title: Separating Ultrafiltration Membrane Adsorption from Plasma Protein Binding
claim: Nonspecific adsorption to an ultrafiltration membrane is an assay effect distinct from plasma protein binding. Characterize membrane recovery over the tested concentration range before interpreting an ultrafiltrate-to-total concentration ratio as the unbound fraction fu. Concentration-dependent membrane loss does not by itself establish concentration-dependent plasma binding.
conditions: Ultrafiltration is used to measure unbound analyte in plasma.
Membrane recovery controls and plasma measurements use a documented, compatible concentration range and preparation procedure.
required_inputs: Paired total and ultrafiltrate concentrations with units and assay limits.
Membrane or device recovery controls over the relevant concentration range; the validated recovery/correction definition.
Species, plasma source, disease state, sample preparation, temperature and incubation conditions where recorded.
limitations: This is a method-level inference from an adsorption-sensitive assay, not a universal numerical correction.
Different matrices, filters and preparation methods require separate qualification.
Do not infer a target-species fu or substitute membrane binding for plasma binding.
downstream_use: Qualify fu data before calculating free concentration or free-exposure PK/PD indices; keep the measured binding relationship and assay uncertainty attached.

title: Comparing Formulation Effects on Systemic and Site-of-Action Exposure
claim: Compare formulations using concentration-time measurements in both the systemic matrix and the relevant target-site matrix. Estimate exposure over the same stated window, retain the actual administered amount and formulation batch, and distinguish changes in systemic exposure from changes in local exposure. This comparison tests a formulation hypothesis; it does not imply that a carrier formulation increases penetration or improves efficacy.
conditions: The formulations contain the same analyte or have an explicit component-resolved comparison basis.
Route, dose, sampling window, assay basis and study population are matched or differences are reported.
For pulmonary studies, lavage-derived epithelial lining fluid (ELF) exposure requires a documented dilution correction.
required_inputs: Formulation composition/batch, actual analyte dose, route and event times.
Systemic and target-site concentration-time observations with units, assay limits, total/free basis and experimental-unit identifiers.
AUC integration windows and methods for each matrix; dose-normalization assumptions if normalization is used.
If a PD relationship is claimed: separately measured response, baseline, endpoint time and control group.
limitations: A formulation effect in one study is not a transferable effect size, direction or efficacy guarantee.
Total site concentration may differ from active unbound exposure; binding differences cannot be assumed absent.
Destructive sampling does not provide individual longitudinal profiles.
Differences between PK and PD study populations limit linkage; exposure comparison alone does not establish clinical benefit or safety.
downstream_use: Assess whether a formulation changes the exposure profile relevant to the stated question, then evaluate PD and uncertainty separately.

title: Distinguishing Measured Total Site Exposure from Modeled Unbound Exposure
claim: Persistent total concentrations at a tissue or fluid site can motivate a binding or sequestration hypothesis, but total measurements alone do not identify the binding site or establish the pharmacologically active fraction. Keep measured total exposure separate from model-predicted unbound exposure.
conditions: Paired systemic and site concentration data are available and their assay basis is known.
A binding explanation is treated as a candidate mechanism requiring independent support.
required_inputs: Site and systemic concentrations, matrix identity, units, sampling window and total/free analyte basis.
If a binding model is evaluated: explicit equations, parameter units, fixed versus estimated status, site volume assumptions and supporting binding evidence.
Direct free or activity-linked measurements when available to assess the proposed active fraction.
limitations: A slow total concentration decline does not uniquely identify a target-mediated mechanism.
Fitted binding, volume or partition parameters are not independent raw measurements.
No numerical site-binding parameter, fraction or site volume is transferable from the cited example.
downstream_use: Prevent total tissue AUC from being automatically used as an unbound PK/PD driver; compare alternative explanations and mark unmeasured active exposure as unresolved.

title: Designing Preclinical Regimens to Match a Qualified Reference Exposure Profile
claim: When an appropriate reference concentration-time profile is available, simulate candidate animal regimens to compare profile shape and exposure with the reference, including the consequences of different terminal half-lives. Evaluate experimental feasibility alongside matching quality; the selected animal regimen remains study-specific.
conditions: A qualified reference profile for the intended analyte, matrix, total/free basis and regimen is explicitly supplied.
The animal PK model is qualified within the route, dose and study-state range used in the design.
This method does not create human reference data for a target lacking human PK.
required_inputs: Reference profile or distribution with provenance, regimen, units, matrix and exposure window.
Animal PK model, parameter uncertainty, actual dosing constraints and candidate administration schedules.
Matched comparison criteria for time course, exposure and feasible sampling confirmation.
limitations: Matching plasma exposure does not guarantee matched tissue exposure or PD response.
Different disease states or nonlinear PK can invalidate simple schedule translation.
No source dose, dosing interval or percentile range is a universal requirement.
downstream_use: Design an explicitly bounded animal exposure-matching experiment; do not infer a human recommended dose from the matching exercise.

title: Assessing Disease-State and Study Differences Before Transferring Animal PK
claim: When PK estimates differ across disease models or studies, retain infection or disease state, severity, route, dose range, body size and study design as potential explanations. A cross-study contrast does not isolate the causal effect of disease or establish a universal direction of clearance change.
conditions: Animal PK data are compared across disease states, strains or study designs.
Parameter definitions and absolute versus body-weight-normalized units are made comparable first.
required_inputs: Study-specific concentration-time data or qualified parameter estimates with uncertainty.
Disease-state and severity descriptors, biological population, dosing route/range and body weight.
Model structure, assay method and sampling design for each study.
limitations: Study-level confounding prevents attributing all differences to one physiological cause.
Do not transfer a clearance multiplier or disease effect from another analyte.
downstream_use: Decide whether a PK source is applicable to the intended PD model and whether matched PK data or an explicit sensitivity scenario is needed.

title: Urea Dilution Correction for Lavage-Derived Epithelial Lining Fluid Concentrations
claim: Under the urea dilution method, apparent ELF volume is V_ELF = V_BALF × U_BALF / U_plasma and apparent analyte concentration is C_ELF = C_BALF × U_plasma / U_BALF. Urea concentrations must use the same units; the corrected analyte concentration retains the units of C_BALF. The result is a dilution-corrected concentration, not a direct measurement of unbound or active exposure.
conditions: Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and the blood reference are paired to the same animal and sampling occasion.
The protocol qualifies urea as a dilution marker under its collection conditions.
The urea denominator is measured and quantifiable; an absent or invalid denominator prevents numerical correction.
required_inputs: Measured analyte concentration in BALF with calibration, assay limits and analyte basis.
Paired BALF and plasma urea concentrations with matching units and assay provenance.
Recovered lavage volume when V_ELF is needed; sample identifiers and collection times.
limitations: Marker equilibration and collection conditions affect interpretation.
The formula does not identify binding, intracellular exposure or pharmacological activity.
Do not substitute zero for BLQ values or import a universal assay limit/outlier threshold from the cited study.
downstream_use: Produce a traceable apparent ELF concentration for site-exposure analysis while retaining the raw BALF and urea measurements.

title: Matrix-Specific Bioanalysis and Tissue Homogenate Concentration Normalization
claim: Quantification across plasma or serum, bile, urine and tissue homogenates requires matrix-specific calibration and a documented analytical method. For tissue homogenates, retain tissue mass, added diluent and processing factors so an assay concentration can be related to the declared tissue concentration basis. Assays measuring chemical analyte and assays measuring antimicrobial activity are not interchangeable observations.
conditions: Several biological matrices or analytical methods contribute to one PK analysis.
Calibration, extraction recovery, selectivity and quantification limits are qualified for each analyte/matrix combination.
required_inputs: Analyte definition, matrix identity and assay method, including whether concentration is chemical or activity-derived.
Matrix-specific calibration range, LLOQ/ULOQ, recovery, precision and accuracy records.
Tissue wet mass, homogenization diluent/volume and subsequent dilution or concentration factors, with units.
Raw reported result and calculation showing the conversion to the stated final basis.
limitations: A validated method for one analyte/matrix does not validate another combination.
A tissue homogenate concentration is not an unbound extracellular or intracellular concentration.
The cited extraction protocol and numerical assay criteria are not universal defaults.
downstream_use: Harmonize concentration units without losing the original matrix, assay or mass/volume basis before tissue/plasma comparison.

title: Qualifying Aggregate Exposure Reporting for Multi-Component Formulations
claim: For a multi-component formulation, compare component-resolved concentration-time profiles and exposures with the aggregate measurement before simplifying reporting. Compare AUC over the same window and concentration basis, and account for component dose fractions and batch composition. Similar aggregate exposure alone does not establish equal component disposition or potency.
conditions: The analytical method can resolve the relevant components or explicitly reports unresolved groups.
Component and aggregate concentrations use a compatible mass or molar definition.
The comparison uses the same subjects/design and single-dose or repeated-dose exposure window.
required_inputs: Component-resolved and aggregate concentration-time data with assay limits and units.
Administered amount and component abundance for each formulation batch.
AUC definition/window and model or integration method; parameter uncertainty where available.
limitations: Component ratios may vary between batches.
Similar half-lives or summed AUC do not prove identical clearance, volume, tissue distribution or pharmacodynamic potency.
The method does not supply a universally acceptable similarity margin or a default one-compartment model.
downstream_use: Decide whether aggregate PK reporting answers the intended question or component-specific exposure must be retained.

title: Charge and Divalent-Ion Context for Binding to Anionic Membrane Targets
claim: For a cationic ligand whose action depends on interaction with an anionic membrane target, target charge and competing divalent ions are mechanistically relevant to binding. The cited mechanism involves negatively charged lipid-A/LPS phosphate groups and Mg2+/Ca2+ bridges. Addition of cationic groups such as L-Ara4N or phosphoethanolamine (PEtN) can reduce net negative charge; applying this mechanism to a new ligand requires evidence that the same interaction governs its binding.
conditions: A cationic ligand and an anionic lipid-A/LPS target are independently supported for the system of interest.
Target chemistry and assay ion conditions are specified rather than inferred from the antimicrobial label alone.
required_inputs: Ligand charge state and target chemical composition under the relevant assay conditions.
Mg2+/Ca2+ and other relevant medium composition; binding or activity measurements under documented conditions.
Evidence for the proposed target modification and its relation to binding affinity, if that mechanism is modeled.
limitations: This is a mechanism-specific consideration, not a universal law of permeability, antibacterial activity or resistance.
Net charge alone does not determine KD or a clinical efficacy threshold.
A change in bacterial growth or susceptibility does not by itself establish the chemical mechanism.
downstream_use: Use supported physicochemical features to motivate a binding hypothesis or controlled comparison; do not assign a fixed potency shift or resistance threshold.

title: Bias in Parameter Estimates from BQL Handling Methods
claim: Omission of BQL data causes substantial bias in parameter estimates (e.g., absorption rate constant KA, mean transit time MTT, clearance CL, drug effect SLOP). Substitution with LOQ/2 yields unpredictable bias patterns, sometimes reducing and sometimes inflating bias compared to omission. The M3 method (likelihood-based) generally provides unbiased parameter estimates.
conditions: Applicable to nonlinear mixed-effects models (e.g., NONMEM).
Validated for BQL occurring in absorption phases, elimination phases, and indirect response PD models.
Bias magnitude increases with higher LOQ levels and higher percentages of BQL data.
required_inputs: Concentration data with defined LOQ.
Structural PK/PD model specification.
Software capable of likelihood-based estimation (e.g., NONMEM VI with F_FLAG for M3).
limitations: M3 method requires longer runtimes and has a lower rate of successful minimization/covariance steps compared to FOCE.
Results are based on simulation studies; real-world applicability depends on correct structural model specification.
Laplacian estimation (required for M2/M3 in this study) had higher non-successful termination rates than FOCE.
downstream_use: Select M3 (or equivalent likelihood-based censoring method) as the primary strategy for handling BQL data in population PK/PD modeling to minimize bias. Avoid simple omission or LOQ/2 substitution unless justified by specific constraints.

title: Two-Panel VPC for Censored Data Diagnostics
claim: Standard VPCs are insufficient for models with BQL data. A two-panel VPC is recommended: the top panel displays prediction intervals for continuous data above LOQ, and the bottom panel displays the simulation-based confidence interval for the fraction of BQL observations over time. This diagnostic clearly identifies model misspecification caused by incorrect BQL handling.
conditions: Model contains non-randomly censored data (BQL).
Sufficient data points above LOQ to calculate percentiles for the top panel.
Software capable of simulating censored data and calculating fraction of BQL.
required_inputs: Final model parameter estimates.
Observed data with BQL flags.
Simulation engine capable of generating 500+ datasets for VPC.
Plotting tool capable of dual-panel visualization.
limitations: Percentiles for observed data can only be calculated for percentiles where BQL data constitute a smaller fraction than the percentile in question.
Misspecification in the VPC could also result from incorrect structural models, not just BQL handling.
downstream_use: Use the two-panel VPC to validate that the chosen BQL handling method (e.g., M3) correctly captures the distribution of both quantifiable and censored data. Use the BQL fraction panel to detect bias in absorption or effect parameters that might be invisible in standard VPCs.

title: Implementation of Likelihood-Based BQL Methods (M2/M3)
claim: The M3 method is implemented in NONMEM VI using the F_FLAG functionality, where F_FLAG=0 indicates a prediction (above LOQ) and F_FLAG=1 indicates a likelihood (below LOQ). The M2 method uses YLO functionality. M3 consistently outperforms M2 in reducing bias across tested models.
conditions: Use of NONMEM VI or equivalent software supporting simultaneous continuous/categorical likelihood modeling.
Log-transformation of the dependent variable is applied to avoid negative predictions.
Residual error models must be specified to handle the log-scale or combined error structures appropriately.
required_inputs: NONMEM VI software.
Data file with F_FLAG or YLO columns.
Model code specifying the likelihood contribution for BQL observations.
limitations: Specific to NONMEM VI implementation details (F_FLAG/YLO).
Requires careful specification of residual error models (e.g., additive component on normal scale for log-transformed data).
Higher computational burden and convergence issues compared to FOCE.
downstream_use: Implement M3 using F_FLAG for population PK/PD modeling. Ensure residual error models are compatible with the log-transformation and censoring mechanism.

title: pcVPC Principle and Normalization
claim: Prediction-corrected VPCs (pcVPC) remove variability arising from differences in independent variables (e.g., dose, covariates) within a bin by normalizing the dependent variable (observed and simulated) based on the typical population prediction for the median independent variable in that bin.
conditions: Applicable when traditional VPCs are hampered by binning across large variability in dose or influential covariates.
Requires a mixed-effects model capable of generating typical population predictions (PRED).
For log-transformed dependent variables, the transformation must be adjusted to allow correct prediction correction.
required_inputs: Fitted mixed-effects model (fixed and random effects).
Observed data with independent variables (time, dose, covariates).
Typical population predictions (PRED) for each observation.
Median typical population prediction for each bin of independent variables.
limitations: Prediction correction transforms the y-axis scale, making it less intuitive than raw concentration units.

Censored data (e.g., BQL) cannot be directly handled by standard pcVPC rank-based methods; they must be omitted from both observed and simulated datasets before calculating statistics, requiring accurate prediction of censoring frequency.
Does not replace the need for other diagnostics; it is one tool in a toolbox.
downstream_use: Model qualification and diagnostic evaluation of population PK/PD models, specifically for assessing random effects structure and structural model misspecification in the presence of covariate or dose variability.

title: pcVPC for Adaptive Dose Adjustments
claim: pcVPCs are readily applicable to data from studies with a priori or a posteriori dose adaptations (e.g., therapeutic drug monitoring), where traditional VPCs can be misleading or uninformative due to the correlation between dose adjustments and the dependent variable.
conditions: Study design involves dose adjustments based on observed concentrations or other dependent variable-related factors.
The dose adjustment algorithm may not be well-documented or fully reproducible in simulations.
Traditional VPCs show decreasing observed variability over time due to dose adjustments, which is not captured by simulations using realized designs.
required_inputs: Dataset with adaptive dosing history.
Model predictions for the realized design.
Identification of bins for prediction correction.
limitations: Simulations based on realized designs do not maintain the correlation between dose alterations and previous observed concentrations, which pcVPC corrects for.
If a dose adjustment algorithm is simulated, it may not accurately mimic real-life adjustments, leading to deceptive results; pcVPC based on realized design is preferred in these cases.
downstream_use: Validating model predictive performance in clinical or preclinical studies with adaptive dosing protocols, ensuring that observed variability is correctly attributed to random effects rather than design artifacts.

title: pvcVPC and Variability Correction
claim: Prediction- and variability-corrected VPCs (pvcVPC) further normalize the dependent variable by the typical variability (standard deviation) of the prediction-corrected values, accounting for non-constant relative variability across bins.
conditions: Expected relative variability differs between observations within a bin due to parameter dependencies or non-proportional residual error models.
Used when pcVPC alone is insufficient to account for heteroscedasticity in the corrected data.
required_inputs: Prediction-corrected dependent variable (pcY).
Standard deviation of simulated pcY values.
Median standard deviation of pcY for the specific bin.
limitations: In the examples investigated, pvcVPCs showed only marginal diagnostic advantage over pcVPCs, possibly due to similar expected variability within bins.
Adds complexity to the diagnostic plot interpretation.
downstream_use: Advanced model diagnostics where residual error structure or parameter-specific variability contributions need to be explicitly normalized to isolate structural model misspecification.

title: Unified Information-Theoretic Identifiability Criterion
claim: Identifiability can be assessed by analyzing the relationship between the determinant of the Fisher Information Matrix (|MF|) and the residual noise variance (σ²). For structurally identifiable fixed-effects models, log|MF| shows a continuous linear relationship with log(σ²) and approaches infinity as σ² approaches zero. For mixed-effects models, the relationship is continuous but asymptotes to a constant value rather than infinity.
conditions: Applicable to both fixed-effects and mixed-effects (population) PK/PD models.
Requires computation of the Jacobian matrix and the Fisher Information Matrix.
Assumes equal variances across observation points (though this can be relaxed).
required_inputs: Structural model equations (fixed and random effects).
Design points (observation times).
Parameter vector (Θ) and variance-covariance matrix of random effects (Ω).
Residual error model (σ²).
limitations: A full-rank local information matrix does not guarantee global identifiability.
The method is model- and design-specific.
Does not explicitly assess deterministic identifiability directly, but allows inference via Cramér-Rao bounds on parameter precision.
downstream_use: Use this method to screen for local/design-dependent identifiability issues in proposed PK/PD model structures before data collection or model fitting. It helps identify parameters that may be unidentifiable under specific designs, requiring fixing or re-parameterization.

title: Independence of Fixed- and Random-Effects Identifiability
claim: The identifiability of random-effects parameters (variances/covariances) is not strictly dependent on the identifiability of their corresponding fixed-effects parameters. In the cited examples, random-effect parameters were identifiable even when their corresponding fixed-effect parameters were unidentifiable. However, the source notes that in its limited examples, identifiable fixed effects always had identifiable corresponding random effects; the reverse case (identifiable fixed/unidentifiable random) was not demonstrated as a general rule.
conditions: Applies to nonlinear mixed-effects models (population PK/PD).
Demonstrated in the cited Bateman/Dost model examples under specified fixed/random-effect and covariance structures. Do not infer a symmetric implication or a universal effect of fixing F.
Source examples show random effects can be identifiable despite unidentifiable fixed effects (e.g., ωV3 identifiable while V3 unidentifiable).
required_inputs: Mixed-effects model specification.
Population Fisher Information Matrix including terms for random effects.
limitations: No standard rule exists to predict random-effect identifiability from fixed-effect identifiability; each must be assessed.
Interactions between covariances in the Ω matrix may affect identifiability, which was not fully explored in the source examples.
The opposite direction was not demonstrated in the limited examples and cannot be inferred from them; assess fixed and random-effect identifiability under the stated candidate model/design.
downstream_use: When building population models, do not assume that fixing a fixed-effect parameter resolves identifiability issues for its associated random-effect parameter. Assess both separately using the FIM criterion, noting that random-effect identifiability can persist even when fixed-effect identifiability fails.

title: Case Deletion for Identifying Unidentifiable Parameters
claim: Specific unidentifiable parameters can be identified via a case deletion methodology: removing the column corresponding to a specific parameter from the Jacobian matrix and observing if the log|MF| vs log(σ²) relationship becomes continuous/linear (indicating the removed parameter was the source of unidentifiability).
conditions: Used when a model is determined to be unidentifiable.
Requires iterative assessment of individual parameters.
required_inputs: Jacobian matrix of the model.
Parameter-specific columns for deletion.
limitations: Computationally intensive for models with many parameters.
Relies on the assumption that removing the unidentifiable parameter restores identifiability for the remaining set.
downstream_use: Use this diagnostic step to pinpoint which specific parameters (e.g., F in a one-compartment oral model) are causing structural unidentifiability, allowing for targeted model simplification or parameter fixing.

title: Route-Specific Identifiability Assessment for Parent-Metabolite Models
claim: Assess parent-metabolite model identifiability separately for each observation and route configuration. Metabolite volumes and absorbed or formed fractions can be confounded, but which combinations are identifiable depends on the equations, measured analytes, design and fixed assumptions. Evaluate fixed and random effects separately rather than assuming that fixing one volume or fraction solves every model.
conditions: Parent and metabolite structural/observation equations are explicitly defined.
IV and extravascular models are assessed using their actual parameter sets and data.
required_inputs: Parent and metabolite input, formation, elimination and observation equations.
Measured analytes, route, sampling design and proposed parameter values for local information analysis.
List of estimated/fixed parameters, random effects and covariance assumptions with their justification.
limitations: The cited example demonstrates a diagnostic procedure, not a universal parameter-fixing prescription.
Local information results do not by themselves establish global identifiability or predictive validity.
downstream_use: Identify parameter combinations that the proposed data can support and justify simplification or additional measurements before fitting.

title: Stochastic Simulation and Estimation (SSE) for Design Evaluation
claim: Stochastic Simulation and Estimation (SSE) is a valuable method for evaluating the efficiency of sparse sampling designs. By simulating multiple datasets (e.g., 1000 replicates) from a known 'true' model and fitting them with candidate models, one can quantify the probability (power) of correctly identifying the true model structure under different sampling constraints.
conditions: Requires a well-characterized 'true' model from prior rich data.
Computational intensity: requires fitting thousands of datasets.
Model selection criteria must be predefined (e.g., ΔOFV > 3.84 for 1 df).
required_inputs: Final population PK model parameters and variability estimates.
Candidate model structures for comparison.
Software capable of automated simulation and fitting (e.g., NONMEM with PsN SSE script).
limitations: Results are dependent on the accuracy of the 'true' model used for simulation.
Computationally expensive.
Does not account for all real-world data collection errors or protocol deviations.
downstream_use: Prospective evaluation of sampling strategies before conducting a new study to minimize resource use while maintaining model identifiability.

title: Bayesian NCA for Serial Sacrifice Designs
claim: A Bayesian approach using MCMC (BUGS) can estimate the posterior distribution of AUC0-∞, tissue-to-plasma AUC ratios, and Drug Targeting Index (DTI) in serial sacrifice designs, providing valid uncertainty estimates (credible intervals) where frequentist methods (Bailer, Yuan) fail to account for within-animal plasma-tissue correlation or underestimate variance.
conditions: Study design must be serial sacrifice (destructive sampling) with sparse data (one sample per animal).
Concentrations are assumed log-normally distributed.
Terminal elimination follows first-order kinetics.
Non-informative (vague) priors are used unless prior knowledge is available.
Within-animal correlation between plasma and tissue concentrations is modeled via a bivariate normal likelihood.
required_inputs: Concentration data (plasma and tissue) at discrete time points.
Time points for sampling.
Assumption of log-normality for concentration data.
Definition of terminal phase (e.g., last 3 time points) for λz estimation.
limitations: Requires Bayesian statistical expertise and MCMC software (e.g., OpenBUGS).
Prior specification is subjective, though vague priors minimize this.
Assumes linear distributional kinetics (no saturation of efflux transporters in the model structure, though inference on ratios remains valid).
Does not replace compartmental modeling for mechanistic insight but improves NCA parameter uncertainty.
downstream_use: Statistical comparison of tissue penetration (partition coefficients) between genotypes or formulations in preclinical PK studies; quantifying uncertainty in exposure metrics derived from destructive sampling.

title: Modeling Within-Animal Plasma-Tissue Correlation
claim: In serial sacrifice designs, plasma and tissue concentrations measured from the same animal at the same time point are correlated. The Bayesian model explicitly accounts for this by using a bivariate normal distribution for log-transformed concentrations, improving the precision of AUC ratio estimates compared to methods that treat them as independent.
conditions: Paired plasma and tissue samples are collected from the same individual animal at each time point.
In the source model, the precision matrix (inverse covariance) has a Wishart prior; the covariance matrix has the corresponding Inverse-Wishart prior.
required_inputs: Paired concentration data (C_plasma, C_tissue) for each animal at each time point.
Log-transformed concentration values.
limitations: The cited model uses a time-specific covariance matrix Sigma_j for each sampling time point j.
Requires sufficient data points to estimate the covariance matrix reliably.
downstream_use: Accurate estimation of tissue-to-plasma partition coefficients (Kp) and their confidence intervals in preclinical drug distribution studies.

title: Estimation of Terminal Elimination Rate (λz) in Sparse Data
claim: The terminal elimination rate constant (λz) is estimated by linear regression on log-transformed concentrations at the last three sampling time points. In the Bayesian framework, λz is treated as a random variable with a uniform prior, allowing its uncertainty to propagate into the AUC0-∞ calculation.
conditions: Terminal phase data must be available (at least 3 points).
First-order elimination kinetics are assumed for the terminal phase.
Concentrations at terminal points are log-normally distributed.
required_inputs: Concentration values at the last three time points.
Time points corresponding to the terminal phase.
limitations: The method uses a fixed number of points (last 3) rather than an adaptive regression (like Phoenix WinNonlin's best-fit search), which may affect accuracy if the terminal phase is not clearly defined by these points.
Assumes log-normality for the terminal phase data.
downstream_use: Calculation of AUC0-∞ (AUC0-t + Ct/λz) and subsequent exposure metrics in sparse sampling studies.

title: Comparison with Frequentist Methods (Bailer/Yuan)
claim: The Bayesian NCA approach provides wider, more conservative credible intervals for AUC and partition coefficients compared to Yuan's method (which underestimates variance due to double usage of the last time point) and jackknife resampling (which can be unreliable with small sample sizes). The Bayesian posterior median is a robust estimator for skewed distributions.
conditions: Small sample sizes per time point (e.g., n=4 animals per time point).
Sparse sampling design where individual trajectories are not observable.
required_inputs: Simulation or experimental data from serial sacrifice designs.
Comparison metrics: Bias, Coverage probability of 95% intervals.
limitations: Bayesian methods require MCMC convergence diagnostics (trace plots, Gelman-Rubin).
Interpretation of credible intervals differs from confidence intervals (probability statement about the parameter vs. the procedure).
downstream_use: Justification for using Bayesian NCA over standard software (e.g., WinNonlin) for statistical inference on tissue distribution parameters in preclinical studies.

title: Semimechanistic PK/PD Model Structure for Time-Kill Curves
claim: The PK/PD model divides the bacterial population into two subpopulations: a growing drug-susceptible population (S) and a resting drug-insusceptible population (R). The transfer from S to R (k_SR) is proportional to the total bacterial concentration (S+R), modeling phenotypic switching to a persister state at high densities. The drug effect is modeled as an Emax function increasing the killing rate of the S population.
conditions: In vitro time-kill experiments
Constant antibiotic concentrations
Bacterial growth to stationary phase
required_inputs: Time-course bacterial counts (CFU/ml)
Antibiotic concentrations over time
MIC values
limitations: In vitro model; does not account for host immune response or in vivo PK variability
Assumes first-order degradation for unstable drugs
Effect delay modeled via link compartment
downstream_use: Prediction of bacterial kill curves under various concentration-time profiles; comparison of antibiotic efficacy.

title: Separating Incubation Stability from Pharmacodynamic Effect Delay
claim: In an in vitro time-kill experiment, measure concentration stability before assuming constant exposure. If degradation is detected, obtain sufficient time-course measurements to characterize it; a first-order degradation model is a candidate only when supported. Evaluate a separate effect-delay component when concentration and killing trajectories support it, rather than forcing delay or degradation into every experiment.
conditions: Incubation concentration may change over the observation window.
The concentration assay and bacterial-count timing are documented.
required_inputs: Measured concentrations at the beginning and end of incubation and additional times when instability is suspected.
Time-matched bacterial counts, control growth and assay limits.
Candidate degradation and delay equations with units and parameter provenance.
limitations: First-order degradation is a model assumption, not a universal stability law.
Sparse observations can prevent estimation of a delay constant.
Improved fit does not independently identify the biological source of delay.
downstream_use: Separate changing exposure from delayed response before interpreting potency or kill-rate estimates.

title: Residual Error and Mixture Model for Inoculum Variability
claim: To handle replicate variability and inoculum heterogeneity, the residual error was divided into a consistent difference between replicates and a replicate-specific difference. A mixture model was used to allocate experiments to two classes: those starting in logarithmic growth phase (all susceptible) and those approaching stationary phase (mixed susceptible/resting).
conditions: Multiple replicates per experiment
Variability in starting inoculum growth phase
required_inputs: Replicate data structure
Starting inoculum status (log vs stationary)
limitations: Complexity of error model
Assumption that inoculum variability is the primary source of between-experiment variation
downstream_use: Improved model fit and parameter precision by accounting for experimental noise and biological variability in starting conditions.

title: Experiment-Level Case Deletion for Time-Kill Parameter Robustness
claim: Assess internal robustness by refitting after deleting an experiment or an experimental day and comparing parameter estimates with the full-data fit. If a parameter is sensitive to one experiment, disclose that dependence. A fixed-parameter sensitivity refit is a separate analysis and does not change the final model unless an explicit model-selection decision is made.
conditions: Experiment/day membership is known and deletion preserves the intended experimental-unit grouping.
The model can be re-estimated using comparable fitting settings.
required_inputs: Full and subset datasets with experiment identifiers.
Full-data and deletion-refit parameter estimates, convergence records and objective-function outputs.
For any fixed-parameter sensitivity analysis: the tested value, units, rationale and explicit final-model decision.
limitations: Internal case deletion does not establish external predictive validity.
Instability can reflect limited design information, model misspecification or influential observations.
No universal objective-function threshold or fixed delay constant is supplied by this method card.
downstream_use: Report parameter-specific fragility and preserve the distinction between the selected model and sensitivity refits.

title: Interlaboratory Variability in Hepatocyte CLint
claim: In vitro CLint values for the same compound can vary significantly across laboratories (CVs up to 99.8%), and this variability is not dependent on the number of published values (n). This variability propagates into IVIVE predictions, often resulting in systematic underprediction for high-clearance compounds.
conditions: Applies to human hepatocyte-based IVIVE.
Variability is driven by experimental procedure differences (e.g., shaking intensity) rather than just donor variability.
High permeability compounds (low rotatable bonds) are more susceptible to this variability due to unstirred water layer (UWL) effects.
required_inputs: Multiple published CLint values for the same compound from different sources.
Physicochemical properties (logD, rotatable bonds, protein binding).
limitations: Retrospective analysis of existing literature; does not provide a universal correction factor.
Does not account for all potential sources of experimental error.
Findings are specific to the dataset of 50 compounds analyzed.
downstream_use: Use this to justify caution when selecting in vitro data for IVIVE. If multiple CLint values exist, assess their consistency. If variability is high, consider the impact on predicted hepatic clearance (CLH) and acknowledge uncertainty in human simulations.

title: Physicochemical Context for IVIVE Reliability
claim: Lipophilicity (logD), intrinsic clearance and plasma binding can help contextualize IVIVE uncertainty. In the cited retrospective multi-compound analysis, lower lipophilicity, lower intrinsic clearance and lower binding were associated with more accurate predictions within the evaluated subset. These associations do not determine the accuracy of a new compound or justify an automatic empirical correction.
conditions: Hepatocyte-based clearance extrapolation is being assessed.
The cited property/accuracy analysis involved 31 compounds with uniform predictions and only six accurate cases.
Property definitions, assay conditions and the numerical clearance basis are retained when comparing sources.
required_inputs: logD with its measurement/condition provenance; fraction unbound and plasma/blood basis.
In vitro intrinsic clearance, scaling method and units; observed in vivo reference only when available for retrospective qualification.
Assay and source provenance, including selection of the comparison dataset.
limitations: The reported associations are observational and based on a limited selected sample.
Dataset thresholds and a two-fold accuracy definition are not universal acceptance criteria.
Physicochemical properties alone do not identify the cause or magnitude of extrapolation error.
downstream_use: Use property and assay context to prioritize uncertainty analysis or additional qualification, not to assign a target clearance or mandatory correction.

title: Incubation Mixing and Unstirred-Water-Layer Effects in Hepatocyte Clearance Assays
claim: Mixing conditions can influence apparent permeability and measured intrinsic clearance in hepatocyte incubations. The cited analysis proposes unstirred-water-layer (UWL) effects as one explanation for interlaboratory differences, particularly for permeable compounds; rotatable-bond count was used as an indirect property correlate, not a measurement of permeability.
conditions: Hepatocyte incubation results from different protocols or laboratories are compared.
Mixing, assay duration and compound-property information are available or explicitly missing.
required_inputs: Incubation protocol, shaking/static conditions and cell preparation.
CLint values with units, replicate uncertainty and source provenance.
Measured permeability when available; rotatable bonds and other physicochemical descriptors labeled as indirect descriptors.
limitations: The compilation did not directly establish UWL causality for every compound.
No universal shaking correction, fold increase or permeability value follows from rotatable-bond count.
downstream_use: Retain mixing conditions in IVIVE data qualification and represent unexplained protocol differences as uncertainty rather than silently pooling results.

title: Qualifying Allometric Clearance Scaling for Macromolecules
claim: Simple allometry is a candidate for macromolecule clearance when the relevant elimination mechanism is comparable across species. The cited multi-compound evaluation found useful average performance for proteins and peptides, but species-dependent target binding and nonlinear PK produced exceptions. A fixed exponent is a justified scenario choice, not a universal property of all macromolecules.
conditions: The compound is a macromolecule and the dominant elimination mechanism is characterized.
Species binding/activity, dose range and PK linearity are assessed before transfer.
required_inputs: Animal clearance and body weight with parameter basis and uncertainty.
Target body weight, proposed scaling equation and exponent with provenance.
Evidence for comparable elimination mechanisms and target binding across species.
limitations: Molecular size alone does not qualify a scaling method.
A good average result in a reference dataset does not establish target-specific accuracy.
Receptor-mediated elimination or nonlinear PK may require a different bridge or explicit sensitivity scenarios.
downstream_use: Compare qualified clearance-scaling scenarios and preserve uncertainty; do not import a universal exponent or reference-compound parameter.

title: Hepatic vs. Renal Elimination in Small-Molecule Scaling
claim: Elimination pathway helps qualify small-molecule clearance scaling. In the cited multi-compound evaluation, simple allometry performed better on average for predominantly renal elimination than for hepatic elimination, particularly low-extraction hepatic compounds. Maximum life-span potential (MLP) or brain-weight (BRW) corrections were empirical alternatives, not guaranteed improvements for a new compound.
conditions: A small molecule is being evaluated for cross-species clearance scaling.
The renal/hepatic contribution and relevant binding or extraction context are supported.
Candidate correction methods are explicitly defined and compared rather than triggered as universal physiological rules.
required_inputs: Animal clearance with species, route, blood/plasma and total/unbound basis, units, body weight and uncertainty.
Target-species body weight for the intended projection.
Supported renal/hepatic contribution and binding/extraction context.
Maximum life-span potential (MLP) values only if evaluating an MLP-corrected candidate.
Brain weight (BRW) values only if evaluating a BRW-corrected candidate.
Simple-allometry exponent and its uncertainty when estimated from the animal data; this is a downstream estimate, not a raw measurement.
limitations: Average method performance in the reference dataset is not target-specific accuracy.
Low extraction and species-specific metabolism can leave substantial uncertainty.
No fixed exponent boundary alone establishes that MLP or BRW correction is appropriate.
downstream_use: Use elimination-pathway evidence to compare scaling candidates and retain method uncertainty.

title: Qualifying Liver-Blood-Flow-Based Clearance Scaling
claim: Liver-blood-flow-based scaling is a candidate extrapolation method when a reference species has compatible clearance and physiological-flow data. The cited multi-compound study found the method useful with primate data, but performance depended on compound class and reference species. This empirical result is not proof that flow limits the target compound clearance.
conditions: Reference-species clearance and body weight are available with unambiguous units.
Reference and target liver blood flow are qualified for the population and expressed on the same absolute or per-body-weight basis.
required_inputs: Reference-species clearance, body weight and parameter basis.
Reference and target liver blood flow with units and provenance.
Target body weight if converting per-body-weight flow to absolute flow; explicit scaling equation.
limitations: The reference study does not establish a universally best species or flow constant.
Nonhepatic clearance, binding and nonlinear processes may invalidate the bridge.
downstream_use: Use as an explicitly qualified comparison scenario, keeping dimensional consistency and method uncertainty.

title: Exponent Rule-Corrected Allometry (ROE) Methodology
claim: Exponent rule-corrected allometry (ROE) is an empirical candidate that selects a correction based on the fitted simple-allometry exponent b: in the cited rule, no correction for b < 0.71, MLP correction for 0.71 ≤ b < 1, and BRW correction for b ≥ 1. These cutoffs define that historical method; they are not universal physiological boundaries or guarantees of predictive improvement.
conditions: Multiple species data available for simple allometry fit.
Exponent b is calculated from the log CL vs log BW regression.
Species-specific MLP and BRW values are available.
required_inputs: Simple allometry exponent (b).
Species-specific MLP values (e.g., Mouse 2.7, Human 93.4).
Species-specific BRW values (e.g., Mouse 1.65%, Human 2%).
limitations: Empirical exponent cutoffs are method-specific.
The source did not show universal benefit for macromolecules or renally eliminated small molecules.
Low-clearance hepatic compounds can remain poorly predicted; compare alternatives and report uncertainty.
downstream_use: Evaluate ROE as one documented empirical scaling candidate when its assumptions and species data are applicable, without treating its cutoffs as mandatory project policy.

title: Distinction Between Uncertainty and Variability in Translation
claim: In translational PK/PD modeling, 'uncertainty' refers to limited knowledge of the system (e.g., scaling error) and decreases as information accumulates, whereas 'variability' is an inherent property of the system (e.g., inter-individual differences) that does not decrease with larger sample sizes. Conflating these leads to misinterpretation of prediction intervals.
conditions: Applicable when defining input distributions for Monte Carlo simulations.
Requires explicit labeling of whether a distribution represents scaling uncertainty or population variability.
required_inputs: Point estimates for PK/PD parameters.
Literature or empirical data on the accuracy of scaling methods (to define uncertainty ranges).
Knowledge of population variability if distinct from scaling uncertainty.
limitations: The source notes that literature on correlations between PK/PD parameter uncertainties is scarce.
PD uncertainty is highly project-specific and harder to generalize than PK uncertainty.
downstream_use: Guides the construction of input distributions for prospective human simulations, ensuring that confidence intervals reflect knowledge gaps rather than assumed biological spread.

title: Monte Carlo Integration of Multi-Source Uncertainty
claim: Monte Carlo simulation is an effective method to integrate multiple sources of uncertainty (e.g., clearance prediction error, volume of distribution scaling error, PD potency uncertainty) into a single empirical distribution of the predicted human dose. This approach handles both closed-form PK/PD models and complex nonlinear models where analytical solutions are unavailable.
conditions: Requires defining probability distributions (e.g., log-normal) for each uncertain parameter.
Suitable for ranking compounds or assessing feasibility when point estimates are insufficient.
Computational feasibility is high for closed-form equations; requires optimization loops for complex ODE models.
required_inputs: PK parameters (CL, Vss, F) with associated uncertainty ranges.
PD parameters (MEC, C_ss, receptor occupancy targets) with associated uncertainty ranges.
PK/PD model structure (e.g., one-compartment, receptor occupancy).
limitations: Assumes independence between parameters unless correlations are explicitly modeled (which is often not done due to lack of data).
Results are prospective scenarios, not validated predictions for a specific target drug.
downstream_use: Generates cumulative probability plots of dose or exposure (Cmax/AUC) to support decision-making in lead optimization and early clinical trial design.

title: Handling Model Structure Uncertainty in Dose Prediction
claim: Uncertainty in the PK/PD model structure itself (e.g., whether the effect is driven by average steady-state concentration C_ss or minimum effective concentration MEC) significantly impacts dose predictions. This structural uncertainty can be quantified by running parallel simulations under different model assumptions and comparing the resulting dose distributions.
conditions: Applicable when the mechanism of action or exposure-response relationship is not fully characterized.
Requires defining distinct scenarios for competing model structures.
required_inputs: Competing PK/PD model equations (e.g., Eq. 2 for C_ss-driven vs. Eq. 3 for MEC-driven).
Parameter estimates for each model scenario.
limitations: Does not resolve which model is correct; it only quantifies the impact of the ambiguity on dose feasibility.
Requires careful communication to avoid confusing decision-makers with multiple conflicting scenarios.
downstream_use: Helps identify compounds that are robust to model ambiguity or highlights those where mechanistic understanding is a critical bottleneck for development.

title: Communication of Uncertainty to Non-Modelers
claim: Effective communication of uncertainty requires translating complex probabilistic outputs into accessible formats, such as cumulative probability plots combined with verbal quantifiers (e.g., 'likely', 'unlikely'). This approach helps non-modeling stakeholders (medicinal chemists, bioscientists) understand risk and make informed decisions without being overwhelmed by technical jargon.
conditions: Target audience includes non-experts in PK/PD modeling.
Focus on 'need-to-know' science rather than exhaustive technical detail.
required_inputs: Output distributions from Monte Carlo simulations.
Clear definitions of verbal quantifiers mapped to probability thresholds.
limitations: Risk of misinterpretation if the distinction between uncertainty and variability is not maintained in the visual language.
Sensitivity plots (one-at-a-time) are limited compared to integrated probabilistic analyses.
downstream_use: Facilitates cross-functional decision-making in drug discovery projects by making uncertainty tangible and actionable.

title: IVIVE Systematic Underprediction of High Extraction Ratio Compounds
claim: IVIVE predictions using the well-stirred model systematically underpredict hepatic clearance (CLH) for high extraction ratio (ER) compounds. While low ER compounds are frequently classified correctly as low ER (>90% accuracy), their numerical CLH predictions are often inaccurate (only ~25-40% within 2-fold). The majority of high ER compounds are misclassified as low or intermediate ER due to underprediction.
conditions: Applies to compounds where hepatic metabolism is the primary elimination route.
Based on analysis of human and rat hepatocyte/microsome data.
Assumes standard physiologically based scaling factors without empirical correction.
required_inputs: In vitro intrinsic clearance (CLint) from microsomes or hepatocytes.
Fraction unbound in blood (fu,B) and incubation (fu,inc).
Liver blood flow (QH) values (e.g., 20.7 ml/min/kg for human, 100 ml/min/kg for rat).
Observed in vivo CLH for validation.
limitations: The study uses known compounds; bias patterns do not determine the target drug's specific clearance.
Does not account for extra-hepatic metabolism or specific transporter effects not captured in the model.
High ER compounds have fewer data points in the dataset, potentially affecting statistical robustness for that range.
downstream_use: Use this to qualify the reliability of IVIVE-derived CLH predictions. If the target drug is suspected to be high ER, expect underprediction and consider empirical scaling factors or alternative models (parallel tube/dispersion) with caution, noting that the source found no significant improvement with parallel tube models for human hepatocytes.

title: Sources of IVIVE Error and Measurement Challenges
claim: Systematic underprediction in IVIVE is multifactorial, stemming from limitations in in vitro systems (e.g., enzyme activity loss, cofactor depletion), measurement errors (e.g., fraction unbound), and biological complexities (e.g., unstirred water layer, protein-facilitated uptake). Low clearance compounds are difficult to measure accurately due to low turnover rates.
conditions: Applies to all IVIVE predictions.
Particularly relevant for low CLint compounds where experimental noise is high relative to signal.
required_inputs: Knowledge of in vitro system limitations (microsomes vs. hepatocytes).
Awareness of potential binding artifacts (e.g., long-chain fatty acids in microsomes).
limitations: The exact mechanism for CLH-dependent underprediction remains undetermined.
Donor variability and cryopreservation effects are noted but not fully resolved in the literature cited.
downstream_use: Contextualize uncertainty in PK/PD modeling. When interpreting IVIVE-derived parameters, acknowledge that underprediction is a known bias, especially for high ER compounds, and that low CLint measurements have high uncertainty.

title: Mechanism of Bias in Free Concentration Derivation
claim: For low extraction ratio drugs, total plasma concentrations are more variable than free plasma concentrations because they reflect both clearance variability and binding variability (Bmax, Kd). Deriving free concentrations by scaling total concentrations with a scalar fu or an independent fu distribution transfers this excess binding variability to the free distribution, causing underestimation of low-quantile free exposures (e.g., Q10%) and biased PTA estimates. As a method inference, correct pairing/joint modeling avoids the specific added back-scaling error from ignoring total/fu dependence; assay error, model misspecification and target uncertainty can still affect overall PTA accuracy.
conditions: Applies under the source low-extraction/back-scaling assumptions, including its free-clearance dependence on binding; applicability must be assessed for the target system.
Bias occurs when free concentrations are derived by scaling total measurements with a scalar fu or a fu distribution independent of the total concentration draw.
Does not apply if free concentrations are directly measured or if paired/joint modeling correctly accounts for the dependence between total and free concentrations.
required_inputs: Total plasma concentration data.
fu value (scalar or distribution) used for scaling.
PK/PD index definition (e.g., fAUC/MIC).
Knowledge of whether fu is treated as independent or paired with total concentration.
limitations: Bias magnitude depends on the specific fu value and its assumed variability.
The general principle applies to low extraction ratio drugs; high extraction drugs may have different clearance dependencies.
Abstract-only or partial text may not cover specific drug examples beyond the general principle.
downstream_use: Guides the selection of PK/PD modeling strategies: prefer direct free concentration measurement or joint modeling of total/free concentrations. Warns against using scalar fu or independent fu distributions to derive free concentrations from total data, as this exacerbates bias in PTA calculations.

title: Impact of fu Variability on PTA and Dose Recommendations
claim: In Monte Carlo simulations where total concentrations are back-scaled to free concentrations using a scalar fu or an independent distribution of fu, the resulting free concentration distribution often exhibits inflated variance compared to the true free distribution. This leads to a negative bias in the estimated PK/PD cutoff (critical MIC) and an overestimation of the dose required to achieve the target PTA (e.g., 90%). The bias is exacerbated when variability in fu is incorrectly added as an independent source of noise during back-calculation, rather than being properly accounted for in the joint total/free relationship.
conditions: Monte Carlo simulations where total concentrations are scaled by fu to estimate free exposure.
Comparison between scalar fu and distributed fu approaches for back-calculation.
A reference free-exposure distribution is needed to quantify bias in this source simulation. It is not a mandatory known truth for prospective PTA based on separately qualified free exposure.
required_inputs: Distribution of fu (e.g., log-normal or uniform) used for scaling.

For source-simulation replication/bias quantification: a declared reference free-exposure distribution. For prospective PTA instead: qualified direct free exposure or a justified joint total/free model and its uncertainty.
Target PTA percentile (e.g., 90%).
Total concentration distribution parameters.
limitations: Experimental data for individual fu distributions are rare; often based on pooled samples.
The study uses simulated data; real-world impact depends on actual binding variability of the specific drug.
The bias direction and magnitude are specific to the simulation assumptions regarding the independence or correlation of fu and total concentration errors.
downstream_use: Prefer qualified direct free-concentration data when available. If only total concentrations and binding information exist, state the scalar-fu approximation and its limitations, or model the joint free/total/binding relation with justified covariance; do not add arbitrary independent fu variability during back-calculation as this increases bias in PTA estimates.

title: Operational Equivalence of fAUC/MIC and fCss/MIC for Continuous Infusion
claim: For constant continuous IV infusion at steady state, fAUC_tau/MIC = tau × fCss/MIC for an explicitly stated time window tau. The source clearance equations share the same algebraic structure after replacing dose with infusion rate, but fAUC/MIC and fCss/MIC are not numerically or dimensionally identical. The binding-variability bias argument can be studied in both settings.
conditions: Continuous intravenous infusion regimen.
Steady-state conditions.
Low extraction ratio drugs where free clearance is independent of fu.
required_inputs: Infusion rate.
Free clearance (CLfree).
MIC.
limitations: Specific to continuous infusion; intermittent dosing requires time-dependent integration.
Assumes linear binding kinetics for the simplification to hold.
downstream_use: Simplifies PK/PD analysis for beta-lactams and other continuous-infusion antimicrobials by recognizing the shared algebraic structure of the clearance equations, while maintaining the distinction between AUC/MIC and Css/MIC quantities.

title: Qualified Alternatives to Independent Free-Fraction Back-Scaling in PTA
claim: Where back-scaling total exposure with an independent fu approximation is inadequate, consider qualified direct free-concentration modeling or a justified joint/deconvolution approach using individual binding information. A total-exposure PTA analysis is a different option only when its target is independently established on a compatible total-concentration basis; merely relabeling a free target is not sufficient.
conditions: PTA uses an explicit free or total exposure index and a compatible target definition.
The dependence of total exposure and binding, extraction assumptions and analytical uncertainty are considered.
required_inputs: Total and/or directly measured free exposure with assay provenance.
Individual binding information or a justified joint distribution, including relevant covariance assumptions.
PK/PD target with free/total basis, exposure window and derivation context.
limitations: Low free concentrations can introduce analytical variability.
Deconvolution depends on distributional and mechanistic assumptions and may require numerical methods.
When the needed information is unavailable, report the approximation and sensitivity rather than claiming bias-free PTA.
downstream_use: Choose an exposure representation consistent with the qualified target and retain the uncertainty of the total/free relationship.

title: PBPK Report Structure and Content Requirements
claim: The cited FDA guidance recommends a specific six-section structure for PBPK study reports: Executive Summary, Introduction, Materials and Methods, Results, Discussion, and Appendices. The Executive Summary should clearly convey how the analysis addresses a specific scientific question in a clinical setting.
conditions: Applicable to IND, NDA, BLA, or ANDA submissions.
Guidance is nonbinding; alternative approaches are permitted if they satisfy statutory requirements.
Content must allow reviewers to duplicate and evaluate modeling results.
required_inputs: Objectives and rationale for the PBPK analysis.
High-level synopsis of drug physicochemical, PK, and PD properties.
Exposure-response relationships for efficacy and safety.
Cross-references to prior PBPK submissions for the same drug substance/product.
limitations: Does not address methodological best practices for conducting PBPK modeling.
Does not specify the appropriateness of PBPK for a specific drug; acceptance is case-by-case.
Does not establish legally enforceable responsibilities.
downstream_use: Structuring the final report for human simulation scenarios to ensure regulatory readiness and traceability of assumptions.

title: Documentation of Modeling Parameters and Assumptions
claim: All system-specific and drug-specific parameters must be clearly specified with their sources and justifications. Key model assumptions impacting application, including biological rationales and mathematical representations, must be explicitly stated.
conditions: Parameter values must be justified with appropriate references.
If multiple sources exist for a parameter, the selection process must be described.
Use of clinical PK data to optimize parameters must be described and justified.
Library models (e.g., virtual populations) must be justified, and modifications must be identified.
required_inputs: Table of drug-dependent parameters (names, values, units, sources).
Prediction algorithms and assumptions.
Procedures for assessing parameter uncertainty (e.g., sensitivity analysis).
Justification for any modifications to library models.
limitations: Does not prescribe specific parameter estimation methods.
Does not define acceptable ranges for parameter uncertainty.
downstream_use: Ensuring transparency in human simulation inputs and enabling reproducibility of the model structure.

title: Simulation Design and Virtual Population Specifications
claim: Simulation design descriptions must include specific operational details: route, dose, formulation, administration time, fasting/fed conditions, dosing regimen, trial duration, virtual population demographics, and number of simulated trials/subjects.
conditions: Applies to model development, verification, and application phases.
Settings for differential equation integrators must be included when applicable.
Demographics and their distributions must be specified for virtual populations.
required_inputs: Route, dose, formulation, and administration conditions.
Dosing regimen details.
Duration of simulated trials.
Virtual population demographics and distribution.
Number of simulation studies and virtual subjects per trial.
Integrator settings.
limitations: Does not specify how to select the virtual population demographics.
Does not define the minimum number of virtual subjects required for statistical validity.
downstream_use: Defining the precise experimental conditions for prospective human concentration/exposure scenarios.

title: Model Verification, Sensitivity Analysis, and Robustness
claim: Sponsors must demonstrate that the PBPK model is appropriate for its intended use and robust to perturbations in uncertain parameters. This requires presenting results from verification methods, confirming model results against observed data, and conducting sensitivity analyses.
conditions: Model verification must cover both drug and system models.
Sensitivity analysis results must be discussed in the context of simulation conditions and clinical relevance.
If parameters are refined during verification, modifications must be described and justified.
If assumptions cannot be confirmed, further verification for untested clinical scenarios is required.
required_inputs: Procedures used for model verification.
Results of sensitivity analyses for uncertain parameters.
Comparison of model-generated simulations to observed data.
Justification for any parameter refinements made during verification.
limitations: Does not define specific statistical metrics for 'robustness' or 'appropriateness'.
Does not specify the threshold for acceptable deviation between simulated and observed data.
downstream_use: Qualifying the reliability of human simulation outputs and identifying sources of uncertainty in the model.

title: Software Documentation and Electronic Submission Standards
claim: Submissions must include the name and version of the software, schematic views of model structures, mathematical equations, parameterization sources, and user manuals. Electronic files must comply with eCTD specifications.
conditions: FDA does not recommend specific software; sponsors must communicate early if using complex models.
Documentation must describe how software vendor changes during development impacted model performance.
Electronic files must adhere to eCTD file format specifications and technical rejection criteria.
required_inputs: Software name and version.
Schematic view of model structure and mathematical equations.
Parameterization of system information and sources of parameter values.
User's manual/instructions for running code.
Compliance with eCTD specifications.
limitations: Does not validate specific software tools.
Does not provide technical details on eCTD file formats beyond referencing external specifications.
downstream_use: Ensuring the technical reproducibility and auditability of the simulation environment.

title: PBPK Platform Qualification and Regulatory Impact
claim: PBPK platforms must be qualified for their intended use before being used to support regulatory decisions. The extent of qualification required depends on the regulatory impact of the modelling (low, moderate, or high). High-impact analyses (e.g., replacing clinical data, predicting DDIs in specific populations) require rigorous demonstration of the platform's ability to predict observed outcomes using pre-specified qualification datasets. Low-impact analyses (e.g., mechanistic understanding where confirmatory PK data exists) may not require formal platform qualification.
conditions: Applicable when PBPK modelling is intended to support a regulatory decision.
Qualification is purpose-specific and platform-version specific.
For high-impact analyses, the science must be mature enough, supported by valid system data and in vitro-in vivo correlations.
required_inputs: Definition of the intended regulatory purpose.
Classification of regulatory impact (low/moderate/high).
For high impact: Pre-specified qualification datasets with in vivo data for probe drugs.
Documentation of system-dependent parameters and their justification.
limitations: Qualification issued within a specific submission is valid only for that submission unless a CHMP qualification opinion exists.
Abstract-only material supports only what appears in the abstract; this guideline is full-text but excerpts are partial.
Does not define specific numerical acceptance criteria for 'adequacy' of prediction; this is case-by-case.
downstream_use: Guides the selection of validation datasets and the level of documentation required for human simulation scenarios. Determines whether a generic PBPK platform can be used or if specific drug-model validation is mandatory.

title: Drug Model Predictive Performance Evaluation
claim: The predictive performance of the specific drug model must be evaluated by comparing simulated plasma concentration-time data against observed individual data from representative in vivo studies. This evaluation should cover different dose levels, single/repeated administration, and relevant populations. Visual predictive plots comparing central trends and variability (5th/95th percentiles) are required. The evaluation must focus on the parts of the model central to the intended purpose (e.g., Cmax/t1/2 for intestinal vs. hepatic metabolism).
conditions: Required before using the model to simulate novel situations (e.g., DDIs, alternate populations).
Simulations should be performed in the population of interest for a large number of individuals (>100 recommended).
Acceptance criteria for prediction closeness depend on regulatory impact and concentration-effect relationships.
required_inputs: Observed individual PK data from representative studies.
Simulated concentration-time profiles.
Statistical metrics (geometric mean, SD, range) and visual plots (linear and semi-log).
Justification for any discrepancies between simulated and observed data.
limitations: Does not prescribe a universal numerical threshold for 'good' prediction; acceptance is context-dependent.
Excerpts do not include the full text of Appendix 2 examples, limiting specific scenario details beyond the general principles.
downstream_use: Provides the standard for validating that a human simulation model is fit for purpose before generating prospective exposure scenarios. Defines the evidence needed to trust simulated PK parameters.

title: Sensitivity Analysis and Parameter Uncertainty
claim: Sensitivity analysis is required to understand how changes in key input parameters (due to uncertainty or variability) influence model output. It should be performed for parameters considered key to the model or uncertain (e.g., those with literature variability, optimized during building, or difficult to measure). A 'worst-case' approach is recommended (e.g., 10-fold for CYP enzymes, 30-fold for transporters). Global or joint sensitivity analyses may be used to assess correlated parameters.
conditions: Must be performed during both model development and application.
Ranges for sensitivity analysis must be pre-specified and justified based on scientific rationale or published data.
Applicable to both system-dependent and drug-dependent parameters.
required_inputs: Identification of key/uncertain parameters.
Justified ranges for parameter variation.
Methodology for global or joint sensitivity analysis if parameters are correlated.
limitations: Does not specify the exact statistical method for sensitivity analysis beyond 'systematic investigation'.
Specific fold-change examples (10-fold/30-fold) are illustrative, not universal mandates for all parameters.
downstream_use: Informs the uncertainty analysis in human simulation scenarios. Helps identify which parameters drive exposure variability and require precise measurement or justification.

title: Reporting of Model Parameters and Assumptions
claim: PBPK reports must explicitly discuss assumptions and their biological/pharmacological rationale. System-dependent parameters (physiology) and drug-specific parameters (physicochemical, ADME) must be presented with sources and justification. Modifications to default system values must be highlighted. Drug-specific parameters should be reported with mean and variability (SD or range). If parameters are estimated, the estimation method and identifiability issues must be described.
conditions: Applies to all PBPK reports intended for regulatory assessment.
Literature references for system parameters must be provided as full articles.
Identifiability issues (e.g., correlated Ki and kinact) must be addressed with additional data or discussion.
required_inputs: Tabular summary of drug-specific parameters (mean, SD/range, source).
Documentation of any modifications to default system-dependent parameters.
Description of estimation methods for fitted parameters.
limitations: Does not define specific physiological values; relies on external literature.
Excerpts do not include the full list of 'Pharmacokinetic parameters used' beyond the definitions provided in chunk 0023.
downstream_use: Ensures transparency in human simulation inputs. Allows reviewers to assess the biological plausibility of the model structure and parameter choices.

title: Standard Broth Microdilution Conditions for Non-Fastidious Organisms
claim: For non-fastidious organisms (e.g., Enterobacterales, Staphylococcus spp., Pseudomonas spp.), MIC determination uses Cation-Adjusted Mueller-Hinton Broth (CAMHB) with a final inoculum of 5x10^5 CFU/mL (range 2x10^5 to 8x10^5 CFU/mL) and incubation at 35±1°C for 18±2 hours in sealed panels under air.
conditions: Applicable to rapidly growing aerobic bacteria listed in Table 1a.
Inoculum must be verified by viable counts.
Standard reading is the lowest concentration completely inhibiting visible growth.
required_inputs: Organism species identification
Antimicrobial agent identity
Standardized inoculum preparation (McFarland 0.5 adjusted to target CFU/mL)
limitations: Does not apply to fastidious organisms without the appropriate protocol; does not apply to Mycobacteria.

Before using the generic protocol, verify the current validated method for the actual agent-organism pair, including medium and endpoint applicability. This card does not contain agent-specific exceptions.
downstream_use: Ensures MIC values used in PK/PD modeling are derived from a standardized, reproducible reference method, reducing methodological variability in exposure-response analysis.

title: Methodology for Fastidious Organisms
claim: For fastidious organisms (e.g., Streptococcus spp., Haemophilus influenzae, Campylobacter spp.), MIC determination uses MH-F broth (CAMHB with 5% lysed horse blood and 20 mg/L beta-NAD). Incubation conditions vary by species (e.g., 35±1°C for 18±2h for Streptococcus; 41±1°C for 24±1h for Campylobacter).
conditions: Applicable to organisms listed in Table 1b.
Inoculum target remains 5x10^5 CFU/mL.
Extended incubation (40-44h) may be required if growth is insufficient after 16-20h for certain species.
required_inputs: Confirmation of organism fastidiousness
Preparation of MH-F broth with correct supplements
Species-specific incubation parameters (temperature, atmosphere, duration)
limitations: Growth phase of initial culture significantly affects final inoculum viability for fastidious organisms.
Requires at least two passages on suitable agar media when retrieved from freezer storage.
downstream_use: Provides the correct experimental context for MIC data generation for fastidious pathogens, ensuring comparability with EUCAST breakpoints/ECOFFs.

title: Broth Microdilution Method and MIC Definition
claim: For an agent-organism pair for which broth microdilution is the qualified reference method, record the MIC as the lowest antimicrobial concentration meeting the applicable growth-inhibition endpoint, expressed in mg/L or µg/mL. The standard endpoint is complete visible-growth inhibition; method and endpoint applicability must be verified before use.
conditions: Use MH-F broth (Mueller-Hinton broth + 5% lysed horse blood + 20 mg/L β-NAD) for fastidious organisms.
Standard MH broth for non-fastidious organisms.
Results must be recorded as MIC values, not just categorical susceptibility.
required_inputs: Antimicrobial concentration series with units.
Microorganism identity and the qualified assay method for the agent-organism pair.
Broth composition, incubation protocol and endpoint definition with method/version provenance.
limitations: Broth microdilution and complete-inhibition reading are not universal for every agent-organism pair.
Specific exceptions must be checked in the applicable assay protocol; this generic card does not prescribe those drug-specific procedures.
Text extraction does not verify visual growth patterns; requires trained manual or calibrated automated reading.
downstream_use: Defines the fundamental data type (MIC in mg/L) and experimental conditions required for PK/PD modeling inputs.

title: Validity Criteria for MIC Assays
claim: MIC results are only valid if: (1) positive growth control shows obvious button or definite turbidity, (2) pure culture is confirmed via subculture, and (3) inoculum is correct at 5 x 10^5 CFU/mL.
conditions: Inoculum verification: 10 µL from growth control diluted in 10 mL saline; 100 µL spread on agar should yield 20-80 colonies.
Purity check: Subculture from growth-control well immediately after inoculation.
required_inputs: Positive growth control well status.
Purity subculture results.
Inoculum density verification data.
limitations: Failure to meet these criteria invalidates the MIC result for that isolate/agent combination.
downstream_use: Quality control filter for data cleaning; invalid assays must be excluded from PK/PD analysis.

title: Standard MIC Endpoint Reading Rules
