claim: MIC is read manually as the lowest concentration completely inhibiting growth. For trailing endpoints (gradual fading over 2-3 wells), read at complete inhibition unless specific exceptions apply. Haze/turbidity without a pellet (e.g., Pseudomonas/Acinetobacter) is considered growth.
conditions: Manual reading is preferred; automated readers must be calibrated to manual reading.
Round-bottom wells: growth appears as button/pellet. Flat-bottom: scattered.
Trailing endpoints: Read at first well with complete inhibition (clear broth).
required_inputs: Visual assessment of well turbidity/pellet.
Concentration series order.
limitations: Subjectivity in complete inhibition versus trailing growth requires trained personnel or calibrated automation.
Apply this endpoint only after confirming it is appropriate for the actual agent-organism pair and assay protocol. Drug-specific exceptions are outside this card.
downstream_use: Standardizes the interpretation of raw assay data into numerical MIC values.

title: Handling Skipped Wells
claim: A 'skipped well' (no growth bordered by growth) indicates potential error (inoculation, contamination, heterogenous resistance). For a single skipped well, retest or read the highest MIC value to avoid false susceptibility. Do not report results if more than one skipped well occurs.
conditions: Single skipped well: Retest or use highest MIC value.
Multiple skipped wells: Result invalid.
required_inputs: Pattern of growth/no-growth across concentration series.
limitations: Reading the highest MIC value in a single-skip scenario may overestimate resistance if the skip was technical error.
downstream_use: Data cleaning rule for handling anomalous MIC assay patterns.

title: Quality Control and Interpretation
claim: MIC values for relevant Quality Control (QC) strains must be within acceptable ranges before reporting clinical isolate results. MIC values are interpreted into susceptibility categories (S, I, R) according to current EUCAST Breakpoint Tables.
conditions: QC strain MICs must be in range.
Use current EUCAST Breakpoint Tables for S/I/R categorization.
required_inputs: QC strain MIC results.
Current EUCAST Breakpoint Tables.
limitations: Breakpoints are dynamic; must use current version.
QC failure invalidates the batch/run.
downstream_use: Final step in converting numerical MIC to clinical susceptibility category, which may be used for binary PK/PD analysis.

title: MIDD Evidence Assessment Framework
claim: MIDD evidence is defined as model outcomes determined by an assessment framework to be appropriate for answering a specific question of interest. The framework requires explicit definition of the Question of Interest, Context of Use, Model Influence, Consequence of Wrong Decision, Model Risk, and Model Impact.
conditions: Applicable to all M&S methods (popPK, PBPK, exposure-response, etc.)
Requires multidisciplinary team assessment
Model risk is derived from model influence and consequence of wrong decision
required_inputs: Explicitly stated Question of Interest
Description of model role/scope and data used
Rating and justification for Model Influence and Consequence of Wrong Decision
limitations: Does not prescribe specific numerical thresholds for model acceptance
Does not replace topic-specific ICH guidelines (e.g., E4, E5, E9)
Abstract-only material supports only what appears in the abstract (not applicable here as full text is provided)
downstream_use: Structuring the initial project plan and defining the criteria for accepting PK/PD models as evidence for decision-making.

title: Model Evaluation Standards: Verification and Validation
claim: Model evaluation must include Verification (ensuring code/equations are error-free) and Validation/Applicability Assessment (assessing performance/robustness). Evaluation must be commensurate with Model Risk. Key activities include assessing data relevance, model structure consistency with knowledge, and external validation.
conditions: Verification of user-generated code is mandatory
Validation must assess adequacy/relevance of data and model assumptions
External validation is encouraged and may be essential depending on risk
required_inputs: Documented verification of code/equations
Justification for data inclusion/exclusion
Description of model assumptions and alternatives considered
Graphical and numerical diagnostics
limitations: High-level recommendations; specific technical standards depend on the M&S method used
Does not define specific goodness-of-fit metrics for specific model types
downstream_use: Guiding the technical execution of PK/PD model building, ensuring code integrity and scientific justification for model structure and parameters.

title: MIDD Reporting: MAP and MAR Requirements
claim: Model Analysis Plans (MAP) should be pre-defined before data access/analysis. Model Analysis Reports (MAR) must document results, evaluation against technical criteria, and deviations from the MAP. All supporting data, code, and definition files must be available for regulatory review.
conditions: MAPs define planned evaluation activities and technical criteria
MARs include executive summary, objectives, data/methods, results, and discussion
Changes to planned analyses must be justified and documented
required_inputs: Pre-defined MAP with objectives and methods
MAR with detailed results and evaluation against technical criteria
User-generated code and data files
limitations: Structure can be adjusted to specific M&S methods
Does not specify file formats for code/data beyond 'available for review'
downstream_use: Structuring the final deliverables and ensuring traceability of the PK/PD analysis from planning to final report.

title: Lambda Z Estimation Methodology (Best Fit)
claim: Phoenix's 'Best Fit' method automatically determines points for Lambda Z calculation by performing linear regressions of ln(concentration) vs time on subsets of data points (starting from the last 3 non-zero points post-Cmax). It selects the regression with the largest adjusted R². If adjusted R² values are within 0.0001, the regression with more points is chosen. Lambda Z is defined as the negative of the estimated slope and must be positive.
conditions: Concentration data must be positive (log-transformable).
Points prior to Cmax or end of infusion are excluded unless specifically requested.
Minimum of 3 data points required for automatic selection.
Slope must be negative for Lambda Z to be valid.
required_inputs: Concentration-time data
Cmax identification
Infusion stop time (if applicable)
limitations: Cannot estimate if fewer than 3 positive concentration values exist after Cmax (non-bolus) or 2 (bolus).
Fails if slope is not negative.
Fails if time difference between first and last points in range is < 1e-10.
downstream_use: Determines whether terminal half-life and extrapolated AUC can be calculated. Failure to estimate Lambda Z limits PK parameters to those independent of terminal slope (e.g., AUClast, Cmax).

title: Manual Time Range Selection for Slope Estimation
claim: Users can manually specify the time range for Lambda Z or Slope estimation. Phoenix performs linear regression of ln(concentration) (or raw values for drug effect) on the user-specified points. The estimated slope must be negative for Lambda Z (which is then negated to be positive). For drug effect models, slopes can be positive or negative and are reported as-is.
conditions: User must specify the time range.
For Lambda Z, the resulting slope must be negative.
For drug effect Slope 1/2, linear or log regression can be chosen, and slope sign is not constrained to negative.
required_inputs: User-defined time range
Concentration or effect data
limitations: If the user-specified range contains fewer than two non-missing observations, estimation fails.
Manual selection bypasses the automatic 'Best Fit' logic but still requires valid data points for regression.
downstream_use: Allows override of automatic selection when automatic methods fail or select inappropriate points due to noise or sparse sampling.

title: Handling of Failed Lambda Z Estimation
claim: When Lambda Z cannot be estimated (due to insufficient points, non-negative slope, or invalid time range), Phoenix omits the curve fit for that subject. However, parameters independent of Lambda Z (Cmax, Tmax, AUClast) are still reported. A warning is issued in the text output indicating Lambda Z was not estimable.
conditions: Automatic range selection requested but insufficient points.
User-specified range has <2 non-missing observations.
Slope is not negative.
Time range width is negligible (<1e-10).
required_inputs: NCA object configuration
Data profile
limitations: Extrapolated AUC (AUCinf) and terminal half-life cannot be calculated.
Interpretation of terminal phase is not possible for that subject.
downstream_use: Guides interpretation of incomplete PK profiles. Researchers must decide whether to exclude these subjects or rely on partial exposure metrics (AUClast).

title: Drug Effect Model Slope Estimation
claim: For NCA drug effect models, Phoenix estimates two slopes: Slope 1 (beginning of data) and Slope 2 (end of data). It uses the same adjusted R² selection logic as Lambda Z (min 3 points) but allows linear or log regression and does not negate the slope (can be positive or negative). If only one range is specified, the other is automatically determined.
conditions: Applicable to drug effect (PD) models, not just concentration PK.
Regression can be linear or log-transformed.
Slope sign is not constrained.
required_inputs: Effect-time data
Optional user-specified ranges for Slope 1 or 2
limitations: Same point-count and data validity constraints as Lambda Z (min 3 points for automatic selection).
downstream_use: Quantifies onset and offset kinetics of pharmacodynamic effects.

title: Absolute vs. Apparent PK Parameters
claim: For extravascular (oral) administration, Clearance and Volume of Distribution are reported as apparent parameters (CL/F, Vz/F) because the fraction of dose absorbed (F) cannot be estimated from plasma data alone. Absolute CL and Vz are only computed for IV Bolus or Infusion models.
conditions: Extravascular dosing model (e.g., Model 200)
IV Bolus or Infusion dosing
required_inputs: Dose
Concentration-time data
Dosing route
limitations: Apparent parameters (CL/F, Vz/F) are not directly comparable to absolute IV parameters without knowing F.
Vss is not computed for extravascular models because MRTINF includes mean input time.
downstream_use: Correct interpretation of PK parameters for translation; avoiding direct comparison of oral CL/F with IV CL.

title: Terminal Slope (Lambda Z) Estimation and Diagnostics
claim: Lambda Z is estimated via linear regression of log concentration (Y) vs. time (X) (or log excretion rate vs. midpoint for urine); lambda_z is the negative fitted slope. Diagnostics include Rsq (goodness of fit), Corr_XY (correlation), and Span (ratio of Lambda Z window to half-life). Parameters like AUCINF and Vz are calculated using either the last observed (obs) or last predicted (pred) concentration/rate.
conditions: Terminal log-linear phase exists
Sufficient points in terminal phase
required_inputs: Time-concentration pairs
Lambda_z_lower/upper bounds
limitations: If Lambda Z cannot be estimated, No_points_lambda_z is set to zero and extrapolated parameters are not computed.
Span and Rsq are critical for assessing the validity of the terminal slope.
downstream_use: Assessment of NCA model fit quality; determination of whether extrapolated parameters (AUCINF) are reliable.

title: Steady-State NCA Metrics
claim: Steady-state analysis requires a defined dosing interval (Tau). Key parameters include Cavg (AUC_TAU/Tau), Ctau (concentration at end of interval), and Accumulation Index. Fluctuation% and Swing are calculated based on Cmax and Cmin/Ctau within the interval.
conditions: Multiple dosing regimen
Defined Tau
required_inputs: Tau (dosing interval)
Concentration-time data within interval
limitations: Cmin and Ctau may differ depending on regulatory definitions; both are output.
AUC_TAU calculation handles small sampling deviations by estimating concentration at Tau.
downstream_use: Exposure-response analysis for multiple-dose regimens; PK/PD index calculation (e.g., AUC/MIC, Cmax/MIC).

title: Interval Data (Urine) NCA Formulas
claim: For interval data (e.g., urine), excretion rate is calculated as (Concentration * Volume) / (Ending Time - Starting Time). Lambda Z is estimated using midpoints of collection intervals vs. log excretion rates. Amount_Recovered is the cumulative amount eliminated.
conditions: Urine or other interval-collected data
required_inputs: Start/End times
Concentration
Volume
limitations: Midpoint is used for time axis in regression.
AURC_INF is theoretically equal to Amount_Recovered but differs due to experimental error.
downstream_use: Renal clearance estimation; mass balance analysis.

title: AUC Estimation via Linear Combinations of Mean Concentrations
claim: In destructive sampling designs, the AUC for a specific dosing regimen can be estimated using linear combinations of mean concentrations measured at discrete time points, rather than integrating individual subject trajectories.
conditions: Experimental unit must be sacrificed to obtain concentration data (destructive/terminal sampling).
Multiple subjects are sampled at each time point to allow calculation of mean concentrations.
The method applies to metabolite or drug concentration over time.
required_inputs: Mean concentration values at specific time points for each dosing regimen.
Time points at which samples were collected.
Sample sizes per time point (implied for variance estimation, though not explicitly detailed in abstract).
limitations: Does not reconstruct individual trajectories.
Abstract does not specify the exact weighting scheme or variance estimation method for the linear combination.
Applicability to non-uniform time spacing or complex designs requires checking the full method details (not available in abstract).
downstream_use: Interpreting group-level PK parameters from terminal sacrifice studies. Validating whether reported AUCs in such studies are derived from this or similar group-mean based methods.

title: Statistical Testing of AUC Equality in Destructive Designs
claim: Contrasts among AUC estimates derived from destructive sampling data can be readily constructed and tested to determine if AUCs are equal among different dosing regimens.
conditions: Comparing multiple dosing regimens.
Data is derived from destructive sampling (group means at time points).
Goal is to test for equality of exposure (AUC) across regimens.
required_inputs: Estimated AUCs for each regimen (derived via the linear combination method).
Variance/covariance structure of the mean concentrations (implied for contrast testing).
limitations: Abstract confirms the ability to test contrasts but does not detail the specific statistical test (e.g., t-test, ANOVA, mixed model) or assumptions (normality, homoscedasticity).
Does not address PK/PD target attainment directly, only statistical equality of exposure.
downstream_use: Designing statistical analysis plans for destructive sampling PK studies. Interpreting p-values or confidence intervals for AUC comparisons in such studies.

title: One-Species Scaling Coefficients for Human CL
claim: Data-driven one-species methods for predicting human clearance (CL) were derived as: CL(human)/kg = 0.152 x CL(rat)/kg, CL(human)/kg = 0.410 x CL(dog)/kg, and CL(human)/kg = 0.407 x CL(monkey)/kg. The monkey method coefficient (0.407) was similar to the monkey LBF method (0.467), while rat (0.152) and dog (0.410) coefficients differed significantly from their respective LBF methods (0.247 and 0.700).
conditions: Applicable for prospective human CL prediction when only one animal species data is available.
Coefficients are specific to the dataset (n=102) and method derivation.
Not a universal constant; applicability depends on compound class and similarity to training set.
required_inputs: Animal CL data (rat, dog, or monkey) normalized to body weight (CL/kg).
Human body weight (implied by /kg normalization in formula).
limitations: Abstract-only source; full methodology for coefficient derivation not visible.
Coefficients are fixed values from this specific study; not validated for all drug classes.
Does not account for protein binding or specific metabolic pathways beyond the aggregate CL data.
downstream_use: Use these specific linear scaling factors as candidate methods for human CL prediction in translation modules, comparing against standard allometric scaling.

title: Two-Species Allometric Scaling Methods
claim: New two-species methods were developed as CL(human) = a(rat-dog) * W(human)^0.628 (rat-dog method) and CL(human) = a(rat-monkey) * W(human)^0.650 (rat-monkey method), where 'a' is the coefficient obtained allometrically from the corresponding two species. These methods showed predictive performance comparable to three-species-based Rule of Exponents (ROE).
conditions: Requires CL data from two specific species pairs (rat+dog or rat+monkey).
Exponents (0.628 and 0.650) are fixed for these specific methods.
Applicable when two-species data is available but three-species data is not.
required_inputs: CL data from rat and dog, OR rat and monkey.
Human body weight (W).
Allometric coefficient 'a' derived from the two animal species.
limitations: Fixed exponents may not apply to all compounds.
Abstract does not detail how 'a' is calculated beyond 'obtained allometrically'.
Performance is 'comparable' to ROE, not necessarily superior in all cases.
downstream_use: Implement as alternative translation methods when only two species are available, potentially reducing data requirements compared to standard ROE.

title: Performance Comparison and Species Count Necessity
claim: Testing on 26 Wyeth compounds showed that the new rat, dog, monkey, rat-dog, and rat-monkey methods provided improved predictions for the majority of compounds compared to the Rule of Exponents (ROE). This suggests that using three or more species in an allometrically based approach may not be necessary for predicting human exposure.
conditions: Based on a validation set of 26 compounds.
Comparison is against standard ROE.
Focus is on clearance prediction accuracy.
required_inputs: Validation dataset of compounds with animal and human CL data.
limitations: Validation set size (n=26) is small.
Abstract does not specify the statistical metrics of 'improved predictions' (e.g., AAFE, bias).
Generalizability to other drug classes beyond the Wyeth dataset is unknown.
downstream_use: Supports the feasibility of using limited species data (1 or 2 species) for human PK prediction, challenging the necessity of multi-species datasets for all cases.

title: Human CL Prediction Method Performance
claim: In the 19-drug subset analyzed, in vivo methods (particularly two-species allometry, rat-dog) generally performed better than IVIVE methods for predicting human intravenous clearance. Maximum success rates for predicting human CL were 100% (10-fold error), 94% (threefold), and 78% (twofold).
conditions: Applicable to prospective human PK simulation
Requires preclinical in vivo data from at least two species (typically rat and dog)
IVIVE methods require specific binding assumptions (microsomal/plasma binding)
required_inputs: Preclinical in vivo clearance data (rat, dog)
In vitro microsomal/hepatocyte stability data (for IVIVE)
Plasma protein binding data (for IVIVE binding corrections)
limitations: Abstract-only source; full methodology details unavailable
Performance metrics are aggregate across 19 drugs; applicability to specific target drug unknown
IVIVE accuracy varies significantly with binding assumptions
downstream_use: Selecting appropriate translation method for human PK simulation; justifying use of allometry vs. IVIVE based on available data types

title: IVIVE Binding Assumptions Impact Accuracy
claim: IVIVE methods using microsomes incorporating both plasma and microsomal binding, and hepatocytes not incorporating binding, achieved ~75-78% predictions within twofold error. Other binding assumption combinations were much less accurate.
conditions: Use when IVIVE is selected over allometry
Requires accurate measurement of plasma and microsomal binding fractions
required_inputs: Microsomal intrinsic clearance
Hepatocyte intrinsic clearance
Plasma protein binding (fu)
Microsomal binding data
limitations: Abstract does not specify exact equations for 'fu intercept method' or specific binding correction formulas
Generalizability to new compounds not guaranteed
downstream_use: Guiding selection of binding correction strategy in IVIVE models

title: Oral AUC Prediction Limitations
claim: Prediction of oral AUC was consistent with i.v. CL predictions, but the greatest challenge was estimating human bioavailability (F).
conditions: Applicable when predicting oral exposure from preclinical data
Requires separate estimation of F
required_inputs: Predicted human CL
Estimated human bioavailability (F)
Preclinical oral PK data
limitations: Abstract does not detail methods for estimating F
High uncertainty in F estimation limits oral AUC prediction accuracy
downstream_use: Highlighting uncertainty in oral exposure predictions; justifying IV-only simulations if F cannot be reliably estimated

title: Microbiological Data Requirements for PK-PD Analysis
claim: Adequate microbiological data, including MIC distributions for relevant pathogens and time-kill studies, are prerequisites for PK-PD analyses. MIC data should be presented by species/genus and separated by resistance status. Time-kill studies help identify the most predictive PK-PD index (concentration-dependent vs. time-dependent).
conditions: MIC distributions must cover the range of interest, including upper-end values (MIC90, ECVs).
Time-kill studies should document changes in organism numbers over a justified time period.
Data should distinguish between wild-type and resistant populations where applicable.
required_inputs: MIC values for clinical isolates relevant to intended indications.
Time-kill curve data showing concentration-dependent or time-dependent activity.
Identification of resistance mechanisms if relevant.
limitations: Abstract-only material supports only what appears in the abstract (not applicable here as full text is provided, but note partial extraction).
Does not specify exact sample sizes for MIC distributions, only that they must be 'adequate'.
downstream_use: Defines the input data required for PK-PD index identification and PTA simulations.

title: Identification of PK-PD Indices and Targets (PDTs)
claim: PK-PD indices (e.g., AUC/MIC, Cmax/MIC, %T>MIC) are identified from nonclinical models (in-vitro or in-vivo). PDTs are defined as the magnitude of the index required to achieve specific effects (net stasis, 1-log10, or 2-log10 CFU reduction). Free drug concentrations are preferred for index calculation unless justified otherwise.
conditions: PDTs are initially derived from nonclinical studies.
Concentration-dependent activity typically links to AUC/MIC or Cmax/MIC; time-dependent activity links to %T>MIC or trough/MIC.
Analyses must report PDTs for stasis, 1-log, and 2-log reductions for each pathogen group.
required_inputs: Nonclinical PK data from animal models or in-vitro systems.
Microbiological effect data (CFU counts) from the same studies.
Protein binding data to convert total to free drug concentrations if necessary.
limitations: Not all agents achieve 2-log10 reductions for all pathogens.
Extrapolation of PDTs to other organisms requires justification of similar behavior.
downstream_use: Provides the target values used in PTA simulations to assess dose regimen adequacy.

title: Clinical PK Data Collection and Population PK Modeling
claim: Clinical PK data from healthy volunteers and infected patients are critical for building POPPK models. Initial models may rely on healthy volunteer data, but must be adjusted to reflect patient variability (e.g., renal hyperfiltration, changes in Vd). Sparse sampling in clinical trials should be guided by optimal sampling designs.
conditions: POPPK models should be developed in accordance with CHMP guidance.
Patient PK data should provide point estimates and variance for PK parameters and covariate effects.
Protein binding must be assessed to determine free drug concentrations for PK-PD analyses.
required_inputs: Intensive PK data from healthy volunteers.
Sparse or intensive PK data from infected patients.
Plasma protein binding data (in-vitro and/or in-vivo).
Concentration-time data in relevant body fluids (e.g., ELF, CSF, urine) if applicable.
limitations: Healthy volunteer data may not fully represent patient PK; adjustments are required.
Inter-individual variability may be greater in patients than in healthy volunteers.
downstream_use: Feeds into Monte Carlo simulations for PTA analysis and E-R relationship modeling.

title: Probability of Target Attainment (PTA) Simulation Methodology
claim: PTA is determined using simulations (typically Monte Carlo) based on POPPK models and nonclinical PDTs. Simulations estimate the probability of achieving the PDT at specific MIC values. Results should be presented by pathogen group and PDT level (stasis, 1-log, 2-log).
conditions: Simulations should use the same PK model from which parameter estimates were obtained.
Inputs include central tendency statistics and variance for PK parameters.
Adjustments for protein binding are required unless binding is low.
If only healthy volunteer data is available, variability must be inflated to reflect patient population.
required_inputs: POPPK model parameters and variances.
Nonclinical PDTs.
MIC distributions for relevant pathogens.
Protein binding data.
limitations: PTA is a probability of achieving a microbiological target, not a probability of clinical cure.
Simulation validity depends on the accuracy of the POPPK model and PDT derivation.
downstream_use: Supports dose regimen selection by demonstrating the likelihood of achieving efficacy targets across the MIC range.

title: Clinical Exposure-Response (E-R) Relationships
claim: Clinical E-R analyses evaluate the relationship between PK parameters (derived from POPPK models) and clinical/microbiological outcomes. These analyses can refine PDTs and support dose adjustments for special populations. They are most useful when there is variability in exposure and outcome.
conditions: Analyses are confined to patients with documented outcomes, adequate PK data, and identified pathogens with MICs.
E-R relationships can be evaluated as continuous or categorical variables.
Model diagnostics and validation are required.
required_inputs: Clinical efficacy and microbiological outcome data.
Individual patient PK data (sparse or intensive).
MICs for pathogens isolated from individual patients.
limitations: E-R analyses may not be feasible if success rates are uniformly high, if combination therapy is used, or if outcomes are heavily confounded.
For licensed agents, E-R analyses require new clinical studies with sparse sampling to be useful.
downstream_use: Provides clinical validation of nonclinical PDTs and identifies the highest MIC treatable with confidence.

title: Beta-Lactamase Inhibitor (BLI) Dose Regimen Identification
claim: BLI dose regimens are identified using PK-PD analyses specific to the BL/BLI combination. The PK-PD index for the BLI (e.g., %T>threshold) is established using nonclinical models mimicking clinical administration. Simulations must account for the variability of both BL and BLI PK and potential interactions.
conditions: BLI investigations must be BL-specific due to varying stability against different beta-lactamases.
Simulations must account for co-administration variability and potential PK interactions.
Renal clearance differences between BL and BLI may necessitate different dose adjustments.
required_inputs: Enzyme kinetics data for BLI inhibitory activity.
In-vitro MICs and time-kill curves for BL alone and BL/BLI combinations.
POPPK models for both BL and BLI.
Nonclinical infection model data for the specific BL/BLI pair.
limitations: Clinical studies often have limited numbers of BL-resistant/BLI-susceptible pathogens, making PK-PD analyses the primary support.
Fixed-dose combinations may be precluded if renal clearance differences require divergent dose adjustments.
downstream_use: Supports the selection of BL/BLI combination regimens and informs labeling for renal impairment.

title: PK Model Parameterization Options
claim: Phoenix supports Micro, Clearance, and Macro parameterizations. Micro uses mass transfer rate constants (e.g., Ke). Clearance uses clearance parameters (e.g., Cl) and supports saturable (Michaelis-Menten) elimination. Macro uses closed-form sums of exponentials and requires a 'stripping dose' assumption to scale predictions for different doses.
conditions: Macro models assume a reference initial dose (stripping dose) to convert fitted concentration curves to other doses.
Clearance parameterization allows switching to saturable kinetics (Km, Vmax).
Macro models are closed-form and cannot handle nonlinear kinetics directly in the same way differential equation models can.
required_inputs: Selection of parameterization type (Micro, Clearance, Macro, Macro1).
For Macro: Definition of stripping dose (A1Strip).
For Clearance: Km and Vmax if saturable elimination is selected.
limitations: Macro models require an assumption about the size of the initial dose used for fitting.
Closed-form models (Macro) are limited to linear kinetics and single observed variables.
Covariates in closed-form models must be constant during observation.
downstream_use: Selecting the appropriate structural model representation for PK analysis. Ensuring correct parameter mapping for dose scaling in simulation.

title: Residual Error Model Selection
claim: Residual error models include Additive, Multiplicative, Power, and Mixed (Add+Mult, Mix Ratio). For PK models, Multiplicative or Power error models are preferred because PK concentrations often span several orders of magnitude, whereas Additive error has large relative errors at low concentrations. For PD models, Additive error is often the first choice due to narrower effect ranges.
conditions: PK models: Prefer Multiplicative or Power error models.
PD models: Prefer Additive error models.
Log-additive error models transform predictions and observations to log-space for fitting, improving performance/accuracy for FOCE engines.
required_inputs: Selection of error model type (Additive, Multiplicative, Power, etc.).
Standard deviation (Stdev) or power exponent values.
For Mixed models: Definition of multiplicative sigma or mix ratio parameters.
limitations: Residual error cannot be less than 0.001 for most engines.
Log-additive models truncate zero/negative values to 1/4 of the smallest positive observation.
Mixed error models require specific formula implementations (e.g., using sigma() function for Add+Mult).
downstream_use: Defining the statistical error structure for model fitting. Interpreting residual plots and model diagnostics.

title: BQL Data Handling in Maximum Likelihood Models
claim: Phoenix handles Below Quantification Limit (BQL) data by using maximum likelihood estimation with censored data. When BQL is enabled, the engine reverts to the Laplacian method. Censored observations (CObsBQL != 0) use the cumulative distribution function for likelihood calculation, while non-censored values use the probability density function.
conditions: BQL option must be selected in the model configuration.
Data must include a column flagging censored vs. non-censored values (e.g., CObsBQL).
Static LLOQ can be used if no BQL flag column is mapped, but mapped columns override static values.
required_inputs: Observation data with BQL flags.
LLOQ values (either static or per-row).
Selection of 'BQL?' checkbox in model options.
limitations: Log-likelihood calculations may overflow if censoring numbers are very small, particularly with multiplicative error models.
BQL handling is specific to Maximum Likelihood engines (e.g., Laplacian).
downstream_use: Accurate parameter estimation in the presence of censored PK data. Avoiding bias from imputing BQL values as zero or LLOQ/2.

title: Structural Model Configuration Details
claim: Model structure is defined by number of compartments (1-3) and absorption type (IV or Extravascular). Extravascular absorption adds Ka. Micro parameterization allows setting Ka=Ke. Clearance parameterization adds inter-compartmental clearances. An elimination compartment (urinecpt) can be added for urine data, which is ignored in steady-state dosing.
conditions: Micro parameterization allows Ka=Ke constraint.
Clearance parameterization with elimination compartment removes 'Closed form?' option.
Infusions require mapping rate contexts (A1 Rate or Aa Rate).
required_inputs: Number of compartments (1-3).
Absorption type (IV or Extravascular).
Optional: Time lag (tlag), Elimination compartment flag.
limitations: Adding an elimination compartment to a Clearance model disables closed-form options.
Steady-state dosing ignores the urinecpt statement.
downstream_use: Configuring the differential equations or algebraic expressions for PK simulation. Mapping data columns to model parameters.

title: AUC Estimation and Testing for Destructive Sampling
claim: When only one measurement per experimental unit is available (destructive sampling), AUC must be estimated using mean concentration values at measurement times. The variance of this estimator can be derived via linear combination of these means.
conditions: Destructive sampling design (one data point per subject/unit).
Group-level mean concentrations are available at specific time points.
Comparison of AUCs between two groups.
required_inputs: Mean concentration values at each measurement time point for each group.
Sample sizes and variances for the mean concentrations at each time point.
Time points for sampling.
limitations: Abstract-only source; specific formulas for the linear combination estimator are not provided in the excerpt.
Does not address longitudinal sampling or individual NCA.
Does not specify handling of BLQ or censoring in this specific estimator context.
downstream_use: Guides the statistical approach for comparing exposure metrics in destructive sampling studies (e.g., tissue distribution studies) rather than using individual-level NCA.

title: Recommendation for Hypothesis Testing of AUC Equality
claim: Welch's test for non-pairwise contrasts is recommended for testing the null hypothesis of equality between two AUCs in destructive sampling designs. The previously suggested normal approximation of the test statistic is inadequate because it exceeds the nominal alpha-level.
conditions: Hypothesis testing of AUC equality between two groups.
Destructive sampling context.
Simulation studies support the recommendation over normal approximation.
required_inputs: Estimated AUCs and their variances for the groups being compared.
Degrees of freedom or sample size information for Welch's test.
limitations: Abstract-only source; does not provide the specific implementation details of Welch's test for this specific AUC estimator.
Does not specify if this applies to multi-group comparisons beyond two groups.
Does not define the exact alpha-level control mechanism beyond rejecting the normal approximation.
downstream_use: Informs the statistical testing module for AUC comparisons in destructive sampling studies, ensuring type I error control.

title: AUC Interpolation Methods
claim: PKNCA supports three interpolation methods for AUC calculation between points: 'lin up/log down' (default, for exogenous substances with first-order elimination), 'linear' (for endogenous substances or non-first-order elimination), and 'lin-log' (linear before Tmax, log after). Zero-interpolation rules apply when both concentrations are zero.
conditions: Exogenous vs endogenous substance distinction
First-order vs non-first-order elimination assumption
Explicit user selection of method
required_inputs: Concentration-time data points
Tmax determination
LLOQ status
limitations: Package defaults are not project approval
Other NCA tools may not describe interpolation as zero
Method choice affects calculated AUC values
downstream_use: NCA calculation configuration

title: AUC Extrapolation Methods
claim: Three extrapolation methods are defined for the tail of the concentration-time curve: 'AUClast' (no extrapolation, integral is zero), 'AUCall' (no extrapolation if the last measured concentration is above LOQ; otherwise linear triangle integration from the last quantifiable point to the subsequent zero-concentration time, under the stated PKNCA convention), and 'AUCinf' (extrapolation using the equation C_last/lambda_z, requiring half-life estimation).
conditions: Last concentration relative to LLOQ
Availability of terminal half-life (lambda_z) for AUCinf
Explicit user selection of method
required_inputs: Last measured concentration (Clast)
Terminal elimination rate constant (lambda_z) for AUCinf
LLOQ value
limitations: AUCinf requires reliable lambda_z estimation
AUCall behavior depends on whether Clast is above or below LLOQ
Extrapolation choices are explicit settings, not automatic defaults
downstream_use: Total exposure calculation (AUCinf/AUCall)

title: Positional BLQ Handling Logic
claim: BLQ values are categorized by their position in the concentration-time profile: 'first' (up to first non-BLQ), 'middle' (between first and last non-BLQ), 'last' (after last non-BLQ), or relative to Tmax ('before.tmax', 'after.tmax'). Each category can be independently configured to 'drop', 'keep', or set to a specific numeric value.
conditions: Concentration values are considered BLQ if they are 0.
NA values are handled by `clean.conc.na` before BLQ logic is applied.
The method for handling NA can affect which points are subsequently classified as BLQ or 'middle'.
required_inputs: Concentration vector (`conc`)
Time vector (`time`)
BLQ handling strategy (`conc.blq`): scalar or list with keys 'first', 'middle', 'last', 'before.tmax', 'after.tmax'
NA handling strategy (`conc.na`)
limitations: BLQ is defined strictly as 0 in this implementation.
The output depends on the order of operations: NA handling precedes BLQ handling.
Does not specify statistical imputation methods beyond setting to a fixed number or dropping.
downstream_use: Preprocessing step for NCA or compartmental modeling to ensure consistent handling of censored data before parameter estimation.

title: NA and BLQ Interaction in Data Cleaning
claim: NA concentrations are processed before BLQ values. The specific method used to handle NA values can alter the classification of subsequent points as BLQ or 'middle' BLQ, thereby influencing the final cleaned dataset.
conditions: NA handling is delegated to `clean.conc.na()`.
The interaction between NA handling and BLQ classification is explicit in the documentation.
required_inputs: NA handling strategy (`conc.na`)
limitations: The specific logic of `clean.conc.na` is not detailed in this excerpt, only its precedence.
Users must be aware that changing NA handling changes BLQ classification.
downstream_use: Ensuring reproducible data cleaning pipelines where missing data and censored data are not conflated or mishandled due to processing order.

title: Sparse Sampling NCA Methodology and Output Structure
claim: When the Sparse Sampling option is enabled in Phoenix NCA, the engine computes mean concentration or rate at each unique time value/interval across subjects. It estimates standard parameters plus specific standard errors (SE_Cmax, SE_AUClast, SE_AUCall for plasma; SE_Max_Rate, SE_AURC_last, SE_AURC_all for urine). Output worksheets are renamed to 'Mean Curve Final Parameters' and 'Mean Curve Summary Table' to indicate group-level estimands.
conditions: Applicable to pre-clinical sparse sampling designs.
Requires loading an NCA model with the Sparse Sampling option enabled.
Data is treated as a special case of plasma or urine concentration data.
required_inputs: Concentration or rate data with subject IDs and time points.
Configuration of NCA model with Sparse Sampling option active.
limitations: Outputs represent group-level means, not individual trajectories.
Standard errors are derived from the mean curve structure, not individual variability directly.
downstream_use: Use for analyzing pre-clinical PK studies where individual full profiles are not available. Interpret parameters as mean curve estimates with associated uncertainty metrics.

title: Limitation of Sparse AUC Standard Errors with Log-Trapezoidal Rules
claim: The standard error calculations for AUC (SE_AUClast and SE_AUCall) in the sparse sampling module depend on AUC being a linear combination of the mean concentrations. Consequently, SE_AUClast and SE_AUCall are NOT included in the output when log-trapezoidal rules are specified as the method for computing AUC.
conditions: Applies when log-trapezoidal integration is selected for AUC calculation.
Applies to sparse sampling data structures.
required_inputs: Selection of log-trapezoidal rule for AUC computation in Phoenix settings.
limitations: Users cannot obtain SE_AUClast/SE_AUCall if log-trapezoidal rules are used.
Linear trapezoidal rules are required to generate these specific SE metrics.
downstream_use: When reporting uncertainty for AUC in sparse pre-clinical studies, verify if linear or log-trapezoidal rules were used. If log-trapezoidal was used, alternative uncertainty metrics or linear rule justification may be needed.

title: Interpretation of SE_AUClast vs SE_AUCall in Sparse Data
claim: SE_AUClast and SE_AUCall provide measurements of uncertainty for AUClast and AUCall, respectively. They are usually the same. Differences between these parameter values are only observed if some measurements were flagged as BQL (below the quantitation limit).
conditions: Sparse sampling data processing.
Presence of BQL data points may cause divergence between SE_AUClast and SE_AUCall.
required_inputs: Data with potential BQL flags.
Sparse sampling NCA model configuration.
limitations: The distinction relies on BQL handling; if no BQLs exist, the SEs are identical.
Does not address the underlying statistical validity of the SE method itself, only the software output behavior.
downstream_use: Use the difference (or lack thereof) between SE_AUClast and SE_AUCall to diagnose the impact of BQL data on the mean curve uncertainty estimates.

title: MRT Definition in Michaelis-Menten Systems
claim: In systems with Michaelis-Menten elimination, Mean Residence Time (MRT) is defined as a function of the steady-state volume of distribution and time-average clearance, where time-average clearance is calculated as Dose/AUC.
conditions: Drug elimination follows Michaelis-Menten kinetics.
Intravenous administration into one- or two-compartment systems.
Applicability check required: Dose/AUC represents time-average clearance, not necessarily constant clearance.
required_inputs: Dose
Area Under the Curve (AUC)
Steady-state volume of distribution (Vss)
limitations: Abstract-only source; specific equations for Vss derivation in nonlinear contexts are not provided.
Does not specify handling of BLQ or censoring in the nonlinear context.
Specific numerical thresholds for 'validity' are not detailed in the abstract.
downstream_use: Use this definition to interpret MRT in nonlinear PK studies. Do not assume linear clearance assumptions apply. Use Dose/AUC as the operational definition for time-average clearance in these specific nonlinear models.

title: Discrepancy between Proposed MRT and Moment Theory (AUMC/AUC)
claim: For Michaelis-Menten systems, the MRT calculated using the proposed method (based on Vss and Dose/AUC) differs from the MRT calculated using standard moment theory (AUMC/AUC).
conditions: Nonlinear elimination kinetics (Michaelis-Menten).
Comparison of two distinct MRT calculation methodologies.
required_inputs: Area Under the Moment Curve (AUMC)
Area Under the Curve (AUC)
Dose
limitations: The magnitude of the difference is not quantified in the abstract.
The specific conditions under which one method is preferred over the other for regulatory or clinical decision-making are not explicitly stated beyond 'clarifying residence time derivations'.
downstream_use: When analyzing nonlinear PK data, explicitly state which MRT definition is being used. Do not interchangeably use AUMC/AUC and the Vss/(Dose/AUC) derived MRT without acknowledging the theoretical difference demonstrated in this source.

title: Validation of MRT via Dose Elimination and Area Attainment
claim: The validity of the proposed MRT calculation method is assessed by examining the percentage of administered dose eliminated and the percentage of total area attained at the calculated MRT compared to the moment theory result (AUMC/AUC).
conditions: Validation of nonlinear PK parameter estimation methods.
Assessment of how well the calculated MRT represents the actual disposition characteristics.
required_inputs: Time-concentration data to calculate cumulative dose eliminated.
Time-concentration data to calculate cumulative area attained.
limitations: Abstract does not provide the specific percentage thresholds for acceptance.
Does not specify if this validation applies to single-dose or multiple-dose scenarios explicitly, though 'single dose' is mentioned in related article titles in the metadata.
downstream_use: Use this conceptual framework to validate nonlinear PK models. If the calculated MRT does not correspond to a logical percentage of dose eliminated or area attained, the model or parameter estimation may be flawed.

title: Direct Calculation of MM Parameters from MRT-Dose Relationship
claim: The study provides direct methods for calculating Michaelis-Menten parameters (Vmax, Km) based on the relationship between Mean Residence Time (MRT) and dose.
conditions: Nonlinear elimination kinetics.
Availability of MRT values across different doses.
required_inputs: MRT values calculated at multiple dose levels.
Dose levels.
limitations: The specific algebraic equations for this direct calculation are not present in the abstract.
Requires accurate MRT calculation, which itself depends on the correct definition (see Card 1).
downstream_use: Potential method for estimating nonlinear parameters without full compartmental fitting if MRT can be reliably estimated from concentration-time data. Requires full-text access to implement the specific equations.

title: Molecular-Weight-Normalized Systemic Metabolite Formation
claim: For a qualified parent-to-metabolite pathway, the systemically available fraction of the parent dose represented by a metabolite can be estimated from metabolite AUC and independently qualified systemic metabolite clearance, with molecular-weight conversion. Compare formed-metabolite kinetics with direct metabolite dosing when available; do not assume formation-limited or elimination-limited kinetics for every pair.
conditions: Requires a defined parent/metabolite identity and formation stoichiometry, linear exposure-clearance relationship over the evaluated range, and appropriately integrated metabolite exposure.
Direct metabolite IV data can qualify systemic metabolite clearance; apparent clearance after an incompletely available route must not substitute without correction.
required_inputs: Parent dose and molecular weight; metabolite molecular weight and formation stoichiometry.
Metabolite AUC after parent dosing, its units/window/extrapolation qualification, and systemic metabolite CL from an applicable independent dataset.
Parent and metabolite concentration-time profiles and dose/route records for comparing formation and disappearance kinetics.
limitations: For one-to-one molar formation and compatible mass units: f_systemic_metabolite=AUC_metabolite*CL_metabolite/Dose_parent*(MW_parent/MW_metabolite). Multiply by100 only to express percent.

This is systemic metabolite availability, not necessarily total metabolic conversion or intestinal fraction absorbed. Other formation/elimination routes and first-pass loss can prevent identification of total conversion.
No source-pair fraction, half-life or kinetic dominance is retained as a default. Nonlinear or coupled formation/elimination may require a different model.
downstream_use: Qualify analyte-specific metabolite contributions and mass-versus-molar accounting in conditional parent-metabolite translation.
retrieval_keywords: parent metabolite molecular weight molar mass systemic formation fraction clearance AUC

title: Phoenix NCA Model Selection and Input Requirements
claim: Phoenix NCA uses specific model IDs based on matrix and dose type: 200 (extravascular plasma), 201 (IV bolus plasma), 202 (constant infusion plasma), 210-212 (urine variants), and 220 (drug effect). Plasma models require 'time of last dose' and 'Tau' (for steady-state); infusion models also require 'length of infusion'. Urine models assume single-dose data.
conditions: Applicable when configuring NCA objects in Phoenix workflows.
Requires correct identification of dose type (extravascular, IV bolus, infusion) and matrix (plasma/blood vs. urine).
required_inputs: Raw concentration or effect data
Dose type specification
Time of last dose
Tau (dose interval) for steady-state plasma models
Length of infusion for model 202
Baseline effect and threshold (optional) for model 220
limitations: Does not specify the mathematical formulas for parameters (referenced as separate 'NCA parameter formulas' section).
Does not define default settings for lambda_z or AUC extrapolation.
Software-specific implementation; not a general PK theory reference.
downstream_use: Guides correct object configuration for PK analysis. Ensures appropriate handling of infusion inputs and steady-state assumptions.

title: Steady-State and Sparse Sampling Assumptions in Phoenix NCA
claim: Phoenix NCA models 200-202 (plasma/blood) support both single-dose and steady-state data. For steady-state, the computation assumes equal dosing intervals (Tau) for each profile and that data is from a 'final' dose at steady state. Models 210-212 (urine) assume single-dose data. The engine supports rich datasets and sparsely-sampled studies (e.g., toxicokinetics).
conditions: When analyzing steady-state data, Tau must be provided and assumed constant across profiles.
When analyzing sparse data, the engine's sparse sampling algorithms are applied.
Urine models (210-212) are restricted to single-dose assumptions.
required_inputs: Tau (dose interval) for steady-state analysis
Identification of 'final' dose data points
limitations: Assumes equal dosing intervals for steady-state; does not explicitly describe handling of unequal intervals in this excerpt.
Does not detail the specific algorithm for sparse sampling (e.g., L-FOCE vs. other methods).
downstream_use: Informs data preparation steps (e.g., ensuring Tau is defined for steady-state studies). Clarifies that urine analysis is limited to single-dose contexts in this software version.

title: Sparse NCA Mean Curve and Nominal Time Requirement
claim: For sparse sampling analysis, the NCA object calculates a mean concentration curve by taking the mean concentration value for each unique time value. It is recommended to use nominal time rather than actual time for these analyses to ensure correct grouping.
conditions: Sparse sampling design
Plasma or urine concentration data
required_inputs: Concentration data
Time values (nominal preferred)
Subject identifiers
limitations: Using actual time instead of nominal time may disrupt the mean curve calculation logic.
This is a software implementation detail, not a universal statistical rule for all sparse methods.
downstream_use: Data preparation for sparse NCA analysis; ensuring time variables are formatted as nominal categories.

title: Unbiased Sparse NCA Estimation Conditions
claim: For batch designs with multiple time points per subject, the documented Phoenix sparse sampling methodology requires equal sample sizes per time point for its unbiased-estimate claim. The documentation also requires no missing data for the sparse routines. These implementation-specific conditions do not establish that all unequal-n destructive-sampling AUC estimators are biased.
conditions: Sparse sampling design
Batch designs with multiple time points per subject
required_inputs: Complete dataset with no missing observations
Balanced sample sizes across time points
limitations: In the documented Phoenix batch implementation, unequal sample sizes per time point introduce bias in parameter estimates.
Missing data violates the unbiasedness condition for these specific sparse routines.
downstream_use: Quality control of sparse datasets before analysis; identifying bias risks in unbalanced designs.

title: Standard Error Calculation for Sparse AUC and Cmax
claim: Standard errors for mean Cmax and AUC are calculated to account for correlations from repeated sampling of individual animals. SE for Cmax is the sample standard deviation of y-values at Tmax divided by sqrt(n). SE for AUC uses a method (Nedelman and Jia 1998; Holder 2001) involving sample variances and covariances between time points.
conditions: Sparse sampling with repeated measures on subjects
Linear trapezoidal rule used for AUC
required_inputs: Concentration values at unique times
Subject IDs to identify repeated measures
Covariance data between time points
limitations: Requires calculation of sample covariance between concentrations at different times.
If r_ij=1 and r_i=1 or r_j=1, covariance s_ij is set to 0.
downstream_use: Interpreting uncertainty in sparse PK parameters; understanding how software handles correlated errors.

title: Handling of Inserted C0 in Sparse AUC
claim: When a non-zero C0 is inserted at dose time t0, the AUC estimate includes an additional constant term C* = C0(t1-t0)/2. The inserted C0 is treated as a constant, so its estimation variance is not duplicated in the Var(AUC) computation.
conditions: Sparse NCA analysis where C0 is estimated/inserted
required_inputs: Estimated C0 value
Time points t0 and t1
limitations: The variance of the estimated C0 is not propagated into the AUC variance calculation in this specific implementation.
downstream_use: Understanding bias/variance trade-offs when imputing C0 in sparse designs.

title: Bioanalytical Method Validation Scope and Elements
claim: Full validation is required for bioanalytical methods quantifying analytes in clinical and nonclinical studies. For chromatographic methods, this includes selectivity, specificity, matrix effect, calibration curve/range (LLOQ to ULOQ), accuracy, precision, carry-over, dilution integrity, stability, and reinjection reproducibility. For LBAs, it includes specificity, selectivity, calibration curve/range, accuracy, precision, carry-over, dilution linearity, and stability.
conditions: Applicable to establishing new methods or repurposing commercial kits/literature methods.
Applies to both chemical and biological drugs.
required_inputs: Defined analyte and matrix.
Reference standards and internal standards (IS).
Blank matrix samples from multiple sources/lots.
limitations: Abstract-only material supports only what appears in the abstract.
Does not validate specific experimental data, only the method framework.
downstream_use: Defines the quality control framework for any PK data used in EDA or modeling. Determines if concentration data is fit for purpose.

title: Selectivity and Specificity Criteria
claim: Selectivity is the ability to differentiate the analyte from interfering substances in blank matrix. For chromatography, interference response must be no more than 20% of analyte response at LLOQ and no more than 5% of IS response. For LBA specificity, target-analyte accuracy at the LLOQ and ULOQ in the presence of related molecules at their anticipated maximal concentrations must be within ±25% of nominal. Specificity involves differentiating the analyte from structurally similar substances (metabolites, isomers).
conditions: Selectivity evaluated using blank samples from at least 6 sources (chromatography) or 10 sources (LBA).
Haemolysed and lipaemic matrices must be tested if relevant to the study population.
required_inputs: Blank matrix samples from multiple donors/lots.
Interfering substances (metabolites, concomitant meds) at anticipated concentrations.
limitations: Does not guarantee specificity for all possible interferents, only those tested.
Back-conversion of metabolites to parent must be evaluated if relevant.
downstream_use: Ensures measured concentrations reflect the target analyte. Critical for interpreting PK data in complex matrices or when metabolites are active.

title: Stability and Recovery Requirements
claim: Stability must be assessed for freeze-thaw (min 3 cycles), bench-top, long-term storage, and processed samples. Conditions must mirror study sample handling. Recovery (extraction efficiency) does not need to be 100% but must be consistent. Recovery is determined by comparing processed spiked samples to processed blanks spiked post-extraction.
conditions: Stability tests must use the same matrix, anticoagulant, and container materials as study samples.
Recovery experiments typically use low, medium, and high QC concentrations.
required_inputs: QC samples at low and high concentrations.
Storage and handling logs for study samples.
Extraction procedure details.
limitations: For chemical drugs, demonstrated stability at one temperature (e.g., -20°C) can be extrapolated to lower temperatures under the source guidance. For biological drugs, a bracketing approach can support intermediate storage temperatures when stability has been demonstrated at both bracketing endpoints.
Recovery is not a measure of accuracy, but consistency is required for accuracy.
downstream_use: Validates that measured concentrations are not artifacts of sample handling. Inconsistent recovery or instability invalidates PK data interpretation.

title: Handling Endogenous Analytes
claim: For analytes that are also endogenous molecules, standard validation is complicated by background levels. Approaches include Surrogate Matrix, Surrogate Analyte, Background Subtraction, and Standard Addition. For QCs spiked with authentic analyte in matrix containing endogenous analyte, Accuracy (%) = 100 × (measured concentration of the spiked sample - endogenous concentration) / nominal added concentration. For unspiked endogenous QCs, only precision can be determined.
conditions: Endogenous concentration in matrix should be low (<20% of LLOQ) for standard approaches.
Surrogate approaches require parallelism and matrix effect evaluation against authentic matrix.
required_inputs: Endogenous concentration levels in blank matrix.
Surrogate standards or stripped matrix if applicable.
limitations: Surrogate matrix/analyte approaches may have different matrix effects/recoveries than authentic matrix.
Standard addition is only for linear response platforms.
downstream_use: Critical for PK/PD of endogenous compounds or replacement therapies. Prevents overestimation of exposure due to background noise.

title: Definition and Linking of Secondary Parameters
claim: Secondary parameters (renal clearance, bioavailability, ratios) are calculated by linking two intervals: a 'requesting interval' (where the result is reported) and a 'reference interval' (which supplies the cross-profile value, e.g., plasma AUC for renal clearance). These are not selected automatically by default interval tables but must be requested by name.
conditions: Requires explicit request of the parameter (e.g., `clr.last`, `f.obs`).
Linking is achieved via `interval_id` in the reference row and `<parameter>_ref` in the requesting row.
If not manually linked, PKNCA attempts to derive the reference by finding the profile with the fewest differing group columns.
required_inputs: Concentration data with group columns (e.g., PCSPEC, Analyte).
Interval specification data frame with `interval_id` and `<parameter>_ref` columns.
Explicit request for the secondary parameter in the interval specification.
limitations: Sparse concentration data (`sparse = TRUE`) is not supported for secondary parameters.
Automatic derivation fails if multiple profiles are equally close (ambiguous reference), resulting in NA unless `group_ref` is used.
downstream_use: Used to calculate renal clearance (AE/plasma AUC), absolute bioavailability (test/ref dose-normalized AUC), and accumulation/metabolite ratios.

title: Unit Handling in Secondary Parameters
claim: Units for secondary parameters are a quotient of the units from the requesting and reference intervals. The result's units are determined by the specific groups involved (e.g., urinary amount units divided by plasma AUC units for renal clearance). If units are convertible, the result may be standardized to a fraction; otherwise, composite units are retained.
conditions: Units are defined per group in the concentration/dose data.
The `units` table in `PKNCAdata` must contain rows for each group pair involved in the calculation.
If units are dimensionless (convertible), `PPSTRESU` becomes 'fraction' with a conversion factor.
required_inputs: Concentration units (`concu`) and dose units (`doseu`) specified per group.
Correct unit definitions in the `units` argument of `PKNCAdata`.
limitations: Units that cannot be reconciled (e.g., IU/mL vs mg/L) result in composite units rather than NA.
Molecular-weight adjustment for metabolite ratios is not currently available.
downstream_use: Ensures correct dimensional analysis for renal clearance (e.g., mg/(hr*ng/mL)) and bioavailability (dimensionless fraction if units match).

title: Exclusion Propagation in Secondary Parameters
claim: Exclusions applied to input values (e.g., insufficient points for half-life calculation) propagate to the secondary parameter result. If the reference interval's AUC is excluded due to poor fit or insufficient data, the dependent secondary parameter (e.g., renal clearance) is also excluded with the same reason.
conditions: Exclusions must be set during the calculation phase (within `pk.nca` or interval specification).
Post-hoc exclusion functions (`exclude_nca_*`) on finished results do not propagate across links.
required_inputs: Interval specification with exclusion criteria (e.g., `min.hl.points`).
Correct linkage between requesting and reference intervals.
limitations: Exclusions applied after calculation do not propagate to linked secondary parameters.
This behavior distinguishes PKNCA's integrated calculation from post-hoc division of results tables.
downstream_use: Prevents reporting of invalid secondary parameters derived from invalid primary parameters (e.g., renal clearance from an excluded AUC).

title: Statistical Analysis of Resistance Trends
claim: Trends in CFR over time were assessed using the Cochran-Armitage test for trend. Confidence intervals for CFR were calculated using the Newcombe-Wilson method without continuity correction. Statistical significance (p < 0.05) indicates a trend in the ability to achieve PD targets, but clinical significance must be evaluated separately.
conditions: Applied to CFR values grouped into time intervals (e.g., 3-year periods).
Used to determine if changes in MIC distributions significantly impacted predicted efficacy.
required_inputs: CFR values for each time interval.
Sample sizes/isolate counts for each interval (implicit in the test).
Significance level (alpha = 0.05).
limitations: Statistical significance does not guarantee clinical relevance (e.g., small CFR declines may be statistically significant but clinically negligible).
Depends on the accuracy of the underlying MIC surveillance data.
Does not adjust for multiple comparisons across multiple regimens in the description.
downstream_use: Provides a quantitative measure of whether resistance trends are strong enough to alter the predicted efficacy of a drug regimen over time.

title: PopPK Data Requirements and Sampling Strategy
claim: Population PK analysis requires PK data of sufficient quantity and quality from subjects representing the indicated population. Sampling schedules should be optimized to estimate parameters and covariate effects with defined precision. For time-varying covariates or between-occasion variability, multiple samples per individual at more than one occasion are required.
conditions: Data must represent the target population.
Sampling around Tmax is required if Cmax is used for E-R analysis.
Missing data handling must be justified (e.g., sensitivity analysis).
required_inputs: Rich or sparse PK sampling data.
Covariate data (intrinsic/extrinsic).
Study design details (dose, frequency, duration).
limitations: Stand-alone studies may miss interactions or lack target population representation.
High shrinkage (>20-30%) reduces reliability of EBEs for E-R analysis.
downstream_use: Designing sampling schemes for clinical trials; assessing data adequacy for model building.

title: Model Development and Covariate Identification
claim: Structural models should be informed by data exploration and scientific rationale. Covariate-parameter relationships should be based on biology, physiology, or allometry. Correct identification of covariate relationships is essential for applying models to untested scenarios. Outliers should be handled with prespecified criteria, and missing data/BLQ must be addressed with appropriate methods.
conditions: Structural model must account for covariance between parameters (e.g., CL and V) if relevant.
Covariate analysis methods (stepwise, full model, Lasso) must be justified.
Outlier removal is discouraged unless due to protocol violation/human error.
required_inputs: Observed PK data.
Prior knowledge of drug ADME.
Covariate definitions.
limitations: Inappropriate structural models can lead to incorrect covariate identification.
Parameter identifiability issues may arise (indicated by high condition number >1000).
downstream_use: Building mechanistic or empirical PK models; identifying covariates for dose adjustment.

title: Model Validation and Diagnostic Criteria
claim: Model validation is critical and requires multiple methods. Goodness-of-fit (GOF) plots (DV vs IPRED/xPRED, residuals vs predictions/time) and simulation-based diagnostics (VPC, pcVPC, NPC, NPDE) are used. High shrinkage obscures EBE-based diagnostics, making simulation-based checks more informative. External validation uses data not used for model building.
conditions: No single validation method is sufficient.
Shrinkage >20-30% limits utility of individual diagnostics.
External validation requires data excluded from model development; independent studies or a predeclared held-out set may supply them.
required_inputs: Model predictions (IPRED, xPRED).
Residuals (IWRES, xWRES).
Random effects distributions.
Test dataset for external validation.
limitations: Internal validation relies on the same data used for building.
Data splitting reduces power to detect covariates.
Shrinkage affects reliability of individual post-hoc estimates.
downstream_use: Qualifying models for regulatory submission or internal decision-making; assessing model robustness.

title: Simulation Strategies for Exposure Prediction
claim: Simulations can predict exposures for untested regimens or populations. Strategies include: (1) Fixed-effect estimates for typical profiles; (2) Uncertainty in fixed effects to assess probability of exposure cutoffs; (3) Between-subject variability (BSV) and residual error to show individual concentration ranges. Correlations between random effects must be accounted for to avoid unrealistic parameter combinations.
conditions: Models must be revalidated if the simulation purpose differs from the original model purpose.
Simulations for future populations must account for uncertainty in BSV and fixed effects.
Demographic variables for simulation should reflect the target population.
required_inputs: Validated population PK model.
Parameter estimates and uncertainty.
Covariate distributions and correlations.
Residual error model.
limitations: Predictions based on typical parameters are not mean predictions.
Uncertainty increases when simulating beyond clinically studied scenarios.
Shrinkage limits reliability of individual predictions if not accounted for.
downstream_use: Prospective human PK prediction; dose regimen selection; exposure-response analysis.

title: Reporting and Traceability Requirements
claim: Population PK reports must include executive summaries, detailed methods (model equations, software, handling of outliers/missing data), and results presented as effects on clinically relevant exposures. Datasets and model files must be traceable, with unique subject identifiers linking to clinical trial data. All conclusions must be reproducible with submitted codes and data.
conditions: Results should be presented as effects on exposure, not just model parameters.
Traceability between model output and E-R datasets is required.
Software and version must be reported.
required_inputs: Final model code/scripts.
Datasets used for model building and evaluation.
Define files and reviewer guides.
limitations: Lack of traceability hinders regulatory review.
Inconsistent reporting formats reduce efficiency.
downstream_use: Preparing regulatory submissions; ensuring reproducibility of PK analyses.

title: Treatment Duration and Response Endpoint in PK/PD Index Qualification
claim: An index supported for one response endpoint and treatment duration is not automatically qualified for another. Compare candidate exposure indices against the declared endpoint/window and design; a switch in the best-fitting index in a source experiment illustrates this limitation, not a universal rule assigning an index to short or long treatment.
conditions: Conditional antibacterial exposure-response comparisons with matched organism/site context.
Different endpoints, such as viable counts and survival, represent different estimands and may require different observation models.
required_inputs: Qualified exposure profiles with free/total basis, index units and integration window.
Organism susceptibility measurements and assay provenance.
Response measurements, treatment duration, response-assessment time and treatment-start/control definitions.
Dose schedules and a design capable of distinguishing candidate index predictions.
limitations: Do not transfer the source study index winner, treatment durations, numerical targets or regimen superiority.
Association between an index and an endpoint is not a proven mechanism or clinical transport guarantee.
Unmatched exposure support or sparse designs can prevent meaningful index comparison.
downstream_use: Requalify an index when changing the endpoint or treatment window; preserve uncertainty rather than assigning a generic winner.

title: Equilibrium Dialysis and Ultrafiltration Method Comparability
claim: Binding estimates from equilibrium dialysis and ultrafiltration require analyte- and matrix-specific qualification. Compare recoverability and quantification of each relevant component in donor, receiver or filtrate fractions; agreement in one experiment does not establish universal assay equivalence.
conditions: Binding measurements for a defined analyte or multicomponent mixture in a declared biological matrix.
Assay conditions must permit interpretation of the sampled free/total fractions and quantitative recovery.
required_inputs: Analyte/component identities, concentration levels, matrix species and preparation.
Equilibration/separation conditions, device and membrane information, and matched concentration measurements with assay limits.
Nonspecific device binding/recovery controls and independently prepared assay replicates.
limitations: A component not quantified in a receiver fraction is not automatically absent or fully bound; consider assay sensitivity, transport and loss.
Do not transfer source incubation time, centrifugation settings, device brand, measured binding percentages or method agreement as universal defaults.
Analytical replicate counts do not create independent biological samples.
downstream_use: Select and qualify a binding assay before deriving fu or comparing matrices/species.

title: Depletion Slope Qualification and Intrinsic Clearance Units
claim: Under qualified first-order depletion conditions, regress ln(concentration remaining) or ln(percent remaining) against incubation time over an eligible linear interval. The negative slope is an apparent disappearance rate, not an in vivo hepatic clearance. Assay normalization, physiological scaling and binding qualification are separate steps.
conditions: Measured substrate depletion in a defined microsomal or cellular assay, with time and concentration units retained.
The selected interval must support the kinetic approximation; substrate concentration, protein/cell loading, cofactor, pH and temperature are assay-specific qualifications.
required_inputs: Incubation time and quantified concentration or normalized percent remaining, with censoring and normalization provenance.
Assay protocol, matrix, protein/cell loading, incubation volume and appropriate stability/recovery controls.
Only for downstream IVIVE: qualified assay-to-CLint conversion, physiological scaling quantities, flow and matrix/binding basis consistent with the selected equation.
limitations: Do not import a source compound half-life, CLint, tested substrate level, fixed regression interval or assay recipe.
Loss from nonspecific binding or instability can be mistaken for metabolic disappearance; bulk depletion does not identify a specific enzyme contribution.
CLint per protein mass, per cell number and per body mass are distinct quantities; conflicting source denominators must be resolved before numerical reuse.
The image-only assay-conversion equation is not supplied here as an executable formula. Already-unbound-corrected CLint must not receive a second incubation-binding correction.
downstream_use: Prepare an auditable depletion estimate and determine which assay-specific inputs are still needed before IVIVE.

title: EUCAST ECOFF Definition and Derivation
claim: ECOFFs (and TECOFFs) distinguish microorganisms without (wild type) and with phenotypically detectable acquired resistance mechanisms. ECOFFs are based on at least 5 distributions, while TECOFFs are based on 3 or 4.
conditions: Applicable for distinguishing wild-type vs non-wild-type phenotypes
Requires sufficient distribution data (>=5 for ECOFF, 3-4 for TECOFF)
required_inputs: MIC or zone diameter distributions
Curated data compliant with EUCAST SOP 10
limitations: ECOFFs are not clinical breakpoints
Do not represent rates of resistance
Based on phenotypic detection of acquired resistance mechanisms
downstream_use: Used as reference material for epidemiological surveillance and as a basis for clinical breakpoint decisions.

title: Aggregation and Weighting of MIC Distributions
claim: MIC distributions are aggregated from worldwide sources. 'Aggregated weighted distributions' convert each individual distribution to contribute equally to the common distribution, preventing large datasets from drowning out smaller ones.
conditions: Data must be representative of reference broth microdilution (ISO-20776-2) or calibrated methods
Truncated distributions at the lower end are excluded
required_inputs: Multiple MIC distributions from various sources/geographies/time periods
Compliance with EUCAST SOP 10
limitations: Different methods do not give exactly the same results (variation up to one doubling dilution)
Cannot be used to infer rates of resistance or compare resistance over time/geography
downstream_use: Provides a robust reference distribution for wild-type susceptibility calibration.

title: Methodological Calibration and Data Exclusion
claim: MIC data is primarily from EUCAST/CLSI methods calibrated to ISO 20776-1/2. Zone data is exclusively from EUCAST disk diffusion. 10-20% of contributions are excluded, commonly due to 'lower end truncation'.
conditions: MIC methods must be reference or calibrated to reference
Zone data must be quality-controlled EUCAST disk diffusion
required_inputs: Method metadata for each distribution
Quality control data
limitations: If a local distribution's wild-type mode differs by >=2 two-fold dilutions from the website's aggregated mode, it indicates methodological error or inadequate material
downstream_use: Ensures comparability of MIC/Zone data across different laboratories and time periods.

title: Conditional Metal Availability and Transport-Dependent Susceptibility
claim: When uptake of a compound depends on an iron-binding moiety and microbial iron transport, iron availability in the assay can change measured susceptibility and its relationship to exposure-response. Treat metal content and transport biology as applicability variables; a result for one structural mechanism does not justify iron-depleted testing for every antimicrobial.
conditions: A supported iron-chelation/transport-dependent uptake mechanism is relevant to the studied compound and organism.
Medium modification must follow a qualified method with reproducible controls; the source case alone is not a generic assay prescription.
required_inputs: Evidence for the relevant chemical moiety, metal-binding behavior and uptake mechanism.
Measured or specified medium iron content, assay protocol, organism identity and quality-control results.
Matched susceptibility measurements and exposure-response context under the compared conditions.
limitations: A catechol moiety or molecular formula alone does not establish transporter recognition, potency or in vivo efficacy.
Do not import the source compound medium recipe, numerical MIC changes or target values.
Broth metal availability is a model of a biological environment, not a direct measurement of infection-site chemistry.
downstream_use: Flag chemically mediated assay-context dependence when qualifying MIC and transporting a PK/PD target.

title: Dynamic In-Vitro Exposure Profile and Medium-Binding Qualification
claim: A dynamic in-vitro PK/PD experiment should verify the achieved concentration-time profile against the intended profile and qualify unbound exposure in its own medium. Flow-based elimination, dosing inputs and measured assay limits must be documented rather than assuming the nominal regimen was achieved.
conditions: An in-vitro exposure-response system with a declared compartment/flow configuration and sampling design.
The medium and temperature are controlled and applicable analytical methods are available.
required_inputs: System volume and flow/input schedule with units; intended concentration-time profile and independently measured concentration samples.
Medium composition, analyte binding/recovery measurements and quantification limits.
Microbial counts, sampling times and controls for growth, dilution or washout where relevant.
limitations: The source half-life, assay range, exposure error and fu are not transferable settings.
Medium binding does not establish plasma binding. Unquantifiable terminal samples can prevent verification of the intended elimination slope.
An in-vitro system does not reproduce host immunity or all site distribution processes.
downstream_use: Qualify realized exposures before calculating PK/PD indices or interpreting killing/regrowth.

title: Descriptive Calculation and Provenance Rules
