claim: EDA may execute descriptive formulas (e.g., unit conversion, dose normalization, log transformations) only when definitions are established, inputs are available, and no new scientific assumptions are introduced. Original values, units, formula sources, and handling of missing/censored values must be preserved. Source-reported values must be distinguished from EDA-calculated values.
conditions: Definition established
Inputs available
No new scientific assumption
required_inputs: Original values/units
Formula source/definition
Input links
Grouping/calculation scale
Missing/censored handling rules
limitations: Normalization alone does not establish dose proportionality
Group baselines do not create individual pairing
No arbitrary constants added to zero/censored counts
downstream_use: Preparation of clean datasets for PK/PD modeling and exposure-response analysis.

title: Assay Validation and Endogenous Analyte Handling
claim: For analytes that are also endogenous molecules, standard validation is complicated. Approaches include Surrogate Matrix, Surrogate Analyte, Background Subtraction, and Standard Addition. For QCs spiked with authentic analyte in matrix containing endogenous analyte, Accuracy (%) = 100 × (measured concentration of the spiked sample - endogenous concentration) / nominal added concentration. For unspiked endogenous QCs, only precision can be determined.
conditions: Analyte is endogenous
Matrix interference present
required_inputs: Endogenous concentration levels
Calibration standards
QC samples
limitations: Endogenous levels may vary by age, gender, race, etc.
Surrogate matrices may differ in recovery/matrix effects
downstream_use: Assay qualification and data quality assessment.

title: PK/PD Index Calculation and Unit Consistency
claim: Ratios such as fAUC/MIC or Cmax/MIC require matched strain MIC, compatible units, and explicit definitions. PKNCA examples show that ratios of different units (e.g., ng/mL vs mg/L) must be converted to a common basis before calculation to avoid dimensionless errors.
conditions: Exposure-response analysis
Multiple analytes or matrices
required_inputs: Concentration values
MIC values
Unit conversion factors
Analyte definitions
limitations: Concentration records alone do not supply an integrated exposure endpoint
Different quantities/windows require separate panels
downstream_use: PK/PD index calculation and target attainment analysis.

title: Multiple Dose Levels and Dose Normalization
claim: Dose normalization requires an interpretable denominator (e.g., mg/kg). Salt vs. free base, active moiety, and administered mixture vs. measured component distinctions must be preserved. Normalization does not prove proportionality or linear disposition.
conditions: Multiple dose levels
Dose-dependent effects
required_inputs: Explicit dose per profile
Dose unit/basis
Route/formulation
Concentration basis. Explicit link between administered entity (salt/free base, active moiety or mixture) and measured analyte/component.
limitations: Zero-dose controls remain unnormalized
Normalization cannot resolve incompatible analytes/matrices
downstream_use: Dose-scaling assessment and human scenario preparation.

title: Repeated Dosing and Time Origin Definition
claim: Data must distinguish between time since first dose and time since most recent dose. Actual vs. nominal timing must be preserved. A scheduled predose sample is not automatically a verified trough. Steady state is not established by repeated dosing alone.
conditions: Multiple dosing occasions
Steady-state assessment
required_inputs: Dose dates/times
Intervals
Sampling times
Departures from schedule
limitations: Changing concentrations need not reflect accumulation
Timing description does not estimate between-occasion variability
downstream_use: Longitudinal PK analysis and regimen comparison.

title: Matrix and Analyte Specificity in Visualization
claim: Plasma, tissue homogenate, and lavage fluid concentrations must be plotted on separate panels or axes due to incompatible units (e.g., mg/L vs mass/g tissue). Whole-lung homogenate is not automatically ELF. Unmatched samples cannot establish tissue/plasma ratios.
conditions: Multiple matrices
Local-site data
required_inputs: Matrix identification
Concentration units
Sampling method
Correction definitions (e.g., urea)
limitations: Do not connect unrelated matrices as a biological time trajectory
Corrected and measured values require distinct labels
downstream_use: Exposure-target comparison and tissue distribution analysis.

title: NCA Model Selection and Input Requirements
claim: Phoenix NCA requires specific model IDs based on matrix and dose type (e.g., 200 for extravascular plasma, 201 for IV bolus). Plasma models require 'time of last dose' and 'Tau' for steady-state. Urine models assume single-dose data and require interval start/end times.
conditions: Non-compartmental analysis
Data structure definition
required_inputs: Matrix type
Dose type
Time of last dose
Tau (if steady-state)
Interval data (if urine)
limitations: Vss is not computed for extravascular dosing
Urine models do not depend on dose type for final parameters
downstream_use: Parameter estimation and model qualification.

title: NCA Terminal Phase Data Requirements and Validity
claim: Terminal-dependent NCA endpoints (lambda_z, t1/2, AUCinf) require explicit verification of terminal phase validity. The last few observations do not automatically constitute a valid terminal phase. Inputs must include quantifiable observations, BLQ status, and dosing/infusion timing to distinguish terminal decline from ongoing input. A universal minimum sampling count or fit-statistic threshold is not established; adequacy is assessed per endpoint.
conditions: Terminal phase estimation requested
Extrapolation required
required_inputs: Concentration-time observations with quantifiability/BLQ flags
Dosing and infusion timing
Endpoint definition and time origin
limitations: Cannot certify usable terminal estimate if inputs are incomplete
Software default acceptance criteria are not sufficient evidence of adequacy
Group-mean terminal curves do not yield individual parameter distributions
downstream_use: NCA endpoint calculation, model qualification

title: Identifiability of Population PK/PD Models
claim: Structural identifiability concerns whether model parameters can be distinguished under ideal input-output data. In the source fixed-effects examples, the Fisher Information Matrix determinant (|MF|) had a continuous log-log relationship with residual variance and approached infinity as residual variance approached zero; the mixed-effects examples had a noninfinite asymptote. These are model- and design-dependent diagnostic conditions, not sufficient proof of global structural uniqueness. Random-effects parameters do not automatically follow the identifiability behavior of corresponding fixed-effects parameters and must be assessed separately.
conditions: Model development
Design optimization
required_inputs: Model structure
Parameterization
Residual variance assumptions
limitations: Positive |MF| values alone are insufficient to confirm identifiability
Nonidentifiable models may also yield positive |MF| values for some residual variances
downstream_use: Model qualification, design optimization

title: Sparse Sampling Design and Estimation Efficiency
claim: The quality of compartment model estimates depends on experimental design. Sparse sampling designs can be evaluated via stochastic simulation and estimation. In the cited study, designs with 3 points per subject required 60 subjects (180 total collections) and 4 points required 50 subjects to achieve >90% success rates in distinguishing the simulated two-compartment model with absorption lag from its no-lag counterpart. Two-point designs did not achieve this success rate even with increased sample size for that comparison in the simulated scenarios; these counts are not universal minimum sampling requirements.
conditions: Limited blood volume per animal
Longitudinal or destructive sampling constraints
required_inputs: Candidate sampling times
Number of subjects
Number of samples per subject
limitations: Efficiency depends on the specific drug and model structure
Sparse designs may obscure absorption-phase details
downstream_use: Study design, data collection planning

title: Residual Error and Censored Data (BLQ) Handling
claim: Residual error models must be specified (e.g., additive, proportional, or combined). For logarithmically transformed data, additive error is often used. Below Limit of Quantification (BLQ) data requires specific handling; simple omission or imputation is not sufficient. Maximum Likelihood methods with censored data options (e.g., M3 method) use the cumulative distribution function for censored values and probability density for non-censored values, often reverting to Laplacian approximation.
conditions: Data contains BLQ values
Log-transformation applied
required_inputs: Observed concentrations
LLOQ values
Censoring flags
limitations: Naive pooled or QRPEM engines may have different constraints
Residual error cannot be less than 0.001 in some software contexts
downstream_use: Model fitting, likelihood calculation

title: Compartmental Model Parameterization and Saturable Kinetics
claim: PK models can be parameterized via Micro (rate constants), Clearance (clearance terms), or Macro (sum of exponentials) approaches. Saturable elimination (Michaelis-Menten) is modeled using Vmax and Km. For extravascular administration, absorption rate (Ka) is added. In some cases, Ka is set equal to Ke. Macro models require a 'stripping dose' assumption to derive volume.
conditions: Non-linear kinetics observed
Specific software implementation (e.g., Phoenix)
required_inputs: Concentration-time data
Dose information
limitations: Macro parameterization requires explicit dose assumptions for volume derivation
Saturable models require sufficient data to estimate Km and Vmax
downstream_use: Structural model selection

title: Model Qualification and Diagnostic Criteria
claim: Model qualification relies on visual predictive checks (VPC), goodness-of-fit plots (observed vs. predicted), and residual diagnostics (e.g., CWRES). For nested models, a decrease in the objective function (reported as -1*log likelihood in S-ADAPT) of 1.92 U (chi-square test, 1 df) was considered significant in the source study. The source study tested suspected outliers and excluded observations using its weighted-residual and fitted-function criteria. For a new analysis, prespecify and justify outlier handling, document exclusions, and assess their influence by refitting the final model to the complete dataset; residual anomalies may reflect model misspecification. Model performance must be evaluated for misspecification relative to the intended objective.
conditions: Model evaluation
Regulatory or scientific qualification
required_inputs: Observed data
Model predictions
Residuals
limitations: Visual inspection is subjective without quantitative thresholds
Outlier exclusion criteria must be predefined
downstream_use: Model acceptance, parameter reporting

title: PK/PD Index Definition and Input Requirements
claim: PK/PD indices must be explicitly defined with their units, exposure window, and concentration basis (total vs. free). MIC-normalized indices require strain-matched MIC data with defined measurement context. Non-MIC-normalized exposure summaries do not require MIC. The label 'fT' is incomplete without specifying the threshold and whether the output is a duration or percentage.
conditions: When calculating or comparing exposure indices.
When distinguishing between exposure summaries and exposure-response fits.
required_inputs: Defined index formula (e.g., fAUC/MIC, fCmax/MIC, %fT>MIC).
Concentration basis (total or unbound/free).
Exposure window (e.g., 24h AUC).
For MIC-normalized indices: Strain-matched MIC value, units, and measurement method.
For fT>MIC: Specific threshold value and definition.
limitations: Do not infer MIC normalization from an abbreviated label.
Do not borrow MICs from other drugs or strains.
An EDA quotient using matched MIC retains the numerator's provenance; the ratio is not a measured concentration.
downstream_use: Preparation of data for index ranking or PD target estimation.

title: Exposure-Response Index Ranking Methodology
claim: Index ranking requires matched response data (e.g., log CFU change) linked to specific regimens and exposures. The design must allow separation of correlated indices (e.g., varying dose frequency vs. total dose) to distinguish which index best predicts effect. Goodness-of-fit (e.g., R² of sigmoid Emax models) is used to compare candidate indices on comparable response data.
conditions: When the objective is to identify the best predictor of antibacterial effect among candidate indices.
When raw response data is available and traceable to PK inputs.
required_inputs: Traceable mapping between regimen, exposure, and biological response.
PD endpoint definition (e.g., change from baseline, survival).
Baseline/untreated control data.
Multiple dose levels or regimens to vary indices independently.
limitations: Exposure values alone do not establish a best index.
If the design does not separate correlated indices, ranking remains unresolved.
Do not fit models or select a 'winning' index in the data-requirements stage; this is a methodological prerequisite.
downstream_use: Selection of the primary PK/PD index for target estimation.

title: PD Target Definition and Estimation
claim: A PD target is a specific magnitude of a PK/PD index associated with a defined effect (e.g., stasis, 1-log kill, 2-log kill) relative to a specified baseline or comparator. Targets can be reported from literature or estimated from new data. Reported targets must retain their original index definition, units, free/total basis, and applicability context.
conditions: When defining a target for later PTA or regimen design.
When using a reported target from external literature.
required_inputs: Desired effect definition (e.g., static, 1-log reduction).
Reference baseline (e.g., untreated control, start of therapy).
Observation time window.
For estimation: Paired exposure-response observations with independent experimental unit identity.
For reported targets: Source, value, index definition, and uncertainty.
limitations: A published PD target is not automatically applicable to the target drug without context matching.
Stasis and log-kill targets are distinct; do not conflate.
Missing target definition is a gap, not a blocker for independent PK work.
downstream_use: Input for PTA (Probability of Target Attainment) simulations.

title: Concentration-Dependent vs. Time-Dependent Killing Patterns
claim: The predictive PK/PD index is determined by the drug's killing kinetics. Concentration-dependent killing (rapid kill, regrowth below MIC) typically correlates best with AUC/MIC or Cmax/MIC. Time-dependent killing correlates best with fT>MIC. Time-kill studies provide initial insight into which index is likely predictive.
conditions: When selecting candidate indices for exposure-response analysis.
When interpreting in vitro time-kill data.
required_inputs: Time-kill study data showing organism numbers over time.
Observation of regrowth patterns relative to MIC.
Comparison of R² values for AUC/MIC, Cmax/MIC, and fT>MIC in exposure-response fits.
limitations: In vitro time-kill data supports its own analysis context but is not automatically animal efficacy.
Closely correlated indices may have similar fits; a small ranking difference alone does not establish a unique causal driver.
Beta-lactams typically favor fT>MIC.
downstream_use: Justification for index selection in PK/PD modeling.

title: Handling of Free Drug and Binding in PK/PD Indices
claim: Free-drug indices (fAUC/MIC, fCmax/MIC, fT>MIC) require accurate protein binding data. Unbound fractions vary by species and matrix (e.g., plasma of neutropenic mice vs. critically ill humans). Binding evidence must be traceable and specific to the matrix and concentration range.
conditions: When calculating free-drug indices.
When translating animal PK/PD data to human scenarios.
required_inputs: Protein binding percentage or unbound fraction (fu) IF deriving unbound exposure from total. If unbound exposure is directly measured, this conversion factor is not required.
Matrix-specific binding data (e.g., plasma, lung homogenate).
Concentration-dependent binding data if non-linear.
limitations: Do not assume one binding value is valid for every matrix or concentration.
Unbound fractions in animal models may differ substantially from human patients.
downstream_use: Conversion of total drug PK to free drug PK for PD target comparison.

title: MIC Distribution and PTA Input Requirements
claim: For a conditional PTA at one MIC, require that MIC value and a matched PD target, exposure basis and simulation distribution. For PTA across a development-relevant MIC range, include values at the upper end and report organism/resistance strata as applicable to EMA antimicrobial guidance. For CFR, require a scenario-representative MIC frequency distribution and denominator; do not use an aggregated ECOFF reference as default local weights.
conditions: When preparing inputs for PTA simulations.
When evaluating the applicability of a PD target to a population.
required_inputs: MIC distributions for relevant pathogens.
Definition of wild-type vs. resistant subpopulations.
Source of MIC data (clinical isolates, ECVs).
limitations: PTA is not probability of clinical cure.
MIC distributions must be representative of the intended clinical use.
Abstract-only material supports only what appears in the abstract.
downstream_use: Calculation of Probability of Target Attainment (PTA) and Cumulative Fraction of Response (CFR).

title: Allometric Scaling Method Selection and Species Constraints
claim: Human clearance prediction by allometry requires a specified species set, scaling method and exponent. In the cited dataset, single-species optimal exponents were 0.65-0.70 for small molecules and 0.75-0.80 for macromolecules; monkey liver-blood-flow scaling had AFE <= 2.0 in that analysis. In that dataset, renal small-molecule simple allometry had lower average error than hepatic small-molecule scaling, especially at low extraction; MLP/BRW corrections reduced some group-level errors. These observations do not fix a default exponent or guarantee a target-drug prediction.
conditions: Applicable when animal PK data is qualified and body weights are available.
Do not pool CL/F with absolute CL or Vz with Vss.
Count unique qualified species, not duplicate publications.
required_inputs: Qualified animal clearance estimates (CL) with provenance.
Body weights for all species used in scaling.
Explicit method specification (e.g., simple allometry, LBF, ROE).
limitations: No universal minimum species count is established.
Prediction error is high for low hepatic extraction ratio drugs using simple allometry.
A good animal regression fit does not validate human prediction accuracy.
downstream_use: Generates prospective human clearance scenarios for dose prediction.

title: Binding and Unbound Exposure Data Requirements
claim: Binding data must distinguish between directly measured unbound concentration, unbound fraction (fu), and bound fraction. Percentage vs. fractional scales must be preserved. Blood/plasma partition information is required only if the task changes concentration basis. One binding value is not valid for every matrix or concentration; concentration-dependent binding may require a model.
conditions: Enable only when the objective requests unbound exposure or a binding correction.
Do not silently copy animal fu into a human prediction or assume fu equals one.
Do not confuse human-source in vitro evidence with human in vivo PK observations.
required_inputs: Requested use (unbound exposure vs. correction).
Measurement method, species, matrix, temperature, pH, and concentration range.
Explicit definition of the binding metric (fu vs. bound fraction).
limitations: Ambiguous definitions (e.g., % vs fraction) must be flagged.
Non-specific binding to filters (e.g., in ultrafiltration) must be corrected for if applicable.
Missing binding data blocks unbound endpoint calculations but not total exposure work.
downstream_use: Enables conversion of total to unbound exposure for PK/PD target matching.

title: Urinary Excretion and Renal Clearance Data Structure
claim: Renal clearance prediction requires urine collection intervals with start/end times relative to dosing, completeness status, volume, and analyte concentration. Interval vs. cumulative quantity must be preserved. Unchanged drug vs. metabolites must be distinguished. A missing interval is not a zero-amount collection.
conditions: Applicable when urinary excretion or renal/nonrenal split is requested.
Reuse qualified plasma exposure definitions with matched total/free basis, units, and analysis window for the intended translation comparison.
Calculation belongs to the later analysis module; this stage assesses data requirements.
required_inputs: Collection intervals (start/end times).
Urine volume and analyte concentration (or reported amount excreted).
Dose basis and route.
Completeness status of each interval.
limitations: Pooled cage data cannot be treated as individual animal trajectories.
Missing data is not zero; it is a gap.
Published same-drug fe/CLR may be used as literature-reported inputs if permissions allow, but are not independently validated.
downstream_use: Supports renal clearance component of total clearance prediction.

title: Uncertainty vs. Variability in Human Prediction
claim: Prediction uncertainty (limited knowledge of the system) is distinct from population variability (biological variation). Uncertainty decreases with information accumulation; variability does not. Human dose prediction models must distinguish scaling methodology uncertainty from target population variability. PD uncertainty varies by biological system and is harder to generalize than PK uncertainty.
conditions: Apply to all prospective human PK/PD scenarios.
Distinguish between model structure uncertainty and parameter uncertainty.
Do not treat generic published human methodological examples as observations for the target drug.
required_inputs: Parameter estimates with associated uncertainty metrics.
Definition of the target population for variability assessment.
Model structure assumptions.
limitations: Tables are limited to showing uncertainty in two parameters at discrete points.
Sensitivity plots communicate uncertainty in only one parameter at a time.
Species differences in underlying biology are a major source of PD uncertainty.
downstream_use: Frames the interpretation of human simulation outputs and feasibility constraints.

title: IVIVE Error Sources and Low-Clearance Challenges
claim: Systematic underprediction in IVIVE is multifactorial, stemming from enzyme activity loss, cofactor depletion, measurement errors in fraction unbound, and unstirred water layer effects. Low clearance compounds are difficult to measure accurately due to low turnover rates, leading to high uncertainty in first-dose estimations. Interlaboratory variability in hepatocyte intrinsic clearance values is significant and not dependent on the number of prediction values.
conditions: Consider when evaluating the reliability of IVIVE-derived clearance predictions.
Note that compounds with lower rotatable bonds and lower lipophilicity may show different variability patterns.
Uniform in vitro values do not guarantee accurate predictions; many uniform predictions are inaccurate.
required_inputs: Source of in vitro data (single vs. multi-lab).
Physicochemical properties (logD, rotatable bonds) if available for context.
Intrinsic clearance values and their variability metrics.
limitations: Experimental procedures (e.g., shaking during incubation) affect results.
Low turnover compounds have large uncertainty in clearance estimation.
High intrinsic clearance compounds also show increased error due to cofactor depletion/permeability limits.
downstream_use: Qualifies the confidence level of IVIVE-based human clearance predictions.

title: Distinction Between Prediction Uncertainty and Population Variability
claim: In human dose prediction, 'uncertainty' refers to limited knowledge of the system (e.g., scaling error) and decreases as information accumulates, whereas 'variability' is an inherent property of the system (e.g., inter-individual differences) that does not decrease with larger sample sizes. Conflating these leads to misinterpretation of prediction intervals.
conditions: Applicable to all prospective human PK/PD simulations.
Requires explicit separation of scaling methodology uncertainty from target population biological variability.
required_inputs: Point estimates for PK parameters (CL, Vss).
Defined uncertainty distributions for scaling parameters.
Defined variability distributions for population parameters.
limitations: PD uncertainty is harder to generalize than PK uncertainty and varies by biological system.
Uncertainty in PD effect depends on the specific preclinical model and study design.
downstream_use: Guides the construction of Monte Carlo simulation inputs and the interpretation of prediction intervals.

title: Monte Carlo Integration of Multi-Source Uncertainty
claim: Monte Carlo simulation is an effective method to integrate multiple sources of uncertainty (e.g., clearance prediction error, volume of distribution scaling error, PD potency uncertainty) into a single empirical distribution of the predicted human dose or exposure. This approach handles both closed-form PK/PD models and complex nonlinear models where analytical solutions are unavailable.
conditions: Used when multiple parameter uncertainties need to be propagated simultaneously.
Requires defining distributions for each uncertain input parameter.
required_inputs: Distributions for PK parameters (e.g., log-normal for Vss to avoid negative values).
Distributions for PD parameters (e.g., MIC, potency).
Computational framework for numerical integration or optimization.
limitations: Computational cost increases with model complexity (e.g., ODE integration per sample).
Correlations between parameter uncertainties are often unknown and may be omitted, potentially underestimating combined uncertainty.
downstream_use: Generates empirical distributions of human dose or exposure metrics (e.g., fAUC/MIC) for PTA/CFR analysis.

title: Human Simulation Input Definitions and Scenario Constraints
claim: Prospective human IV PK curve simulations require explicit definitions of the regimen (dose, basis, bolus/infusion, interval), concentration basis (total/free), and time horizon. Inputs must distinguish existing data from predicted parameters. Vss must not be silently treated as Vc; multi-compartment profiles require distribution parameters beyond total CL and Vss.
conditions: Applies when the project requests a prospective human IV profile.
Prospective predictions use qualified predicted parameters with stated applicability and assumptions.
required_inputs: Proposed human IV regimen details.
Qualified predicted parameters from translation branch.
Explicit uncertainty/assumption treatment for inputs.
limitations: A unique multi-compartment curve cannot be derived from CL and Vss alone.
Measured human variability or clinical validation is not established by this process.
downstream_use: Defines the boundary conditions for simulation execution and identifies missing scientific scenario definitions.

title: Model Parameterization and Structural Assumptions
claim: PK models can be parameterized via Micro (mass transfer rate constants), Clearance (clearance-based differential equations), or Macro (closed-form sum of exponentials). Macro models require a 'stripping dose' assumption to scale predictions to different doses. Saturable elimination requires Km and Vmax parameters.
conditions: Selection of parameterization affects which parameters are primary vs. derived.
Macro models assume a fixed reference dose for scaling.
required_inputs: Choice of parameterization method (Micro, Clearance, Macro).
For Macro: Stripping dose definition.
For Saturable: Km and Vmax.
limitations: Macro models do not directly model volume; it is derived.
Incorrect parameterization can lead to misinterpretation of Vss vs Vc.
downstream_use: Determines the mathematical structure of the simulation engine and the interpretation of fitted parameters.

title: Steady-State and Sparse Sampling Assumptions in NCA
claim: Non-compartmental analysis (NCA) models for steady-state data assume equal dosing intervals (Tau) and that data is from a 'final' dose at steady state. These models support both rich and sparsely-sampled datasets (e.g., toxicokinetics).
conditions: Applicable when deriving exposure metrics from sparse or rich data for simulation validation or input.
Requires explicit definition of Tau for steady-state calculations.
required_inputs: Concentration-time data.
Dosing interval (Tau) for steady-state.
Infusion duration for constant infusion models.
limitations: Assumes steady state has been reached; does not model accumulation dynamics directly.
Sparse sampling may limit the resolution of terminal slope estimation.
downstream_use: Provides exposure metrics (AUC, Cmax) for comparison with simulated profiles or as inputs for PD modeling.

title: Documentation of Modeling Parameters and Assumptions
claim: All system-specific and drug-specific parameters must be clearly specified with their sources and justifications. Key model assumptions impacting application, including biological rationales and mathematical representations, must be explicitly stated. Procedures for assessing uncertainty (e.g., sensitivity analysis) must be provided.
conditions: Required for regulatory or scientific qualification of the simulation model.
Applies to both library models and custom-built models.
required_inputs: Table of parameters with values, units, and sources.
Justification for parameter selection.
Description of uncertainty assessment methods.
limitations: Does not validate the scientific correctness of the parameters, only their documentation.
Library model modifications must be explicitly justified.
downstream_use: Ensures traceability and reproducibility of the human simulation scenario.

title: Bias in Free-Concentration Scaling for PTA
claim: In the low-extraction binding scenarios studied in SUP013, back-calculating free exposure distributions from total concentrations with an average fu can misrepresent the free-exposure variance and bias extreme-quantile PTA/cutoff estimates; incorrectly adding fu variability can increase that bias. This is not a universal prohibition on modeling binding or a guaranteed bias direction for every drug.
conditions: Applies when PK/PD index is based on free drug (e.g., fAUC/MIC, fT>MIC).
Relevant when total concentration data is scaled by fu.
Bias magnitude depends on the true distribution of fu and the target PTA level.
required_inputs: Total concentration data.
fu distribution or scalar value.
PK/PD index definition.
limitations: In SUP013's specified binding/low-extraction simulations, scalar-fu back-calculation from total exposure misrepresented free-exposure variance and extreme-quantile PTA. Test applicability before transferring this limitation.
Incorrectly adding fu variability in the source's back-calculation scenarios increased bias; preserve any justified covariance instead of assuming independent binding draws.
downstream_use: Method qualification for PTA simulations; correction of historical PTA analyses.

title: Distinction Between Per-MIC PTA and MIC-Weighted CFR
claim: Per-MIC PTA requires a defined MIC grid and PK/PD target but does not require an observed MIC distribution. MIC-weighted CFR requires a specific organism population, MIC bins, frequencies, and denominator. These are distinct tasks with different input requirements.
conditions: Per-MIC PTA is a conditional probability given an MIC.
CFR is a population-weighted summary.
Do not infer a population distribution from a single MIC point.
required_inputs: For PTA: MIC value/grid, PK model, PD target.
For CFR: MIC distribution (bins, counts, denominator), PTA at each bin.
limitations: CFR is invalid if the MIC distribution is not representative of the target population.
Open-ended bins or omitted isolates must be handled explicitly.
downstream_use: Separate reporting of susceptibility-specific efficacy vs. population-level coverage.

title: Separation of Variability and Uncertainty in Simulations
claim: Between-unit variability (IIV) must be distinguished from parameter estimation uncertainty. A fitted parameter standard error is not an individual variability distribution. Human IIV cannot be inferred from animal data or parameter SEs without a stated basis.
conditions: When constructing Monte Carlo simulation inputs.
When translating animal PK to human scenarios.
When defining the 'probability' component of PTA.
required_inputs: Explicit definition of IIV distribution.
Explicit definition of parameter uncertainty (if propagated).
Source of variability estimates.
limitations: Group means do not provide individual trajectories.
Technical replicates do not increase biological n.
Animal variability does not automatically translate to human IIV.
downstream_use: Valid Monte Carlo simulation setup; interpretation of PTA confidence intervals.

title: Prospective Human PTA as Scenario-Based Simulation
claim: Human PTA simulations in this project are prospective scenarios based on PopPK models and assumed variability, not observations of the target drug in humans. They require explicit assumptions about human PK variability and PD targets. PTA is not a measure of clinical cure.
conditions: Target drug has no human PK/PD observations.
Human predictions are hypothetical.
PD targets must be qualified for human applicability.
Simulation must account for infection-related PK changes if relevant.
required_inputs: Qualified human PopPK model.
Qualified PD target with human applicability assessment.
Defined dosing scenarios.
Assumed human IIV.
limitations: Not validated against human data.
Sensitive to assumptions about human IIV and PD target transferability.
Does not prove clinical efficacy.
downstream_use: Dose regimen selection for clinical trials; PK/PD cutoff determination.

title: PD Target Definition and Applicability
claim: A PD target (PDT) must specify the effect (e.g., stasis, 1-log kill), index (e.g., fAUC/MIC), units, concentration basis (free/total), and exposure window. A target awaiting fitting is a planned output. A reported target from another context requires explicit applicability assessment before use in PTA.
conditions: Before using a PDT in PTA simulation.
When comparing indices (e.g., fAUC/MIC vs fT>MIC).
When translating animal-derived targets to human scenarios.
required_inputs: Defined effect and endpoint.
Index definition and units.
Free/total basis.
Source of target and its experimental context.
limitations: A target from one species or infection site may not apply to another.
Index ranking requires separated dose/frequency effects.
Do not borrow MICs or targets from other drugs.
downstream_use: Input for PTA simulation; qualification of PK/PD cutoff.

title: Categorical Distinction of Observation Statuses
claim: Observation statuses must be kept distinct: BLQ is not a measured zero; unresolved above-ULOQ is not an exact concentration at the upper limit; 'not sampled' is distinct from 'missing' or 'technical failure'. A stored numeric zero is a placeholder unless verified as a measured zero. EDA must retain these distinctions without collapsing mixed statuses.
conditions: Applicable during initial data inspection and descriptive EDA.
Applies to all concentration-time data regardless of species or route.
Prohibited: Imputing BLQ with zero or LLOQ/2; converting BLQ to missing; treating 'not sampled' as 'missing' without schedule evidence.
required_inputs: Original observation flags and recorded reasons.
Applicable LLOQ/ULOQ or microbial detection limits.
Actual vs. nominal time definitions.
Provenance of any numeric zeros (measured vs. placeholder).
limitations: EDA does not independently validate the assay or infer the missingness mechanism.
Unknown planned sampling is not evidence that a time was scheduled and missed.
Group summaries cannot reconstruct individual records; mixed statuses in pooled data must not be collapsed into one pure category.
downstream_use: Preserves raw data integrity for later NCA or compartmental modeling. Prevents bias introduced by arbitrary imputation. Enables correct identification of censored vs. missing data for likelihood-based modeling.
retrieval_keywords: BLQ, missing, not sampled, technical failure, above-range and assay qualification

title: Prohibition of Default Imputation and Silent Conversion
claim: BLQ data must not be imputed with zero or half-LLOQ by default. Silent conversion of BLQ to missing is prohibited. Substitution of BQL with LOQ/2 has been shown to introduce bias in parameter estimates. Omission of BQL data is also associated with substantial bias. The correct handling (e.g., likelihood-based) is a modeling decision, not an EDA transformation.
conditions: Applies to all EDA stages.
No pcVPC-driven deletion during EDA.
No covariate analysis activation in this assignment.
required_inputs: Raw concentration values.
Explicit BLQ flags.
LLOQ values.
limitations: Simulation results in source literature depend on tested model forms; do not impose a universal BQL method as project policy.
EDA does not fit models or determine the optimal likelihood method for BQL.
Target drug has NO human PK/PD observations; human methodological examples are not observations for the target drug.
downstream_use: Ensures that downstream model fitting receives raw, unaltered data with explicit censoring flags, allowing the modeler to apply appropriate likelihood methods (e.g., M3/M4) rather than relying on biased imputation.
retrieval_keywords: BLQ, missing, not sampled, technical failure, above-range and assay qualification

title: Analyte, Matrix, and Unit Definitions for Descriptive Data
claim: Concentration data must be labeled with the specific matrix (e.g., plasma, serum, tissue homogenate) and analyte identity (parent, metabolite, or specific component of a mixture). Units must specify mass/volume or mass/tissue-mass. Total and free bases are distinct; whole-lung homogenate is not equivalent to epithelial lining fluid (ELF).
conditions: Applicable when cataloging raw concentration-time data for EDA.
Requires explicit distinction between administered dose basis (e.g., salt vs. free base) and measured analyte.
Source-specific numbers (e.g., LLOQ) are not universal thresholds but define the assay's quantifiable range.
required_inputs: Provenance: Source ID and chunk ID for each data point.
Identity: Exact analyte or component identity versus total mixture, with matrix type.
Units: Explicit mass/volume (e.g., mg/L) or mass/tissue-mass (e.g., µg/g) with total/free basis.
Time: Documented time origin (e.g., dose start) and units.
limitations: Group means cannot be treated as individual trajectories.
Technical replicates do not increase biological n.
BLQ is not zero; missing/not-sampled/technical failure are distinct states.
Abstract-only evidence cannot support unreported method details.
downstream_use: Enables valid comparison of exposure metrics (AUC, Cmax) by ensuring denominator and basis consistency. Prevents invalid pooling of incompatible matrices or analytes.
retrieval_keywords: Dose/event/time, analyte, matrix, units and free/total concentration definitions attached to descriptive evidence

title: Bioanalytical Context and Assay Validity
claim: Reported concentrations depend on a defined assay with specific calibration ranges, LLOQ, and stability profiles. QC acceptance criteria (e.g., ±15% of nominal) and stability tests (freeze-thaw, bench-top) validate the data's reliability. Endogenous analytes require specific QC handling (spiked vs. unspiked) to ensure accuracy.
conditions: Applies when evaluating the quality and traceability of concentration data.
Requires knowledge of the assay method (e.g., LC-MS/MS) and matrix-specific validation.
Stability and recovery data must be available to interpret concentration changes over time.
required_inputs: Provenance: Reference to specific validation guidelines (e.g., ICH M10) or study-specific validation reports.
Identity: Assay method name and specific analyte measured.
Prerequisites: Documented LLOQ, ULOQ, and stability conditions (temperature, pH, time).
Missing-input gates: If assay validation details are absent, quantitative-reuse qualification is marked as unresolved; this does not establish invalid data or failed validation.
limitations: A source-reported result is not a new fitted result.
PDF text extraction does not validate table layout or figure accuracy.
Assay limitations (e.g., interference) must be retained in annotations.
downstream_use: Informs whether assay evidence supports quantitative reuse for NCA or compartmental modeling. If stability or selectivity documentation is absent, mark qualification as unresolved and flag dependent reuse for review; absence of documentation alone does not establish invalid data or failed validation.
retrieval_keywords: Dose/event/time, analyte, matrix, units and free/total concentration definitions attached to descriptive evidence

title: Free/Total Basis and Binding Definitions
claim: Free concentration, unbound fraction (fu), and bound fraction are distinct concepts. Percentage vs. fractional scales must be preserved. Directly measured unbound concentrations do not require fu for conversion. Binding data must specify the species, matrix, and experimental conditions (e.g., temperature, pH) under which it was measured.
conditions: Applies when distinguishing between total and unbound exposure.
Requires explicit labeling of whether a value is a measured concentration or a derived fraction.
Blood/plasma partitioning is only relevant if the task requires changing the concentration basis.
required_inputs: Provenance: Source of binding data (e.g., equilibrium dialysis vs. ultrafiltration).
Identity: Specific analyte and matrix for binding measurement.
Prerequisites: Clear distinction between 'free concentration' (mass/volume) and 'fu' (dimensionless fraction).
Missing-input gates: Ambiguous definitions (e.g., 'binding' without specifying free vs. bound) block downstream exposure-response analysis.
limitations: Do not apply fu_incubation corrections if CLint is already unbound; however, blood unbound fraction (fuB) remains a required factor in the well-stirred model equation.
Binding values are source-specific and not universal project policy.
Equilibrium dialysis may detect only specific components (e.g., PMB1) while ultrafiltration detects all, affecting comparability.
downstream_use: Allows correct calculation of unbound exposure metrics. Prevents double-correction errors in PK modeling.
retrieval_keywords: Dose/event/time, analyte, matrix, units and free/total concentration definitions attached to descriptive evidence

title: Dose Basis and Active Moiety Traceability
claim: Dose must be defined by its basis (salt vs. free base, active moiety) and unit (mg/animal vs. mg/kg). Administered dose must be distinguished from measured analyte, especially for prodrugs or mixtures. Dose normalization requires an interpretable denominator.
conditions: Applies when comparing PK across different studies or formulations.
Requires explicit conversion factors if dose basis differs from analyte basis.
Routine unit conversion does not authorize inventing new active-moiety conversions.
required_inputs: Provenance: Source of dose definition and conversion factors.
Identity: Active moiety name and administered form.
Prerequisites: Body weight data if mg/kg normalization is required.
Missing-input gates: If dose basis is ambiguous, comparison is blocked.
limitations: Group means are not individual trajectories.
Batch-to-batch variation in the composition of a multicomponent mixture can affect PK comparability.
Source-specific dose values are not universal.
downstream_use: Enables valid dose-normalized PK comparisons and exposure-response modeling.
retrieval_keywords: Dose/event/time, analyte, matrix, units and free/total concentration definitions attached to descriptive evidence

title: EDA Descriptive Calculations and Provenance
claim: EDA may execute descriptive formulas only when definitions are established, inputs are available, and no new scientific assumptions are introduced. Operations include unit conversion, dose normalization (using known nonzero dose), and response transformations (e.g., log10 of positive counts). Order of operations matters: mean(C_i/D_i) differs from mean(C_i)/mean(D_i). Dose normalization alone does not establish dose proportionality. Censoring is carried as a bound/interval, not an exact point.
conditions: Source summaries are retained without reconstructing unobserved individual values.
Zero-dose controls remain unnormalized.
No arbitrary constants are added to zero or censored counts.
Technical repeats do not increase biological n; pools remain pools.
required_inputs: Established formula definition and source.
Known, nonzero, compatible dose for normalization.
Verified quantitative measurements for maximums.
Stated denominator and unit basis for ratios.
limitations: EDA does not perform AUC integration, terminal-slope selection, or inferential uncertainty estimation.
Missing SD is not zero; unavailable SD is not imputed.
Group baselines do not create individual pairing.
downstream_use: Provides labeled, provenance-tracked descriptive inputs for later NCA or model fitting. Does not authorize model-based inference.
retrieval_keywords: Descriptive transformations versus model-dependent integration or inference

title: Residual Error Model Diagnostics and Definitions
claim: Residual error represents unexplained variability. Diagnostics must evaluate the fit of the residual error model using specific plots: DV vs IPRED/xPRED, |IWRES| vs IPRED/time, and Q-Q plots of random effects. Shrinkage measures the extent to which Empirical Bayes Estimates (EBE) depend on population parameters rather than individual data.
conditions: Applicable during model development and validation.
Requires individual predictions (IPRED) and weighted residuals (IWRES/xWRES).
Time should be evaluated as continuous time and time after dose.
required_inputs: Individual and population predictions.
Weighted residuals (conditional or simulation-based).
Random effects estimates (EBE).
Covariate data for residual diagnostics.
limitations: No single validation method is sufficient; multiple diagnostics are required.
Outliers must be distinguished from model misspecification; removal of outliers requires prespecified criteria and sensitivity analysis.
Shrinkage indicates limited information for individual parameters, affecting reliability of EBEs.
downstream_use: Use diagnostic plots to refine residual error structure (additive/proportional/combined); assess model adequacy; identify outliers for sensitivity analysis.
retrieval_keywords: Residual and censored observation models and structural/practical identifiability

title: External Validation and Simulation Purpose
claim: Model validation must be specific to the intended purpose. External validation uses data not used for model building. Simulations can be based on fixed-effect estimates (typical profile), uncertainty of fixed effects (covariate effects/precision), or between-subject variability (population range). Revalidation is required if the simulation purpose differs from the original model purpose.
conditions: Applicable when preparing a model for prospective prediction or regimen optimization.
Use when distinguishing between descriptive model fit and predictive performance.
required_inputs: Provenance: Separate testing dataset for external validation; simulation settings matching the specific question.
Units/Basis: Concentration-time profiles for typical individuals or population distributions.
Prerequisites: Model must be structurally and deterministically identifiable.
Missing-input gates: If no external data is available, external validation cannot be performed; internal validation only.
limitations: Internal validation (data splitting) may reduce power to detect covariates.
Simulations based on typical estimates do not represent mean predictions unless variability is included.
Source is nonbinding guidance; specific validation strategies are project-dependent.
downstream_use: Conduct external validation if data permits. Select simulation type (fixed-effect vs. variability-based) based on whether the goal is to illustrate typical behavior or population distribution.
retrieval_keywords: Residuals, VPC/pcVPC, convergence, uncertainty and external prediction diagnose different issues

title: Semimechanistic Model Structure for Biphasic Killing
claim: Biphasic time-kill curves (rapid initial killing followed by reduced killing rate) are effectively modeled by dividing the total bacterial population into two subpopulations: a growing drug-susceptible population and a resting insusceptible (persister) population. The drug effect is modeled as an increase in the killing rate of the susceptible state, often using an Emax model. This structure accounts for phenotypic switching rather than assuming a single homogeneous population.
conditions: Applicable when time-kill data shows a decline in killing rate over time not explained by drug degradation.
Requires frequent sampling to distinguish growth phases.
In vitro static or dynamic models; does not automatically imply in vivo efficacy.
required_inputs: Time-series CFU/ml data for control and treatment groups.
Measured drug concentration-time profiles (if dynamic model) or constant concentrations (if static).
MIC values for the specific strain/drug pair.
limitations: The 'persister' state is a phenotypic model construct; it does not prove genetic resistance.
Model predictability is limited to conditions similar to those studied.
Does not account for immune defense or host factors.
downstream_use: Use this structure to fit PK/PD models for drugs exhibiting biphasic killing. Do not assume this structure applies to drugs with monophasic killing or different resistance mechanisms without validation.
retrieval_keywords: Time-kill, regrowth and resistance mechanism interpretation

title: Regrowth Interpretation and Resistance Mechanism Ambiguity
claim: Regrowth after initial killing is a common observation in time-kill studies but does not uniquely identify the underlying resistance mechanism. It may result from the emergence of resistant subpopulations (genetic), phenotypic switching to a persister state, or drug depletion/degradation. In static models, regrowth can occur even at concentrations far exceeding clinically achievable levels, indicating that regrowth is not solely a function of sub-MIC exposure.
conditions: Applies to both static and dynamic in vitro PK/PD models.
Requires careful distinction between 'regrowth due to resistance' and 'regrowth due to drug loss'.
required_inputs: Control growth curves to establish baseline exponential growth.
Drug stability data to rule out degradation as the sole cause of regrowth.
Time-course data showing the transition from killing to regrowth.
limitations: Regrowth alone cannot distinguish between intrinsic, acquired, or adaptive resistance.
In vitro models lack immune system interactions, which may alter regrowth dynamics in vivo.
Abstract-only or partial data may obscure the specific mechanism driving regrowth.
downstream_use: Do not infer a specific genetic resistance mechanism solely from regrowth patterns. Use additional data (e.g., MIC shifts, genetic sequencing) to characterize resistance. Use regrowth data to parameterize models that include both susceptible and resistant/persister states.
retrieval_keywords: Time-kill, regrowth and resistance mechanism interpretation

title: Structured Population Models for Heterogeneous Resistance
claim: Physiologically Structured Population (PSP) models can describe resistance as a selection process based on heterogeneous binding affinities (e.g., K_D distributions) among cells. In this framework, resistance is defined by a critical affinity (K_Dcrit); bacteria with K_D > K_Dcrit survive and grow, while those with K_D < K_Dcrit are killed. This approach models adaptive resistance as a selection of pre-existing heterogeneity rather than a single-step mutation.
conditions: Applicable only when binding-affinity heterogeneity is a supported mechanistic hypothesis; selection of this model requires biological justification.
Requires assumptions about receptor turnover and binding equilibrium.
Static drug concentration assumption simplifies the model but may be violated if bacterial load clears drug.
required_inputs: Distribution of binding affinities (K_D) within the bacterial population.
Maximum efficacy and critical concentration parameters.
Time-kill data for strains with differing susceptibilities.
limitations: This is a specific mechanistic hypothesis (binding affinity selection); it does not apply to all resistance mechanisms (e.g., efflux pumps, enzymatic degradation).
Numeric parameters (e.g., K_Dcrit values) are specific to the studied strain/drug pair and cannot be reused.
Model assumes exponential growth of the resistant subpopulation.
downstream_use: Use PSP models when investigating adaptive resistance driven by molecular heterogeneity. Do not apply this specific mathematical framework to drugs with different mechanisms of action without re-deriving the structural assumptions.
retrieval_keywords: Time-kill, regrowth and resistance mechanism interpretation

title: Allometric Scaling: Inputs, Exponents, and Route Dependence
claim: Allometric scaling is an empirical method correlating physiological parameters with body size (Y = aW^b). For small molecules, human clearance prediction accuracy varies by elimination route: it is generally better for renally eliminated drugs but less accurate for hepatically eliminated drugs unless corrected by maximum life span (MLP) or brain weight (BRW). Optimal exponents are source-specific (e.g., 0.65-0.70 for small molecules, 0.75-0.80 for macro-molecules in cited studies) and not universal constants. Single-species scaling using monkey data often outperforms other species for small molecules.
conditions: Applicable when animal PK data is available for the target drug.
Requires qualified animal estimates for the exact parameter (CL or Vss) with provenance.
Species count and fitted R2 alone do not establish human predictivity; validation requires external evidence or specific method qualification.
Do not pool CL/F with absolute CL or Vz with Vss.
required_inputs: Qualified animal PK parameters (CL, Vss) with units and provenance.
Body weights for all species used in scaling.
Explicit method specification (e.g., simple allometry, MLP-corrected, BRW-corrected).
Justified species/parameter comparability.
limitations: Empirical nature means it does not account for mechanistic differences in metabolism between species.
Prediction error is higher for small molecules with complicated oxidative metabolic pathways and significant cross-species differences in hepatic metabolism.
A universal minimum species count is not established; species count is a data point, not a validation result.
Fixed exponents from literature are examples, not project policy.
downstream_use: Use to generate candidate human PK predictions for early decision-making. Flag predictions for hepatically eliminated small molecules as higher uncertainty. Do not use as a substitute for mechanistic understanding if IVIVE data is available and qualified.
retrieval_keywords: Allometry versus IVIVE: inputs, qualification and species limitations

title: IVIVE: Well-Stirred Model, Binding Corrections, and Interlaboratory Variability
claim: IVIVE predicts hepatic clearance (CLH) using the well-stirred model: CLH = [QH * (fu,B / fu,inc) * CLint] / [QH + (fu,B / fu,inc) * CLint]. Here, QH is liver blood flow, fu,B is fraction unbound in blood, and fu,inc is fraction unbound in incubation. In vitro CLint must be scaled to in vivo CLint using physiological factors (e.g., microsomal protein content, hepatocellularity) before applying the model. Interlaboratory variability in CLint measurements is significant (CVs up to 99.8%), and compounds with lower lipophilicity, lower intrinsic clearance, and lower protein binding tend to have more accurate predictions.
conditions: Applicable when in vitro intrinsic clearance (CLint) data is available from microsomes or hepatocytes.
Requires specific binding data (fu,B and fu,inc) and physiological scaling factors.
Method bias and uncertainty must be assessed for the intended chemical/mechanistic domain.
Human in vitro input permission is distinct from human PK holdout permission.
required_inputs: In vitro intrinsic clearance (CLint) with units and assay conditions.
Fraction unbound in blood (fu,B) and fraction unbound in incubation (fu,inc).
Physiological scaling factors (liver weight, microsomal protein content, hepatocellularity).
Liver blood flow (QH) value for the target species (human).
limitations: Systematic underprediction is common, particularly for high extraction ratio (ER) drugs.
Interlaboratory variability in CLint measurements propagates to prediction error.
Total systemic clearance cannot be derived solely from a hepatic component without evidence of other elimination pathways.
Assay conditions (e.g., shaking during incubation) can affect results; consistency is critical.
downstream_use: Use to generate candidate hepatic clearance predictions. Flag high-ER compounds as high uncertainty due to known underprediction bias. Do not use if binding data or scaling factors are missing or unqualified.
retrieval_keywords: Allometry versus IVIVE: inputs, qualification and species limitations

title: Method Selection and Validation Boundaries
claim: Allometry and IVIVE require different inputs and binding conventions. Allometry is empirical and relies on cross-species similarity; IVIVE is mechanistic and relies on in vitro metabolic stability. Neither method is universally superior. A calibrated one-/two-species approach has method-specific evidence, but this does not authorize arbitrary fixed exponents. A validated human prediction cannot be established solely from good animal regression fit (R2). Human predictions are prospective scenarios; generic published human methodological examples are not observations for the target drug.
conditions: Project must specify which method is being applied and why.
Method-specific correction factors or external calibration evidence must be justified.
Do not treat a project-designed summary as a quoted regulatory requirement.
required_inputs: Explicit method specification for the target drug.
Evidence of method applicability to the target drug's chemical/mechanistic domain.
Distinction between animal internal checks and human validation.
limitations: A calibration coefficient from one drug is not transferable to every drug.
Abstract-only material supports only what appears in the abstract.
PDF text extraction does not inspect figures or validate table layout.
downstream_use: Use to justify the selection of a translation method in the project plan. Document gaps in method qualification. Do not execute numerical workflows based on this card alone.
retrieval_keywords: Allometry versus IVIVE: inputs, qualification and species limitations

title: Distinction between Uncertainty and Variability in Translation
claim: Uncertainty represents limited knowledge of the system and decreases as information accumulates, whereas variability is a property of the system (e.g., genetic/environmental) that does not decrease with larger sample sizes. In scaling, the primary concern is often the inherent uncertainty of the scaling methodology rather than the variability of preclinical input data.
conditions: Applicable when predicting human PK parameters from animal data.
Requires distinguishing between the uncertainty of the point estimate and the population variability of the parameter.
required_inputs: Point estimates of animal PK parameters (e.g., CL, Vss).
Explicit definition of the scaling method used.
Data on the source of error: methodological uncertainty vs. biological variability.
limitations: Does not provide a universal method for quantifying uncertainty; requires case-specific assessment.
Misinterpretation of uncertainty distributions as population variability can lead to incorrect safety margins.
downstream_use: Use this distinction to correctly parameterize Monte Carlo simulations, ensuring that uncertainty distributions are not conflated with between-subject variability models.
retrieval_keywords: Animal parameter uncertainty, scaling-method discrepancy and prospective human uncertainty

title: Quantifying Scaling Uncertainty and Method Discrepancy
claim: Scaling method uncertainty is often represented by log-normal distributions (e.g., 95% probability within threefold of the point estimate). When multiple methods (e.g., allometry and IVIVE) yield different predictions, they should not be treated as independent samples of truth. Instead, discrepancies require investigation into the underlying reasons (e.g., compound-specific suitability), and consensus predictions may be formed by averaging samples from each method's uncertainty distribution.
conditions: Applicable when multiple scaling methods are available or when a single method's uncertainty is characterized by literature benchmarks (e.g., 66-94% accuracy within 2-3 fold).
Requires that the methods are not simply redundant but represent different mechanistic or empirical assumptions.
required_inputs: Point estimates from each scaling method.
Literature-based or empirically derived uncertainty ranges for each method.
Justification for combining methods (e.g., consensus) or selecting one over the other.
limitations: Literature benchmarks for method accuracy are based on historical datasets and may not apply to the specific compound class.
Assuming log-normality is a simplification; actual error distributions may differ.
Discrepancies between methods may indicate a fundamental model misspecification rather than just uncertainty.
downstream_use: Use to construct input distributions for prospective human simulations, ensuring that the spread reflects methodological uncertainty rather than just biological noise.
retrieval_keywords: Animal parameter uncertainty, scaling-method discrepancy and prospective human uncertainty

title: Model Evaluation and Reporting of Translation Uncertainty
claim: Model robustness must be assessed to characterize dependency on data, parameters, and assumptions. Model evaluation should include sensitivity analysis to expose how uncertainty propagates to human predictions. Reporting must include parameter estimates with their associated uncertainty and justify any deviations from the Model Analysis Plan (MAP).
conditions: Applies to all MIDD evidence generation.
Requires predefined technical criteria for model evaluation.
required_inputs: Documented assumptions and method specifications.
Sensitivity analysis results showing impact of parameter uncertainty on human predictions.
Comparison of model outcomes against technical criteria.
limitations: Does not define specific numerical thresholds for 'acceptable' uncertainty, leaving this to project-specific criteria.
External validation is encouraged but may not be available for novel compounds.
downstream_use: Use to structure the Model Analysis Report (MAR) and justify the confidence level of the prospective human dose prediction.
retrieval_keywords: Animal parameter uncertainty, scaling-method discrepancy and prospective human uncertainty

title: Project-Specific Translation Profile Requirements
claim: The project-specific translation profile (MP005) requires qualified animal estimates with provenance, compatible units, and justified species comparability. It mandates preflight checks to ensure unique qualified species counts and prohibits pooling incompatible parameters (e.g., CL/F with absolute CL). Unmet prerequisites block specific predictions.
conditions: Applies when using the project's defined empirical interspecies parameter extrapolation method.
Requires explicit method specification and project permission.
required_inputs: Qualified animal estimates for the exact parameter.
Body weights and units compatible with the scaling equation.
Explicit method specification and justification of comparability.
limitations: This is a project-local draft requirement, not an external scientific law.
Does not establish a universal minimum species count; this is assessed per parameter.
downstream_use: Use to gate the initiation of translation analysis and ensure data integrity before scaling calculations are performed.
retrieval_keywords: Animal parameter uncertainty, scaling-method discrepancy and prospective human uncertainty

title: Required Inputs for Prospective Human IV Simulation
claim: A prospective human IV concentration-time scenario requires a complete, accepted parameter set for a specific compartmental structure, explicit IV regimen details (dose, infusion duration), and an output time grid. Vss must not be silently substituted for Vc. Binding information is required if unbound concentrations are simulated.
conditions: Applicable when no human PK data exists for the target drug.
Requires qualified animal/in vitro parameters translated to human.
required_inputs: Accepted candidate model structure (e.g., 1- or 2-compartment).
Complete parameter set for that structure (CL, Vc, Q, Vp, etc.) with provenance.
IV regimen: dose amount, infusion duration, dosing interval.
Output time grid for simulation.
Explicit uncertainty/assumption treatment for each parameter.
limitations: A unique multi-compartment curve cannot be derived from CL and Vss alone; distribution parameters are required.
Measured human variability is not established; simulations reflect predicted uncertainty, not observed inter-individual variability.
downstream_use: Generate simulated concentration-time profiles for exposure-response analysis or PTA calculations, clearly labeled as prospective predictions.
retrieval_keywords: Required inputs and scenario status of prospective human regimen simulation

title: Uncertainty Quantification via Monte Carlo Simulation
claim: Uncertainty in human dose/exposure predictions should be quantified by integrating uncertainty from all parameter sources using Monte Carlo simulation. Parameters are assigned distributions (e.g., log-normal) rather than point estimates alone. This approach allows communication of the probability of achieving target exposures despite parameter uncertainty.
conditions: Applicable when point estimates are insufficient to convey risk.
Requires defined distributions for key PK/PD parameters (e.g., CL, Vss, KD, koff).
No correlations between parameters were assumed in the cited methodological example.
required_inputs: Point estimates for all PK/PD parameters.
Defined probability distributions (e.g., log-normal) for each uncertain parameter.
Number of Monte Carlo iterations (typically >1,000).
Target exposure metric (e.g., Cmax, AUC, or receptor occupancy threshold).
limitations: Methodological example from SUP011 is for a different drug; it does not provide target-drug parameter values.
Uncertainty in translation (species differences) is a major source of error; human PK uncertainty dominates if animal data is limited.
Does not validate the model; only quantifies uncertainty given the model structure.
downstream_use: Generate empirical distributions of predicted human dose or exposure to support risk assessment and decision-making under uncertainty.
retrieval_keywords: Required inputs and scenario status of prospective human regimen simulation

title: Per-MIC PTA Definition and Calculation Basis
claim: Probability of Target Attainment (PTA) is the probability that at least a specific value of a PK/PD target (PDT) is achieved at a certain MIC. It is calculated by simulating individual exposures (e.g., via Monte Carlo) and determining the proportion of simulated individuals whose exposure index (e.g., fAUC/MIC or %fT>MIC) meets or exceeds the target value for that specific MIC.
conditions: Requires a qualified PK model with explicit parameter/distribution assumptions.
Requires a qualified PD target with defined endpoint, index basis (free/total), and time window.
Applicable when prospective probability of target attainment is needed for specified regimens and susceptibility values.
Must separate uncertainty in parameter estimates from variability between individuals.
required_inputs: Qualified PK scenario with explicit parameter/distribution assumptions.
Qualified PD target with endpoint, index basis, and window.
Specified regimens and susceptibility values (MICs).
Explicit human-variability assumptions if human observations are unavailable.
limitations: PTA is not probability of clinical cure.
Does not establish observed human inter-individual variability (IIV) from animal IIV or parameter standard errors.
Cannot validate human PK/PD in the absence of independent human observations.
Abstract-only or partial excerpts do not support full methodological validation.
downstream_use: Use to determine if a specific dosing regimen achieves a predefined microbiological target for a given MIC, informing dose selection or breakpoint determination.
retrieval_keywords: Per-MIC PTA definition: exposure distribution, target, basis and window

title: Exposure Basis and Protein Binding Bias in PTA
claim: For antimicrobials, the active concentration is the free (unbound) plasma concentration. Computing PTA by scaling total plasma concentrations by an unbound fraction (fu) introduces bias because total concentrations are intrinsically more variable than free concentrations due to binding variability. This bias typically leads to underestimation of the PK/PD cutoff (critical MIC) and overestimation of the dose required to attain a targeted quantile. The bias is greater when the variability of fu is erroneously included in the scaling.
conditions: Applies when converting total measured concentrations to free concentrations for PTA calculation.
Bias direction and size depend on the modeled free/total distributions and assumptions about fu variability.
Specific bias magnitude is source-specific (e.g., greater for high binding or when fu variability is modeled).
required_inputs: Total plasma concentration data.
Unbound fraction (fu) value or distribution.
Knowledge of whether fu is treated as a scalar or a distribution in the simulation.
limitations: This is a methodological warning, not a universal project policy.
Specific bias values (e.g., -20.5%) are specific to the cited study's simulation parameters (fu=0.1, etc.).
Does not apply if free concentrations are measured directly or if fu is constant and known without error.
downstream_use: Guide the selection of input distributions for Monte Carlo simulations: prefer direct free concentration modeling or careful handling of fu variability to avoid biased PTA estimates.
retrieval_keywords: Per-MIC PTA definition: exposure distribution, target, basis and window

title: PTA Interpretation and Regulatory Thresholds
claim: A PTA of 90% is a common benchmark for PK/PD cutoff determination but is not a universal scientific or clinical sufficiency threshold. A PTA <90% may be acceptable if the dose required for >90% PTA is poorly tolerated, or if the infection type is less severe and few organisms have MICs at the upper end of the range. Sponsors must justify the acceptability of PTA <90% based on clinical context.
conditions: Applicable when interpreting PTA results for dose regimen selection or breakpoint setting.
Requires justification for deviating from the 90% benchmark.
Depends on the severity of infection and spontaneous resolution rates.
required_inputs: Calculated PTA values for relevant MICs.
Clinical context regarding infection severity and pathogen burden.
Tolerability data for doses required to achieve higher PTAs.
limitations: PTA is a simulation output, not a direct clinical outcome.
Clinical exposure-response (E-R) relationships are often difficult to establish due to confounding factors (host immunity, adjunctive treatments).
90% is a guideline suggestion, not an absolute biological law.
downstream_use: Inform regulatory submissions and dose selection discussions by justifying the chosen PTA threshold or explaining why a lower PTA is clinically acceptable.
retrieval_keywords: Per-MIC PTA definition: exposure distribution, target, basis and window

title: Experimental Unit Definition and Pseudoreplication
claim: The experimental unit is the smallest biological entity independently assigned to a treatment group. Treating technical replicates (e.g., multiple cells from one mouse) or sub-samples as independent units constitutes pseudoreplication, artificially inflating sample size and invalidating statistical inference.
conditions: Applicable when analyzing data with hierarchical structures (e.g., cells within animals, samples within cages).
Requires clear identification of the unit of randomization.
Applies to both destructive and longitudinal sampling designs.
required_inputs: Explicit definition of the experimental unit for each experiment.
Mapping of each observation to its specific experimental unit ID.
Information on whether units were independently randomized or nested.
limitations: Does not define the statistical model itself, only the unit of analysis.
Cannot resolve ambiguity if the original study design did not specify the unit of randomization.
Abstract-only sources may not provide sufficient detail to distinguish unit types.
downstream_use: Determines the correct denominator for n in statistical tests and guides the selection of mixed-effects models versus simple t-tests/ANOVA.
retrieval_keywords: Destructive samples, pooled specimens, biological and technical replicates: independent experimental units and descriptive uncertainty

title: Handling Pooled Specimens and Unknown Provenance
claim: When specimens are pooled or their origin is unknown, the true experimental unit cannot be reconstructed. If pool membership is unknown, the data cannot support inferential statistics about individual biological variability; such data should be treated as descriptive or excluded from unit-level inference.
conditions: Applies when individual animal IDs are missing or when samples are physically pooled before analysis.
Requires explicit documentation of pooling strategy if available.

Missing individual IDs prevent reconstruction of individual trajectories, but known treatment/time-group provenance can still support labelled aggregate or descriptive analysis. Record the experimental unit from the study design separately from the measurement or pool identity; a group or pooled sample is not automatically an independent experimental unit.
required_inputs: Metadata indicating whether samples are pooled or individual.
Provenance records linking observations to specific biological sources.
Documentation of any technical failures or censoring that might obscure unit identity.
limitations: Cannot recover lost individual-level data.
Does not provide a method to impute missing unit identities.
Pooled data may still be useful for descriptive summaries but not for estimating between-subject variance.
downstream_use: Blocks invented individual trajectories and unsupported inference about individual variability when specimen identity or pool membership is unknown. Preserves labelled aggregate summaries and population methods whose input, sampling and measurement assumptions are supported by the known design; inferential n and uncertainty require a justified unit structure.
retrieval_keywords: Destructive samples, pooled specimens, biological and technical replicates: independent experimental units and descriptive uncertainty

title: Chromatographic Calibration Curve Validation Criteria
claim: For chromatographic methods, the calibration curve must include a blank sample, a zero sample (blank spiked with internal standard), and at least 6 concentration levels of calibration standards (including LLOQ and ULOQ). Blank and zero samples are excluded from regression equation determination. Back-calculated concentrations must be within ±20% at LLOQ and ±15% at all other levels. At least 75% of calibration standards (minimum 6 levels) must meet these criteria. When replicates are used, at least 50% of standards at each concentration level must also meet the accuracy criterion. A failing calibration standard sample is rejected and the curve re-evaluated. For accuracy and precision validation runs, rejection of all replicates of either the LLOQ or ULOQ calibration standard requires rejection of that run, investigation of the failure, and method revision if necessary.
conditions: Applicable to chromatographic bioanalytical methods.
Calibration standards must be prepared in the same biological matrix as study samples.
Regression model and weighting must be defined in written procedures.
Freshly spiked standards required for at least one assessment; frozen standards allowed within stability period.
required_inputs: Calibration standard concentrations (nominal).
Analytical response data for blank, zero, and calibration standards.
Defined regression model and weighting scheme.
Internal standard identity and concentration.
limitations: Source-specific regulatory criteria; not universal project policy.
Does not define QC acceptance criteria (covered in separate section).
Does not address study-run acceptance logic beyond calibration curve failure.
Abstract-only or partial text may omit specific matrix effect handling details.
downstream_use: Use to validate if calibration data meets regulatory acceptance criteria for chromatographic assays. Reject runs if calibration curve fails acceptance criteria. Do not use for QC sample acceptance or study sample quantification logic.
retrieval_keywords: BLQ, missing, not sampled, technical failure, above-range and assay qualification

title: LBA Calibration Curve Validation Criteria
claim: For Ligand Binding Assays (LBA), the calibration curve requires at least 6 concentration levels (including LLOQ/ULOQ) plus a blank sample. Blank is excluded from parameter calculation. Anchor points (below LLOQ/above ULOQ) may be used for curve fitting but have no acceptance criteria. Back-calculated concentrations must be within ±25% at LLOQ/ULOQ and ±20% at other levels. At least 75% of calibration standards (excluding anchor points, min 6 levels) must meet criteria. Surrogate matrix use requires scientific justification and assessment of matrix effect/recovery differences.
conditions: Applicable to LBA methods.
Surrogate matrix use requires scientific justification and comparative assessment against authentic matrix.
4- or 5-parameter logistic models are typical; other models require justification.
Minimum 6 independent runs over several days required for validation.
required_inputs: Calibration standard concentrations (nominal).
Analytical response data for blank and calibration standards.
Justification for surrogate matrix use (if applicable).
