Data from at least 10 different donors for matrix effect assessment (LBA specific).
limitations: Source-specific regulatory criteria; not universal project policy.
Does not define QC acceptance criteria.
Does not address study-run acceptance logic beyond calibration curve failure.
Surrogate analyte approach requires response factor unity check; not covered in this specific calibration section.
downstream_use: Use to validate if calibration data meets regulatory acceptance criteria for LBA assays. Reject runs if calibration curve fails acceptance criteria. Do not use for QC sample acceptance or study sample quantification logic.
retrieval_keywords: BLQ, missing, not sampled, technical failure, above-range and assay qualification

title: Endpoint Independence from Terminal Slope Estimation
claim: Parameters such as Cmax, Tmax, AUClast, and AUMClast do not require Lambda Z estimation and remain reportable when terminal slope estimation fails. Conversely, parameters like AUCinf, Vz, CL, and MRTinf depend on Lambda Z; if Lambda Z is not estimable (e.g., due to insufficient points or non-negative slope), these parameters are omitted or flagged. CLss is a distinct estimand for steady-state data and does not rely on single-dose terminal slope.
conditions: Applicable when terminal phase data is insufficient for regression (e.g., <3 points for non-bolus, <2 for bolus) or slope is not negative.
Software automatically omits Lambda Z-dependent parameters and issues a warning.
required_inputs: Concentration-time data with clear Cmax and Tlast.
Dosing information (bolus vs. infusion) to determine point count requirements for Lambda Z.
limitations: AUClast is truncated at Tlast; it does not represent total exposure if elimination is incomplete.
Software defaults for point counts (e.g., 3 points) are algorithmic constraints, not universal scientific validity criteria.
downstream_use: Report observed exposure metrics (AUClast, Cmax) for PK/PD analysis when terminal phase is undefined. Do not impute or extrapolate CL/Vz without valid Lambda Z.
retrieval_keywords: NCA endpoints with unreliable terminal slope and sparse destructive sampling

title: Sparse Sampling Data Handling and Bias Conditions
claim: For sparse destructive sampling, Phoenix calculates PK parameters from a mean concentration curve derived from unique time points. The Phoenix sparse estimator generates unbiased estimates for batch designs only if equal sample sizes are present per time point; unequal n introduces bias in this specific implementation. Standard errors for AUC (SE_AUClast/SE_AUCall) are computed using linear trapezoidal rules and account for correlations from repeated sampling, but are not output if log trapezoidal rules are specified.
conditions: Data structure must support grouping by unique time points (nominal time recommended).
AUC calculation must use linear trapezoidal rules for SE_AUC computation to be valid.
Equal sample sizes per time point are required for unbiased parameter estimates in batch designs.
required_inputs: Individual subject data with time and concentration.
Subject IDs to calculate correlations for repeated sampling.
Explicit selection of linear trapezoidal rule for AUC calculation.
limitations: Nominal time grouping is a software recommendation for sparse analysis, not a universal substitution rule for actual times.
SE_AUC calculations depend on AUC being a linear combination of mean concentrations; invalid for log-trapezoidal methods.
Missing data in the dataset prevents unbiased estimates in sparse routines.
downstream_use: Use mean-curve parameters for group-level PK characterization. Verify design balance (equal n) before interpreting sparse PK estimates. Do not use log-trapezoidal AUC if SE_AUC is required.
retrieval_keywords: NCA endpoints with unreliable terminal slope and sparse destructive sampling

title: NCA Clearance and Volume Definitions (CL, CL/F, Vss, Vz)
claim: Total body clearance (CL) is calculated as Dose/AUCINF for IV dosing. For extravascular dosing, apparent clearance (CL/F) is used because F cannot be estimated. Volume of distribution at steady state (Vss) is computed as MRTINF * CL (or CLss) and is NOT computed for extravascular dosing because MRTINF includes mean input time. Volume of distribution based on terminal phase (Vz) is Dose/[Lambda_z * AUCINF]; for extravascular dosing, this is effectively Vz/F. Lambda_z is estimated by linear regression of log concentration (Y) on time (X).
conditions: Vss is only valid for IV Bolus and Infusion models.
For infusion models, MRTINF = (AUMCINF/AUCINF) - (Tinf/2). Do not subtract Tinf/2 again when calculating Vss.
For extravascular models (e.g., oral), parameters are apparent (CL/F, Vz/F).
Lambda_z estimation requires sufficient points in the terminal log-linear phase.
required_inputs: Dose (amount)
Concentration-time data (plasma/serum)
AUCINF (extrapolated to infinity)
AUMCINF (extrapolated to infinity)
Lambda_z (terminal slope)
Tinf (infusion duration, if applicable)
limitations: Vss cannot be calculated for extravascular data using standard NCA formulas due to absorption phase influence on MRT.
CL/F and Vz/F are not true physiological parameters but apparent values dependent on F.
NCA parameters assume linear kinetics unless specified otherwise; they do not describe time-varying clearance.
downstream_use: Use CL/CL/F for exposure-response analysis and dose adjustment. Use Vss for understanding tissue distribution extent in IV studies. Use Vz for terminal half-life interpretation. Do not mix apparent and absolute parameters in the same model without explicit F assumptions.
retrieval_keywords: CL, CL/F, Vss, Vz and Vc definitions and conditions

title: Compartmental Model Parameters: Central Volume (Vc) and Flows
claim: In compartmental modeling (e.g., Phoenix NLME), the central compartment is defined by a volume parameter (V) and concentration (C). The default elimination flow from the central compartment is parameterized as Clearance (CL). Inter-compartmental flows between central and peripheral compartments are parameterized as inter-compartmental clearance (Q). Vc is the volume of the central compartment and is distinct from NCA Vz or Vss. In 'Macro' models, concentration is modeled directly using a 'stripping dose' to derive volume, whereas 'Clearance' models use differential equations with explicit CL and Q parameters.
conditions: Vc is a structural parameter in compartmental models, not an NCA output.
In Clearance models, CL is a primary parameter; in Macro models, CL is derived.
Only one central compartment is allowed if microconstants are used.
Concentration parameters (C) are derived from Amount (A) and Volume (V) in amount-based models.
required_inputs: Model structure definition (number of compartments)
Parameterization choice (Clearance vs. Macro/Micro)
Observed concentration data
Dosing events (amount and time)
limitations: Vc is model-dependent and not directly comparable to NCA Vz or Vss without conversion.
Software-specific conventions (e.g., Phoenix NLME) dictate parameter names (CL, Q, V) and default flows.
Identifiability of Vc depends on the richness of the data and model structure.
downstream_use: Use Vc and CL/Q parameters for mechanistic PK modeling, simulation of concentration-time profiles, and covariate analysis. Do not use Vc as a substitute for Vss in steady-state interpretation without model validation.
retrieval_keywords: CL, CL/F, Vss, Vz and Vc definitions and conditions

title: Structural vs. Practical Identifiability and FIM Diagnostics
claim: Global structural identifiability means unique parameter solutions given ideal input-output data; local structural identifiability can allow finitely many alternatives. The source examines continuity and limiting behavior of the FIM determinant as diagnostic conditions in its fixed- and mixed-effects examples. A full-rank local FIM or these diagnostic conditions do not by themselves prove global structural uniqueness. Practical identifiability depends on imperfect data and study design. When the information-matrix approximation is applicable and the FIM is nonsingular, diagonal elements of its inverse provide approximate parameter variances and their square roots provide approximate standard errors; these are not guaranteed achieved precision.
conditions: Applicable to fixed- and mixed-effects PK/PD models.
Requires a defined design (time points) and parameter set.
Assumes the model structure is fixed during assessment.
required_inputs: Model structure (fixed and random effects).
Design variables (sampling times).
Residual error model specification.
Software capable of computing FIM or optimal design metrics (e.g., PFIM, PopED).
limitations: FIM diagnostics are local and design-specific; they do not prove global identifiability across all possible designs.
Numerical accuracy issues can cause unidentifiable models to show small positive determinants instead of zero.
Random effects identifiability does not always mirror fixed effects identifiability.
This is a diagnostic tool, not a proof of scientific validity or model correctness.
downstream_use: Use to screen candidate models for structural identifiability before data collection. Use to evaluate if a proposed sampling schedule provides sufficient information (practical identifiability) to estimate parameters with acceptable precision.
retrieval_keywords: Residual and censored observation models and structural/practical identifiability

title: Handling BQL Data: Likelihood-Based Methods (M2/M3) vs. Substitution
claim: Handling Below Limit of Quantification (BQL) data by omission or substitution (e.g., LOQ/2) can introduce bias in parameter estimates. M2 applies conditional likelihood to observations above LOQ, conditional on their being above LOQ. M3 simultaneously models quantitative observations and the probability that censored observations are below LOQ. In NONMEM VI, M2 uses YLO functionality, and M3 uses F_FLAG. In the source simulations, M2 reduced bias relative to omission but often retained unsatisfactory bias; M3 performed best among the investigated methods, with runtime and convergence tradeoffs. These findings do not guarantee unbiased estimates for other models or designs.
conditions: Applicable when data are censored (BQL) in absorption or elimination phases.
Requires software supporting likelihood-based censoring (e.g., NONMEM VI with LAPLACIAN or specific flags).
Results are conditional on the specific simulation models and censoring patterns tested in the source.
required_inputs: Concentration data with explicit BQL flags or values.
LOQ value.
Software implementation of M2 (YLO) or M3 (F_FLAG) methods.
Residual error model compatible with the chosen likelihood approach.
limitations: M2/M3 performance is conditional on the tested model forms; not a universal guarantee of unbiasedness for all study designs.
Substitution methods (LOQ/2) are crude and suboptimal but may be used if likelihood methods are computationally infeasible.
A successful optimizer run does not validate the model; diagnostic checks (e.g., VPCs for BQL fraction) are required.
Does not address structural identifiability issues unrelated to censoring.
downstream_use: Select M3 (or M2) as the primary method for handling BQL data in population PK modeling. Use VPCs that include BQL fraction diagnostics to validate the censoring model. Avoid omission or simple substitution unless justified by computational constraints and validated via simulation-based diagnostics.
retrieval_keywords: Residual and censored observation models and structural/practical identifiability

title: Shrinkage Impact on Individual vs. Simulation-Based Diagnostics
claim: High standard deviation-based shrinkage (typically >20-30%) causes individual parameters (IPRED, IWRES) and Empirical Bayes Estimates (EBEs) to shrink toward population means, rendering individual-level diagnostic plots uninformative and obscuring covariate correlations. However, simulation-based diagnostics like VPC, pcVPC, NPC, and NPDE are not affected by shrinkage in the same manner and remain informative. Model selection should not be based solely on shrinkage; rather, shrinkage limits the reliability of individual post-hoc estimates for exposure-response analysis.
conditions: Applicable when evaluating mixed-effects models with sparse data or few observations per individual.
Shrinkage is calculated as SD-based; values >20-30% indicate high shrinkage.
Individual plots become less informative but are not inherently invalid if interpreted with caution regarding their reduced power.
required_inputs: Estimated individual parameters (IPRED, IWRES) and population predictions (PRED).
Calculated shrinkage values for random effects.
Simulated datasets for VPC/pcVPC generation.
limitations: High shrinkage does not invalidate the model structure but limits the utility of individual-level diagnostics.
Shrinkage alone is not a criterion for model rejection; it indicates reduced information content in individual estimates.
External source status: FDA guidance is nonbinding; these are contextual guidelines, not mandatory project rules.
downstream_use: Guide the selection of diagnostic tools: rely on simulation-based checks (VPC/pcVPC) when shrinkage is high; use individual diagnostics only when shrinkage is low or for specific covariate screening where shrinkage impact is assessed.
retrieval_keywords: Residuals, VPC/pcVPC, convergence, uncertainty and external prediction diagnose different issues

title: pcVPC Methodology and Censored Data Handling
claim: Prediction-Corrected VPCs (pcVPC) normalize observed and simulated data by the median typical population prediction within bins to remove variability caused by independent variables (e.g., dose, covariates), enhancing the diagnosis of random effects misspecification. For censored data (BLQ), pcVPCs cannot use standard censoring methods because rank order is lost after correction. Instead, censored observations must be omitted from both observed and simulated datasets before calculating statistics, making the pcVPC interpretation heavily dependent on the model's accurate prediction of censoring frequency (e.g., %BLQ vs. time).
conditions: Applicable when independent variables vary within bins, making traditional VPCs uninformative.
Requires accurate modeling of the censoring mechanism (e.g., M3 method) to ensure the pcVPC reflects true model performance.
Log-transformed dependent variables require specific adjustment in the prediction correction formula.
required_inputs: Typical population predictions (PRED) for each observation.
Median PRED for each bin of independent variables.
Simulated datasets reflecting the original design.
Censoring model parameters (if BLQ present).
limitations: pcVPC interpretation is invalid if the model poorly predicts the censoring frequency.
Variability-corrected VPCs (pvcVPC) showed no significant advantage over pcVPCs in source examples.
This is a diagnostic method, not proof of external predictive validity.
downstream_use: Use pcVPC to diagnose structural and random effect misspecification in complex designs; separately assess censoring model adequacy via BLQ frequency plots before trusting pcVPC results.
retrieval_keywords: Residuals, VPC/pcVPC, convergence, uncertainty and external prediction diagnose different issues

title: Baseline vs. Control and Free-Drug Conversion for PK/PD Linkage
claim: In PK/PD modeling, the 'baseline' is the bacterial burden at the start of treatment (time 0), which serves as the stasis reference, distinct from the untreated control group measured at the end of the observation window. To link exposure to effect, total plasma concentrations must be converted to unbound (free) concentrations using experimentally determined protein binding data. The unbound fraction (fu) is a critical parameter; if binding is concentration-independent, a single fu value is applied to total AUC/Cmax to derive fAUC/fCmax for correlation with MIC.
conditions: Applicable when analyzing in vivo infection model data where total drug concentrations are measured.
Requires determination of protein binding in the relevant matrix (e.g., plasma) across the concentration range observed.
Source-specific: In the cited study, binding was constant over the range, allowing a single fu value (0.086) to be used.
required_inputs: Total plasma concentration-time data.
Protein binding data (percentage bound or fu) in the relevant matrix.
Bacterial burden at time 0 (baseline/stasis value).
Bacterial burden at end of treatment window (treated and untreated controls).
MIC values for the specific strains tested.
limitations: Protein binding in animal models (e.g., mice) may differ significantly from humans; direct translation of fu is invalid without human-specific binding data.
If binding is concentration-dependent, a single fu is insufficient; a model of binding kinetics is required.
Group mean baseline values cannot be paired with individual subject trajectories in destructive sampling designs.
downstream_use: Calculate fAUC/MIC, fCmax/MIC, or fT>MIC indices. Use these free-drug indices to fit exposure-response models (e.g., inhibitory sigmoid Emax) to determine PDTs.
retrieval_keywords: Exposure-response linkage to strain/MIC, effect window, baseline, assay and matrix

title: Index Selection and PDT Definition via Time-Kill and In Vivo Models
claim: Time-kill studies provide preliminary insight into the PK/PD index (e.g., AUC/MIC vs. T>MIC) most likely to predict efficacy, but are not a universal mandatory prerequisite for all linkage analyses if in vivo data is sufficient. Nonclinical PD targets (PDTs) are defined as the exposure levels associated with specific bacterial effects: net stasis (0 log10 drop), 1 log10 drop, and 2 log10 drop. The selection of the appropriate index (AUC/MIC, Cmax/MIC, or T>MIC) is guided by the bactericidal pattern observed in time-kill studies (concentration-dependent vs. time-dependent).
conditions: Applicable for defining the primary PK/PD index for subsequent PTA/CFR analysis.

For an MIC-normalized index, use a strain-matched MIC with method, units and measurement context. Use time-kill data to characterize temporal killing or inform index choice when that question requires it; EMA antimicrobial-development guidance separately recommends time-kill studies and relevant MIC distributions for the development package. A full MIC distribution is not required solely to normalize a single-strain index.
PDTs must be defined for specific pathogens or groups of pathogens relevant to the indication.
required_inputs: Time-kill study data showing concentration-dependent or time-dependent killing patterns.
MIC distributions for relevant pathogens.
In vivo efficacy data (CFU counts) at various exposure levels.
Definition of the observation window for effect measurement.
limitations: Time-kill data informs index choice but does not replace the need for in vivo validation of the index.
PDTs derived from animal models require translation to human exposure; species differences in PK and binding must be accounted for.
A PDT is not automatically applicable to all strains; strain-specific MICs and intrinsic resistance mechanisms (e.g., capsule) may alter maximal effect (Emax).
downstream_use: Select the primary PK/PD index for PTA modeling. Define specific PDT values (e.g., fAUC/MIC for stasis) to be used as targets in Monte Carlo simulations.
retrieval_keywords: Exposure-response linkage to strain/MIC, effect window, baseline, assay and matrix

title: Distinction between Index Discrimination and Target Estimation
claim: Cross-index discrimination and within-index target estimation are separate analytical objectives. Index ranking requires a design that separates correlated indices (e.g., varying frequency vs. total dose) and matched exposure-response data; if the design cannot distinguish indices, ranking remains unresolved. Target estimation for a specific index requires defined effect endpoints and matched data, but a reported target from literature does not require raw response data for its registration. A target awaiting estimation is a deferred output, not missing data.
conditions: Applicable when the project requests either index comparison or PD target estimation.
For ranking: The experimental design must vary dosing frequency/interval independently of total dose to separate correlated indices.
For target estimation: Requires source-supported same-drug target or matched exposure-response data.
Project-specific: MAIN.MP009 explicitly separates 'exposure summaries', 'index ranking', and 'PD target tasks'.
required_inputs: Defined PD endpoint, baseline/comparator, and response window.
Traceable mapping between regimen, exposure, and biological response.
For ranking: Regimens that vary frequency/interval to decouple AUC, Cmax, and T>MIC.
For target: Specific effect definition (e.g., stasis, 1-log kill) and index definition (units, free/total basis).
limitations: Exposure values alone do not establish a 'best' index; matched PD data are required.
A winning index from one study is not automatically applicable to another compound, organism, endpoint or experimental context.
Project drafts (IN_MAIN:0045) state that missing PD matching blocks ranking but not independent PK/exposure summaries.
Abstract-only evidence cannot support unreported methods or specific numeric targets.
downstream_use: Determines whether to proceed with index ranking (if design allows) or defer to a single prespecified index for target estimation. Guides the distinction between registering a literature-reported target versus initiating a new fitting workflow.
retrieval_keywords: Dose fractionation: cross-index discrimination versus within-index target fitting

title: Nonlinear PK and Exposure Equivalence in Dose Fractionation
claim: Comparable total daily doses do not guarantee equal AUC or exposure profiles under nonlinear PK conditions. Nonlinear PK examples demonstrate that nonlinear PK behavior can confound interpretation if exposure is not directly measured or qualified. Therefore, dose fractionation comparisons must rely on qualified actual exposures (e.g., measured fAUC) rather than assuming equivalence based on total dose. Index conclusions are also dependent on treatment duration and response endpoint.
conditions: Applicable when PK is nonlinear or when comparing regimens with different frequencies.
Requires direct measurement or qualified modeling of exposure (AUC, Cmax) for each regimen.
Project-specific: IN_EDA:0047 notes that human concentration-time outputs are prospective scenarios, not observations.
External evidence: SUP007 notes that nonlinear PK confounded interpretation in prior studies lacking PK data.
required_inputs: Measured or modeled exposure parameters (AUC, Cmax) for each specific regimen.
Confirmation of PK linearity or explicit handling of nonlinearity.
Source-linked PK observations relevant to the specific PD regimens.
Project-specific: Retain scenario dose/basis and concentration basis without inserting typical values (IN_EDA:0047).
limitations: Total dose equivalence is insufficient for exposure equivalence in nonlinear PK.
Index superiority is context-dependent (e.g., site-specific differences in SUP007).
Project drafts do not authorize numerical fitting or model qualification in this stage; they only define data requirements.
Human IIV cannot be inferred from animal variability or parameter SEs.
downstream_use: Guides the selection of exposure metrics for PD analysis. If exposure equivalence cannot be established due to nonlinear PK or lack of data, index ranking is marked unresolved, and only independent exposure summaries are retained.
retrieval_keywords: Dose fractionation: cross-index discrimination versus within-index target fitting

title: Defining Effect Targets via Baseline (E0) and Model Parameters
claim: PK/PD targets (stasis, log-kill) are derived from the inhibitory sigmoid Emax model parameters (E0, Emax, EC50, Hill coefficient). 'Stasis' is defined as the exposure where the bacterial burden at 24h equals the burden at the start of treatment (B0). A 1-log or 2-log kill target is calculated as B0 minus 1 or 2 log10 CFU. E0 is the model parameter representing the effect in the absence of drug. Reachability of a target depends on whether the fitted response range (E0 - Emax) covers the target value (B0 - k); do not infer reachability from Emax < k alone.
conditions: Applicable when fitting dose-response data to an Emax model.
Requires precise measurement of bacterial burden at time 0 (B0) and at the end of treatment, distinguishing these observations from the fitted model parameter E0.
Source-specific: E0 is the model parameter representing the effect in the absence of drug. B0 is the mean log10 CFU/thigh at 0h in untreated controls (baseline burden).
required_inputs: Provenance: Untreated control bacterial counts at t=0 (baseline) and t=end.
Units: log10 CFU per unit (e.g., CFU/thigh).
Prerequisites: Fitted Emax model parameters (E0, Emax, EC50, Hill coefficient).
limitations: A target is 'not achieved' if the required exposure exceeds the maximum tolerated dose; this does not prove the effect is biologically impossible at higher exposures.
B0 must be measured, not assumed to be the inoculum size if growth occurred in controls. E0 is a fitted parameter, not a direct measurement.
Do not substitute total drug concentration for free drug (fAUC) without verified binding data.
downstream_use: Calculate specific fAUC/MIC or fCmax/MIC values required to achieve stasis or specific log-kill reductions for regimen design.
retrieval_keywords: Stasis, 1-log and 2-log kill targets depend on baseline, time, endpoint and censoring

title: Handling Bacterial Count Censoring and Growth Rate Estimation
claim: Bacterial counts below the assay's limit of detection (e.g., 100 CFU/mL) are censored data, not zero. For quantitative model estimation use a justified censor-aware method; descriptive plots retain <LOD bounds and counts rather than zero. The cited study used a censor-aware likelihood for bacterial counts, distinct from drug-concentration BLQ handling. Growth rates (ψ) are estimated from the slope of the natural logarithm of CFU vs. time (ln(N) vs. t) in the absence of drug or at low concentrations. If fitting on log10 CFU, convert using ψ = ln(10) × slope_log10. In the cited study, the geometric mean of zero-hour measurements was used for N0. Other studies retain actual replicate/time provenance and justify their baseline method.
conditions: Applicable to time-kill curve analysis where counts fall below the detection limit.
Requires explicit definition of the limit of detection (LOD) for the specific assay.
Source-specific: LOD was 100 CFU/mL in the cited gonococcal study.
required_inputs: Provenance: Raw colony counts and dilution factors.
Units: CFU/mL.
Defined assay LOD and censor flags; a justified censor-aware observation model is additionally needed for quantitative fitting, while bounded descriptive displays may remain possible.
Data: Time-series viable counts (CFU/mL) and corresponding time points.
limitations: Do not impute censored bacterial counts as zero or exclude them without statistical adjustment.
Growth rate estimation assumes exponential growth/death; deviations require model adjustment.
This method applies to bacterial burden data, not drug concentration data.
Ensure correct log-base conversion (ln vs log10) to avoid factor-of-2.3 error in ψ.
downstream_use: Accurate estimation of net bacterial growth rates (ψ) for input into PK/PD models (e.g., Regoes model).
retrieval_keywords: Stasis, 1-log and 2-log kill targets depend on baseline, time, endpoint and censoring, natural log slope, ln(10) conversion, geometric mean N0

title: Verified Well-Stirred Model Equation and Binding Correction Logic
claim: The hepatic clearance (CLH) is calculated using the well-stirred model: CLH = [QH * (fu,B / fu,inc) * CLint] / [QH + (fu,B / fu,inc) * CLint]. In this formulation, CLint represents the scaled apparent intrinsic clearance. The term (fu,B / fu,inc) serves as the binding correction factor. If CLint is already reported as unbound intrinsic clearance (CLint,u), the fu,inc correction is already embedded; in this case, the effective intrinsic clearance term becomes A = fu,B * CLint,u, and applying the full (fu,B / fu,inc) ratio again would constitute a double-correction error. The equation structure must be preserved exactly as verified in the source MathML to prevent algebraic misinterpretation.
conditions: Applicable when using the well-stirred model for hepatic clearance prediction.
Requires explicit identification of whether the input CLint is apparent (total) or unbound.
Requires matched units for QH (liver blood flow) and CLint (typically mL/min/kg or mL/min).
Requires distinct values for fu,B (fraction unbound in blood) and fu,inc (fraction unbound in incubation matrix).
required_inputs: Scaled apparent intrinsic clearance (CLint) with units.
Fraction unbound in blood (fu,B).
Fraction unbound in incubation (fu,inc).
Liver blood flow (QH) with units.
Explicit flag indicating if CLint is already unbound (CLint,u) to bypass fu,inc correction.
limitations: The model assumes well-stirred hepatic disposition; it may not apply to parallel-tube or dispersion models.
Does not account for active uptake/efflux transporters unless explicitly modeled.
Source-specific values for QH and scaling factors are not universal constants.
Abstract-only or partial excerpts do not validate the specific numerical values used in the source study.
downstream_use: Calculate predicted human hepatic clearance (CLH) for prospective scenario modeling. Use the result to assess feasibility of dosing regimens or to compare against observed human data if available (noting target drug has no human PK observations).
retrieval_keywords: Binding, blood/plasma, apparent versus unbound intrinsic clearance and IVIVE scaling

title: IVIVE Scaling Inputs and Interlaboratory Variability Constraints
claim: In vitro intrinsic clearance (CLint) values exhibit significant interlaboratory variability, with coefficients of variation (CVs) increasing with CLint magnitude. This variability stems from differences in experimental procedures (e.g., shaking, incubation conditions) and biological scaling factors. Consequently, IVIVE predictions are subject to systematic underprediction, particularly for high-extraction ratio (ER) drugs. The scaling process involves converting in vitro CLint to in vivo CLint using physiological factors (e.g., microsomal protein per gram liver, hepatocellularity). These scaling factors are not universal constants and must be sourced from specific, validated references.
conditions: Applicable when translating in vitro metabolic stability data to in vivo clearance.
Requires knowledge of the specific in vitro system (microsomes vs. hepatocytes) and donor pool characteristics.
Requires awareness of the source of scaling factors (physiological vs. empirical/regression-based).
required_inputs: In vitro CLint data with associated experimental conditions.
Physiological scaling factors (e.g., MPPGL, hepatocellularity) with provenance.
Information on the specific assay protocol (e.g., shaking speed, temperature) to assess comparability.
Data on the number of donors and pooling strategy used in the source study.
limitations: Interlaboratory variability means a single CLint value may not be representative of the population.
Systematic underprediction bias is documented for high-CLint compounds; predictions may be inaccurate.
Source-specific scaling factors cannot be assumed to apply to the target drug without verification.
The method cannot predict non-metabolic clearance pathways (e.g., renal, biliary) unless explicitly included.
downstream_use: Assess the uncertainty and reliability of the predicted CLH. Flag predictions derived from high-CLint data as having higher uncertainty due to documented underprediction bias. Use this to inform sensitivity analysis ranges in human simulation.
retrieval_keywords: Binding, blood/plasma, apparent versus unbound intrinsic clearance and IVIVE scaling

title: Interpretation of Renal Clearance and Urinary Recovery
claim: Renal clearance (CLr) is calculated as the amount excreted unchanged in urine (Ae) divided by the plasma AUC over the same time interval. Low urinary recovery of unchanged drug does not definitively exclude renal contribution to total clearance if the assay lacks specificity for unchanged analyte, if the collection interval is incomplete, or if systemic dose context is missing.
conditions: Applicable when assessing the contribution of renal vs. nonrenal pathways to total clearance.
Requires paired plasma and urine data from the same subject over identical time intervals.
Requires validated assay specificity for the unchanged analyte to distinguish from metabolites.
required_inputs: Plasma concentration-time data for AUC calculation.
Urine concentration and volume data for Ae calculation.
Assay validation data confirming specificity for unchanged drug.
Complete urine collection intervals matching plasma sampling windows.
limitations: Low recovery of unchanged drug in urine does not prove absence of renal elimination if metabolites are not accounted for or if assay specificity is poor.
A low urinary recovery result from one compound or study is not a universal renal-clearance rule.
Renal insufficiency models in animals may not directly translate to human dose adjustment recommendations without clinical validation.
downstream_use: Use to determine if renal function is a significant covariate for clearance. If CLr is negligible relative to total CL, renal dose adjustment may not be required, but this must be confirmed with human data.
retrieval_keywords: Renal/nonrenal clearance, nonlinear elimination, formulation and route limits

title: Nonlinear Elimination and Mean Residence Time (MRT) Interpretation
claim: In systems with Michaelis-Menten (nonlinear) elimination, the standard moment analysis calculation of MRT (AUMC/AUC) does not equal the true Mean Residence Time. For these systems, Dose/AUC represents a time-average clearance, and the true MRT is a function of the steady-state volume of distribution and this time-average clearance. AUMC/AUC is numerically computable but its interpretation as MRT fails under nonlinear conditions.
conditions: Applicable when drug elimination follows Michaelis-Menten kinetics (capacity-limited saturable elimination).
Requires IV administration into a one- or two-compartment system for the cited derivation.
Not applicable to linear first-order elimination where AUMC/AUC is a valid MRT estimate.
required_inputs: Concentration-time data demonstrating nonlinear elimination.
Dose information.
AUC and AUMC calculations (for comparison/contrast).
Steady-state volume of distribution (Vss) if available.
limitations: REF_014 is abstract-only; detailed nonlinear formulas are not fully extracted.
The distinction between 'true MRT' and 'moment MRT' is specific to the theoretical framework of the cited study.
This does not prohibit descriptive AUC calculation, but warns against misinterpreting AUMC/AUC as MRT in nonlinear contexts.
downstream_use: Use to select appropriate PK parameters for nonlinear drugs. Avoid using AUMC/AUC as a proxy for MRT in nonlinear models; prefer Dose/AUC for clearance estimation and specific nonlinear MRT derivations if available.
retrieval_keywords: Renal/nonrenal clearance, nonlinear elimination, formulation and route limits

title: Simulation Types: Typical vs. Mean vs. Uncertainty
claim: Simulations based on fixed-effect estimates illustrate the profile for a typical individual, which generally differs from the population mean prediction. Mean latent-population predictions average over the specified between-subject parameter and relevant covariate distributions, by simulation or suitable integration; measurement residual error is conditional on the requested observed-data estimand. Parameter uncertainty simulations represent uncertainty in estimated parameters and resulting exposures or covariate effects, while BSV simulations describe the distribution of individual predictions.
conditions: Applicable when defining simulation objectives for human PK/PD.
Typical simulations use only fixed-effect parameters.
BSV simulations require random effects; residual error models are required only when predicting observed concentrations.
Uncertainty simulations require estimates of parameter precision (e.g., bootstrap, standard errors).
required_inputs: Fixed-effect parameter estimates (typical values).
Between-subject variability (BSV) estimates (variance/covariance of random effects).
Residual error model parameters.
Parameter uncertainty estimates (e.g., covariance matrix of fixed effects).
limitations: Typical profiles do not represent the population mean.
Ignoring BSV in mean predictions leads to underestimation of exposure range.
Parameter uncertainty is distinct from biological variability; conflating them misrepresents risk.
downstream_use: Select the appropriate simulation type based on the specific question (e.g., typical profile for mechanism, BSV for dose range, uncertainty for confidence intervals).
retrieval_keywords: Typical exposure versus between-person variability versus parameter uncertainty

title: Distinguishing Uncertainty from Variability and Handling Correlations
claim: Uncertainty represents limited knowledge of the system and decreases with information accumulation, whereas variability is a property of the system (e.g., genetic/environmental) that does not decrease with sample size. Simulations accounting for BSV must include correlations between random effects to avoid unrealistic parameter combinations. Independence assumptions for unknown correlations are not established truth and must be explicitly assessed.
conditions: Applicable when propagating uncertainty into dose predictions or simulating population ranges.
Correlations between random effects must be accounted for in BSV simulations.
Uncertainty in scaling methodology is distinct from population variability of a parameter.
required_inputs: Covariance matrix of random effects (to preserve correlations).
Explicit assumption statement if correlations are unknown (e.g., independence assumption).
Source-specific guidance on how to handle unknown correlations (project-local draft policy required).
limitations: Defaulting to independence for unknown correlations is an assumption, not a fact.
Misinterpreting uncertainty distributions as population variability leads to incorrect risk assessment.
PD uncertainty is often more project-specific and harder to generalize than PK uncertainty.
downstream_use: Construct simulation inputs that preserve random effect correlations. Explicitly document any independence assumptions. Use Monte Carlo simulations to integrate all uncertainty sources for dose prediction distributions.
retrieval_keywords: Typical exposure versus between-person variability versus parameter uncertainty

title: Context-Dependent PBPK Reporting and Sensitivity Standards
claim: FDA and EMA guidance documents provide nonbinding recommendations for PBPK report content, including sensitivity analysis and parameter justification. These standards apply specifically to PBPK analyses intended to support regulatory decisions or replace clinical data; they are not mandatory for all simple IV simulations or non-regulatory prospective scenarios. The '10-fold' (CYP) and '30-fold' (transporter) sensitivity ranges cited in EMA guidance are illustrative examples of 'worst-case' approaches, not universal project thresholds.
conditions: Applicable when the simulation is a PBPK analysis intended for regulatory submission or high-impact decision support.
Not applicable to simple compartmental IV simulations where no absorption or mechanistic enzyme/transporter modeling is performed.
Source status is EXTERNAL_SOURCE_NOT_PROJECT_POLICY; these are guidelines, not binding project rules.
required_inputs: Explicit definition of the simulation's intended use (regulatory vs. exploratory).
Identification of the model type (PBPK vs. simple compartmental).
Source-specific justification for any sensitivity ranges used (e.g., literature variability vs. worst-case assumption).
limitations: Guidance documents do not validate specific models or specify project-specific dose levels.
Illustrative fold-change ranges cannot be applied universally to all parameters or all simulation types.
Abstract-only or partial excerpts do not constitute full methodological validation.
downstream_use: Determine whether full PBPK reporting standards (e.g., platform qualification, detailed parameter sourcing) are required for the current simulation task. If the simulation is not PBPK-based or not for regulatory submission, simplified reporting may be acceptable per project draft policy.
retrieval_keywords: Sensitivity analyses and evidence-supported regimen/formulation feasibility

title: Route-Conditional Feasibility and Assumption Labeling
claim: Feasibility of regimen and formulation parameters is route- and model-conditional. The relevance of fed/fasted state, particle size and other formulation inputs depends on the specific formulation, model structure and intended use. Scenarios should explicitly label assumptions, their basis and uncertainty; unsupported assumptions must not be treated as established facts. Sensitivity analysis should address uncertain parameters relevant to the selected model structure.
conditions: IV simulations: Focus sensitivity on CL, Vss/Vc, and infusion duration; exclude absorption parameters.
Oral simulations: Include GI pH, particle size, and absorption rate in sensitivity analysis if modeled.
All simulations: Must distinguish between measured inputs and assumed/prospective inputs.
required_inputs: Route of administration (IV vs. Oral).
Explicit list of assumed parameters (e.g., F, Ka, particle size) with provenance marked as 'assumed' or 'literature-derived'.
Output time grid and dose basis (mg/kg vs. absolute dose).
limitations: A unique multi-compartment curve cannot be derived from CL and Vss alone without additional distribution parameters.
Human variability and clinical validation data are not established for the target drug; simulations are prospective scenarios.
Technical replicates do not increase biological n; group means are not individual trajectories.
downstream_use: Generate a sensitivity analysis plan that perturbs only the parameters relevant to the specific route and model structure. Label all outputs as 'prospective scenario' and flag any parameter lacking experimental or high-quality literature support as an assumption.
retrieval_keywords: Sensitivity analyses and evidence-supported regimen/formulation feasibility

title: Distinction between PTA simulations and clinical efficacy evidence
claim: Probability of Target Attainment (PTA) estimates attainment of a specified PK-PD target under a stated regimen and population or scenario distribution; it is not a direct measure of clinical efficacy or microbiological cure. MIC-normalized targets require a specified MIC value or grid for per-MIC PTA; weighting across MIC values additionally requires a relevant MIC frequency distribution. Clinical exposure-response evidence can inform efficacy but does not alone establish causal clinical efficacy, and such analyses may be infeasible or confounded.
conditions: Applicable when evaluating the evidentiary weight of simulated exposure metrics.
Relevant when distinguishing between nonclinical PK-PD targets and clinical outcomes.
Applies to antimicrobial agents where PTA is used to justify dose selection prior to pivotal efficacy trials.
required_inputs: Nonclinical PK-PD targets (PDTs) derived from in vitro/in vivo models.
Population PK models (initially from healthy volunteers, later from patients).
MIC distributions for relevant pathogens.
Clinical E-R data (if available) to validate or refine nonclinical targets.
limitations: PTA does not account for host factors, adherence, or complex disease states unless explicitly modeled.
Clinical E-R analyses may be impossible if patient numbers are low, success rates are high (lack of failures), or outcomes are confounded by combination therapy.
Simulations cannot replace clinical data for establishing safety or efficacy claims; they only support the rationale for dose selection.
downstream_use: Use PTA to justify dose selection in regulatory submissions, but explicitly state that it is a predictive tool, not proof of clinical cure. Do not interpret high PTA as guaranteed clinical success.
retrieval_keywords: Why prospective exposure or target attainment cannot establish human efficacy or safety

title: Uncertainty vs. Variability in prospective human predictions
claim: Prospective human dose/exposure predictions are characterized by uncertainty (limited knowledge of the system, e.g., scaling errors) rather than just biological variability (system property). Uncertainty in PK parameters (CL, Vss) and PD targets propagates into dose prediction uncertainty, which must be quantified to assess feasibility and safety margins.
conditions: Applicable to all prospective human simulations where no human PK data exists.
Relevant when communicating confidence intervals for predicted exposures to decision-makers.
Applies when distinguishing between inter-individual variability (which persists) and parameter uncertainty (which decreases with data).
required_inputs: Predicted PK parameters (CL, Vss, F) with associated uncertainty distributions (e.g., log-normal).
PD targets (MEC) with uncertainty ranges.
Model structure assumptions (e.g., one- vs. multi-compartment).
Sensitivity analysis results showing impact of parameter uncertainty on dose/exposure.
limitations: Predictions are sensitive to model structure choice; a unique curve cannot be derived from CL and Vss alone without distribution parameters.
Uncertainty in PD parameters often dominates early-stage predictions if biomarkers are not accessible in preclinical species.
Simulated safety margins are prospective estimates, not observed safety data.
downstream_use: Use uncertainty quantification to define the range of plausible human exposures and inform early clinical trial design (e.g., starting dose, safety monitoring). Do not treat point estimates as definitive human values.
retrieval_keywords: Why prospective exposure or target attainment cannot establish human efficacy or safety

title: CFR Calculation Methodology and Denominator Specificity
claim: CFR = sum_i PTA_i * p_i, with PTA_i and p_i both expressed as fractions and p_i = n_i/N for the defined isolate population and time period. The denominator must match the scenario (e.g., all isolates versus a specified species) and time interval used to assess resistance trends. Sum_i p_i = 1 only when the bins exhaust that population and every bin has a matched PTA; otherwise report uncovered or off-scale mass and withhold a complete CFR or provide explicit bounds. A 90% CFR was a study-specific empiric-therapy convention, not a universal regulatory threshold.
conditions: Applicable when Monte Carlo simulation is used to predict microbiological performance.
Requires specific MIC frequency distributions for the target organism population and time period.
PTA must be derived from PK/PD models using appropriate indices (e.g., %fT>MIC for beta-lactams).
required_inputs: Monte Carlo simulation output: PTA values for each MIC dilution.
MIC frequency distribution: Percentage of isolates at each MIC dilution for the specific organism and time period.
Qualified exposure model parameters and a PD target with explicit index, exposure basis and time window; no universal target magnitude is supplied.
limitations: CFR represents microbiological success (target attainment), not clinical cure or safety.
Aggregated reference MIC distributions (e.g., EUCAST) cannot be used as weights for specific clinical populations as they do not represent local resistance rates.
Truncated MIC distributions (lower/upper end) in reference databases are excluded from aggregation, limiting their use for specific scenario weighting if the local distribution differs.
Source-specific thresholds (e.g., 90% CFR) are not universal project policy.
downstream_use: Use CFR to assess trends in microbiological activity over time for specific regimens. Do not use CFR to predict clinical outcomes directly without further clinical correlation. Ensure the MIC distribution used for weighting matches the specific clinical scenario and time period being analyzed.
retrieval_keywords: CFR and weighted attainment: MIC weights, population and denominator

title: MIC Distribution Provenance and Aggregation Constraints
claim: Reference MIC distributions (e.g., EUCAST) are aggregated from diverse sources (human, animal, environmental) and methods (ISO broth microdilution, etc.) to define wild-type distributions and ECOFFs. These aggregated distributions are explicitly stated to NOT represent rates of resistance for any specific agent or location. They are used for ECOFF setting and method calibration, not as representative weights for CFR calculations in specific clinical scenarios.
conditions: Applicable when evaluating the suitability of reference MIC data for weighting PTA.
Requires verification that the source data meets acceptance criteria (e.g., no lower-end truncation, adequate range around mode).
required_inputs: Source metadata for MIC distributions: Method (e.g., ISO 20776-1), source of isolates, year of study.
Acceptance status: 'Approved' or 'Rejected' (e.g., rejected for truncation, few data points, or aberrant mode).
limitations: Aggregated distributions mask local resistance trends and cannot be used to compare resistance rates among agents or over time.
Distributions dominated by outbreak isolates or with uncertain species identification are rejected.
Using aggregated reference data as weights for CFR assumes the local population matches the global aggregate, which is often invalid for specific clinical decision-making.
Abstract-only or partial excerpts cannot validate the full distribution quality.
downstream_use: Use reference distributions to define ECOFFs or calibrate methods. Do not use them as default weights for CFR. If used for hypothetical weighting, the resulting CFR is not a local prediction.
retrieval_keywords: CFR and weighted attainment: MIC weights, population and denominator

title: Conceptual Distinction: Uncertainty vs. Variability
claim: Uncertainty represents limited knowledge of the system and decreases as information accumulates, whereas variability is an inherent property of the system (e.g., genetic or environmental differences) that does not decrease with larger sample sizes. In PK/PD modeling, parameter uncertainty affects the precision of the typical profile estimate, while between-subject variability (BSV) describes the distribution of individual parameters around that typical value.
conditions: Applicable when defining simulation inputs for PTA.
Requires explicit separation of fixed-effect parameter uncertainty from random-effect variability in model specification.
required_inputs: Provenance: External methodological definitions (SUP011, REF_022).
Basis: Distinction between 'limited knowledge' (uncertainty) and 'system property' (variability).
Prerequisite: Clear definition of the 'typical' individual vs. the population distribution.
limitations: Confusing uncertainty with variability leads to incorrect simulation distributions (e.g., treating a wide confidence interval for CL as if it were BSV).
Source-specific examples (e.g., clearance scaling) are illustrative, not target-drug specific.
downstream_use: Guides the correct assignment of input distributions in Monte Carlo simulations: uncertainty distributions for fixed effects vs. variance/covariance matrices for random effects.
retrieval_keywords: Separate target uncertainty, parameter uncertainty and between-unit variability

title: Operationalizing Uncertainty and Variability in PTA Simulations
claim: Simulations can be based on fixed-effect estimates (typical profile), uncertainty of fixed-effect estimates (probability typical subject meets target), or between-subject variability (range of individual predictions). For PTA, one must distinguish between the probability that a *typical* profile meets a target (driven by parameter uncertainty) and the fraction of a *population* meeting a target (driven by BSV).
conditions: Applicable when constructing PTA curves or CFR estimates.
Requires explicit decision on whether to propagate fixed-effect uncertainty into the PTA calculation or treat fixed effects as point estimates.
required_inputs: Provenance: FDA guidance on simulation types (REF_022).
Input: Fixed-effect parameter estimates and their uncertainty (e.g., standard errors, bootstrap distributions).
Input: Between-subject variability estimates (variance/covariance of random effects).
Gate: Must not assume human IIV from animal data without explicit assumption documentation.
limitations: Human IIV cannot be derived from animal IIV or parameter standard errors without independent human observations.
Residual error must be distinguished from BSV when evaluating observed concentration ranges.
downstream_use: Defines the simulation architecture: whether to sample from fixed-effect uncertainty distributions, random-effect distributions, or both, and how to report the resulting PTA/CFR metrics.
retrieval_keywords: Separate target uncertainty, parameter uncertainty and between-unit variability

title: MIC Distribution Aggregation and ECOFF Definition
claim: ECOFFs are epidemiological cut-off values defining the upper end of the wild-type MIC distribution, distinct from clinical breakpoints. Aggregated MIC distributions in the EUCAST database are derived from multiple sources and methods (primarily ISO 20776-1 broth microdilution), incorporating inter-laboratory and temporal variability. These distributions are not representative of resistance rates and cannot be used to infer epidemiological trends over time or geography. ECOFF setting requires at least five valid distributions from separate laboratories, with specific criteria for mode agreement and range coverage.
conditions: Applicable when interpreting MIC data for PTA where the target is defined by wild-type distribution boundaries rather than clinical breakpoints.
Requires that the specific agent-organism combination has a published ECOFF or TECOFF in the EUCAST database.
Methodological variability is accepted if calibrated to reference methods; results rarely vary by more than one doubling dilution step.
required_inputs: Provenance: EUCAST SOP 10.2 compliant data.
Identity: Specific organism and antimicrobial agent pair.
Basis: MIC values in mg/L or µg/mL.
Prerequisite: Confirmation that the data source is calibrated to ISO 20776-1 or equivalent reference methods.
limitations: ECOFFs are not clinical breakpoints and do not indicate therapeutic success or failure.
Aggregated distributions cannot be used to calculate resistance rates or compare resistance across agents/geographies.
Source-specific sample size thresholds (e.g., 15 isolates per distribution, 100 total) are specific to EUCAST ECOFF setting rules, not universal PTA eligibility criteria.
downstream_use: Use ECOFFs to define the wild-type/non-wild-type boundary for PTA calculations if the project policy adopts epidemiological cutoffs as the target. Do not use these distributions to estimate population resistance prevalence.
retrieval_keywords: MIC assay comparability, dilution bins and tails, and target transport applicability

title: MIC Reading Protocols: Trailing Endpoints and Skipped Wells
claim: For the standard endpoint, MIC is the lowest concentration with complete visible growth inhibition unless a qualified agent-organism protocol defines an exception. Trailing growth and skipped wells are distinct patterns; follow the applicable protocol and validity checks rather than inventing a generic percentage-inhibition threshold.
conditions: Conditional broth microdilution interpretation under a declared, applicable reading protocol.
Positive growth control, culture purity and inoculum validity must satisfy that protocol.
required_inputs: Assay protocol/version and applicability to the compound class and organism.
Well-level growth pattern, tested dilution series, medium and incubation conditions.
Growth controls, culture purity and relevant quality-control results.
limitations: Compound-specific medium and endpoint exceptions are excluded from this general card; obtain an applicable assay protocol before interpreting such cases.
Ambiguous growth patterns may require retesting or visual consultation of the source guide.
Do not substitute a partial-inhibition threshold for complete inhibition without protocol support.
downstream_use: Identify whether MIC is interpretable under the declared standard method and flag cases needing a specialized protocol.
retrieval_keywords: MIC assay comparability, dilution bins and tails, and target transport applicability

title: Prefit Individual Concentration-Time Plotting and Event Alignment
claim: Prefit visual examination of concentration-time data requires strict separation of observed records from model-derived values, explicit handling of censoring/missingness as categorical states, and connection of points only within verified serial observation subjects and compatible time references.
conditions: Applies to prefit EDA of concentration-time data.
This card addresses prefit observed-data displays and does not substitute for post-fit diagnostics. Properly labelled exploratory figures can appear in final reports with provenance and limitations.
Assumes source data contains identifiable records, even if some IDs are unresolved.
required_inputs: Conditional input mapping: numeric values only for quantified records; optional summaries/errors only when shown; assay-specific or branch-specific fields only when applicable. Missing fields limit dependent operations, not all displays.
Record/source locator
Study ID
Design
Observation ID
Experimental-unit ID (nullable)
Specimen/pool ID
Technical-repeat ID
Regimen and dose occasion
Route/formulation
Analyte
Matrix
Free/total basis
Time value/unit/origin
Measured value/unit
Quantification status
Nullable serial_observation_subject_id, distinct from experimental_unit_id (e.g. an animal within its randomized cage); required for individual serial lines or paired loops.
limitations: Missingness mechanism is unknown from the plot; visual patterns neither select covariates nor qualify model feasibility.
A semilog visual slope is not a terminal elimination estimate or evidence for a compartment structure.
Unknown serial-subject IDs block individual connections; unknown experimental-unit IDs block independent-unit n/uncertainty, not verified observed subject series.
Unknown limits block numeric boundary placement, not status display.
Unknown time origin permits a source timestamp only if documented; otherwise use a record table.
Missing validation documentation means qualification unestablished, not automatically invalid.
downstream_use: Visual patterns revealed by these plots inform subsequent model development and covariate investigation but do not themselves select covariates or declare model feasibility.

plot_recipe.input_contract: Preserve record/source locator, study, design, observation ID, experimental-unit ID (nullable), specimen/pool ID, technical-repeat ID, regimen and dose occasion, route/formulation, analyte, matrix, free/total basis, time value/unit/origin, measured value/unit and quantification status. Map only available applicable fields; never invent missing identities. Preserve nullable serial_observation_subject_id separately from experimental_unit_id, with its source linkage. Numeric measured value is required only for quantified records; censoring/missing statuses may have a null numeric value. Optional summary/error inputs are needed only when that layer is displayed.
plot_recipe.plot_type: Individual concentration-time scatter with optional verified serial lines; linear and positive-only log-y companion panels.
plot_recipe.axes_and_units: X = actual elapsed time from a documented reference event, in stated units; Y = measured concentration on its stated analyte/matrix/free-total basis and unit. Time since last dose requires verified dose history and dose occasion; retain global documented time for traceability. Positive-only log-y is optional; measured zero remains on the linear panel.

title: Response-Time Plotting and Baseline Reference Integrity
claim: Response-time plots must preserve record-level integrity, distinguishing individual paired baselines from group-level contrasts and concurrent controls. Display conventions must separate observed points from summaries and handle missing/censored data without substitution.
conditions: Applicable to general PK/PD EDA where response is plotted against time.
Requires documented time origin (e.g., dose or treatment start) and explicit response units.
Individual change calculations require verified individual pairing; group-level contrasts require complete compatible inputs.
BLQ and above-range values must be handled as categorical statuses, not numeric substitutions.
required_inputs: Conditional input mapping: numeric values only for quantified records; optional summaries/errors only when shown; assay-specific or branch-specific fields only when applicable. Missing fields limit dependent operations, not all displays.
Record/source locator, study, design, observation ID.
Experimental-unit ID (nullable), specimen/pool ID, technical-repeat ID.
Regimen, dose occasion, route/formulation, analyte, matrix, free/total basis.
Time value, unit, and origin; measured value, unit, and quantification status.
Documented baseline or reference definitions for change calculations.
Nullable serial_observation_subject_id, distinct from experimental_unit_id (e.g. an animal within its randomized cage); required for individual serial lines or paired loops.
limitations: Response-time shape alone is descriptive and does not identify mechanism (e.g., turnover, effect-site delay) or clinical efficacy.
Unknown serial-subject IDs block individual connections; unknown experimental-unit IDs block independent-unit n/uncertainty, not otherwise verified observed subject series.
Unknown limits block numeric boundary placement but not status display.
This is an engineering display contract, not a regulator-mandated layout or scientific law.
downstream_use: Guides the construction of EDA figures for response-time data, ensuring that visual representations accurately reflect data structure, unit integrity, and quantification limits without implying unsupported mechanistic or statistical conclusions.

plot_recipe.input_contract: Preserve record/source locator, study, design, observation ID, experimental-unit ID (nullable), specimen/pool ID, technical-repeat ID, regimen and dose occasion, route/formulation, analyte, matrix, free/total basis, time value/unit/origin, measured value/unit and quantification status. Map only available applicable fields; never invent missing identities. Preserve nullable serial_observation_subject_id separately from experimental_unit_id, with its source linkage. Numeric measured value is required only for quantified records; censoring/missing statuses may have a null numeric value. Optional summary/error inputs are needed only when that layer is displayed.
plot_recipe.plot_type: Observed response versus documented time, with serial-unit lines only when verified; cross-sectional/destructive points otherwise.
plot_recipe.axes_and_units: X = time with explicit origin (e.g. dose or treatment start); Y = the exact response and unit, or explicitly defined change from a named reference. Show treatment start/stop and relevant events if known. Separate endpoints, assays, matrices and reference definitions.
plot_recipe.grouping_and_connections: Separate study, regimen/dose occasion, route/formulation, analyte/matrix/basis and endpoint contexts. Connect only verified serial observations of the same unit in a compatible time reference, ordered by time. Break connections at recorded unresolved missing/censored statuses. No invented scheduled samples or cross-unit lines. Serial-observation subject ID is distinct from experimental-unit ID: a cage/litter may contain several animals. Individual trajectories or paired loops require the same verified serial_observation_subject_id within study and compatible regimen/time/assay context. A shared cage/litter ID alone never authorizes connecting animals. Unknown serial identity blocks individual lines/pairs, not record-level displays; unknown experimental-unit identity blocks independent-unit n/uncertainty, not an otherwise verified observed subject series.
plot_recipe.point_and_summary_layers: Preserve observed values as points at their actual record level. Keep raw observations separate from optional source-reported or explicitly defined descriptive summaries. A labelled group-summary guide is not an individual trajectory. Do not reconstruct individuals from a mean and SD.
plot_recipe.censoring_and_missingness: The plotted variable is response Y, with its actual endpoint, unit and reference. For a confirmed quantifiable-range censor, use Y<its applicable lower limit or Y>its applicable upper limit only when that assay meaning is established. Microbial count detection/quantification limits, bioanalytical limits and response-scale bounds are distinct. Keep unavailable-after-death, missing, not sampled and technical failure separate from censoring; never invent a zero or apply a concentration LLOQ to response Y.
plot_recipe.transformations_and_formula: Individual change = individual endpoint minus that individual's documented baseline, only with verified pairing. An established group endpoint minus group treatment-start reference is allowed with complete compatible inputs but must be labelled group-level. Log transforms require valid positive quantified inputs and a stated reference-unit definition.

title: Exposure-Response Scatterplot and Time-Order Display Conventions
claim: Exposure-response scatter and a time-ordered paired concentration-response loop are distinct displays. A loop requires verified time-matched pairs from the same serial observation subject and compatible context; shared experimental-unit or group identity is insufficient. A loop can suggest time dependence, but its appearance alone identifies neither a specific mechanism nor a model.
conditions: An individual loop requires verified within-subject concentration-response pairing and order.
A separately documented shared regimen exposure may support labelled regimen-assigned scatter without individual PK pairing; never fabricate nearest-time joins.
The display is exploratory, not a model fit or causal identification.
required_inputs: Scatter branch: a supplied qualified exposure metric (e.g. concentration, AUC or Cmax) with source, unit, concentration basis and exposure window, and a measured response with endpoint, unit, reference and response time/window.

Documented individual linkage or explicit shared regimen/group exposure assignment; preserve observation-level IDs and nesting. Unknown independent-unit n stays unknown rather than blocking otherwise qualified record-level scatter.

Loop branch only: time-matched concentration and response with verified serial_observation_subject_id, study/regimen/assay context, measurement timestamps and documented pairing/time-alignment method; no invented nearest-time joins.

Preserve X and Y quantification/censoring/missingness statuses, units and applicable bounds separately. Numeric values are required only for quantitative points; unmatched and censored records stay visible in a companion status/count table.
Optional exposure uncertainty or response summary/error inputs only when supplied or explicitly qualified, with their statistic, scale, unit level and source.
limitations: A visible loop does not prove a specific PK/PD model structure.
Absence of a loop does not prove a direct effect.
Unpaired data cannot be forced into a loop display.
This is an engineering display contract, not a regulatory mandate.

plot_recipe.plot_type: Exposure-response scatter; a time-ordered concentration-response loop only when time-matched within-unit observations are verified. Optional concentration-time and response-time companion panels are separate.
plot_recipe.axes_and_units: X = supplied qualified exposure metric with basis/unit/window; Y = measured response with endpoint/unit/reference/time. For a hysteresis display specifically X = time-matched concentration and Y = response, with arrows or colour indicating verified observation order. A time-X dual-Y display is not the hysteresis loop.
plot_recipe.grouping_and_connections: Require documented linkage within study, individual/regimen, endpoint and compatible assay/time context. Never create closest-row or nearest-time pairs. A supplied shared regimen exposure can be plotted against individual responses only when assignment is known and labelled shared; it is not independent individual PK. For a loop connect only verified ordered pairs, with recorded gaps explicit. Serial-observation subject ID is distinct from experimental-unit ID: a cage/litter may contain several animals. Individual trajectories or paired loops require the same verified serial_observation_subject_id within study and compatible regimen/time/assay context. A shared cage/litter ID alone never authorizes connecting animals. Keep raw observations separate from optional source-reported or explicitly defined descriptive summaries. A labelled group-summary guide is not an individual trajectory. Do not reconstruct individuals from a mean and SD.
plot_recipe.censoring_and_missingness: Preserve X exposure and Y response statuses separately with their units, windows and documented bounds. A censored concentration has its own assay bound; it does not automatically define a bound for derived AUC or another exposure metric. Do not turn a censored X or Y into an exact paired loop point. Display documented inequalities or separate status records, retain unmatched-pair counts/reasons, and do not silently infer a pair from nearest timestamps.

If supplied and compatible, horizontal intervals describe exposure uncertainty and vertical intervals describe the stated response statistic; response spread is not exposure-estimation uncertainty. No invented or universally banned uncertainty bars.

Individual trajectories or paired loops require the same verified serial_observation_subject_id within study and compatible regimen/time/assay context. A shared cage/litter ID alone never authorizes connecting animals. title: Binding Assay and Depletion-Time Exploratory Plots
claim: Binding and depletion data require separate conditional display contracts. Binding plots require explicit concentration stage and fraction definitions; depletion plots require incubation time and measured concentration or established remaining fraction. Display choices are engineering conventions, not scientific mandates.
conditions: Binding and depletion branches are independent; one may be shown without the other.
Unknown metadata is labeled unknown, not silently filled.
Technical repeats are nested and do not increase independent experimental-run or other documented design-unit n.
required_inputs: Conditional input mapping: numeric values only for quantified records; optional summaries/errors only when shown; assay-specific or branch-specific fields only when applicable. Missing fields limit dependent operations, not all displays.
Binding: Concentration (nominal-added vs. measured stage), bound/unbound fraction or percent, species/matrix/assay conditions, sample/run identities.
Depletion: Incubation time, measured parent concentration or established remaining fraction, documented reference relation, assay-series/run/replicate identities.
Assay-specific analytical_series_id, experimental-run ID and specimen/aliquot/technical-repeat linkage; no animal-subject identity required unless that assay design actually uses it.
limitations: Plasma/serum binding data does not automatically supply incubation binding context.
The display itself does not fit depletion slopes or estimate CLint; this is a downstream qualified method.
Unknown assay validation documentation means qualification is unestablished, not that plotting is prohibited.
No source drug values transfer to the current target.
downstream_use: Visual inspection of documented binding measurements or depletion time courses, with assay context and uncertainty; subsequent estimation requires a separate qualified method.

plot_recipe.input_contract: Choose independent branches, never require both: binding needs concentration with nominal-added versus measured stage, named bound/unbound fraction or percent, species/matrix/assay conditions and sample/run identities. Depletion needs incubation time, measured parent concentration or established remaining fraction, documented reference relation and assay-series/run/replicate identities. Preserve independent experimental-run ID separately from analytical series, specimen/aliquot and technical-repeat IDs. Numeric measured values are required only for quantified records; status-only records can have null numeric value. Optional summaries/errors need their own defined inputs.
plot_recipe.plot_type: Separate conditional binding scatter and depletion-time plot; either may be shown independently.
plot_recipe.axes_and_units: Binding: X = clearly defined assay concentration and unit, Y = explicitly bound or unbound fraction (0-1) or percent (0-100), without silently rescaling out-of-range observations. Depletion: X = incubation time/unit; Y = measured parent concentration/unit or established percent remaining. Label assay/species/matrix and known conditions.
plot_recipe.grouping_and_connections: Separate assay series, experimental run, species/matrix, binding method and reference definitions. Use verified analytical_series_id and specimen/aliquot linkage, not an animal-subject ID by default. A same-series depletion guide may link documented successive observations; destructive aliquots must be labelled as a series/group guide, not a repeated specimen trajectory. Technical repeats are nested and do not create independent experimental runs.
plot_recipe.point_and_summary_layers: Preserve observed values as points at their actual record level. Keep raw observations separate from optional source-reported or explicitly defined descriptive summaries. A labelled group-summary guide is not an individual trajectory. Do not reconstruct individuals from a mean and SD.
plot_recipe.censoring_and_missingness: Binding: preserve bound versus unbound fraction/percent, the actual concentration-stage definition and assay-specific qualification/status; an out-of-range fraction is flagged, not clipped or relabelled concentration BLQ. Depletion: retain measured parent concentration status and its actual assay limits. A bound on C_t can be converted to a percent bound only with a documented positive compatible C_ref and inequality propagation. Missing reference blocks normalization only; no zero/half-limit substitution or silent deletion. A censored or uncertain reference is not an exact denominator: retain its status/interval and use normalization only with a qualified uncertainty/interval propagation method. Positivity alone does not qualify a reference as exact.
plot_recipe.transformations_and_formula: Bound and unbound fractions are distinct assay-defined quantities, not interchangeable labels. Only with established numerator/denominator definitions convert fraction to percent by multiplying by 100. For a documented compatible reference qualified for quantitative normalization, percent remaining = 100*C_t/C_ref. Direct pointwise division requires a qualified positive quantified reference, with no unhandled uncertainty or censoring; an uncertain/censored reference requires a qualified uncertainty/interval propagation method instead of silently treating it as exact. C_ref need not be a newly invented t=0 measurement. Retain reference linkage, assay recovery/mass-balance qualifications and raw values.
plot_recipe.uncertainty_and_n: Label displayed record counts separately from known independent experimental-unit n. Preserve supplied statistic, calculation scale and exact SD, SE or CI meaning, including asymmetric interval endpoints. Technical repeats do not increase independent experimental-run or other documented design-unit n; cell-free assays do not require an animal/biological n label. Unknown n or variability stays unknown; no automatic CI or zero-width bar.
plot_recipe.interpretation_limits: Plasma/serum binding does not automatically supply incubation binding. The display does not itself fit a depletion slope or estimate CLint; a separate qualified downstream method may do so. No source drug values transfer to the current target.
plot_recipe.stop_or_fallback: Unknown or nonpositive C_ref blocks percent normalization only: show qualified raw concentration versus incubation time. Unknown assay validation documentation means qualification unestablished, not automatic plotting prohibition. A separately valid binding branch remains available. Unresolved series/run linkage blocks connections or independent-run summaries only, not labelled observed assay records. If reference uncertainty/censoring has no qualified propagation method, retain raw concentration and reference status, omit the dependent normalized value/bound, and state why.
plot_recipe.implementation_conventions: This recipe is an explicitly reviewed engineering display contract, not a regulator-mandated layout or scientific law. Use readable legends, separate aligned panels and visible status/count annotations. No universal numeric completeness threshold. No change to source data or current project Rules.
